days.challenge: Compare an extended favorable metaphor with a comic correction.
days.focus: Good intentions do not erase hurtful behavior.
days.context: Dorry thinks Uncle George’s recent sharpness means he no longer loves her. The narrator pauses to describe the household and Donald’s attempt to understand.
days.contentNote: Donald repeats dated stereotypes about girls. His affection and the narrator’s examples of both children’s abilities need not support those generalizations.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Which Partly Explains Itself; begins “DOROTHY REED was of a somewhat livelier temperament than Donald, and that, as she often could not bu”; ends “oo, with the precious D's wild as young hawks, and Mr. G. as he is of late, and the way things are."”.

questions.prompt: What do the children’s different strengths suggest about their friendship?
facilitatorNotes: Each excels in different subjects, yet each admires the other. Don’s generalizations about girls belong to his limited viewpoint.
evidence: never were brother and sister better friends.

questions.prompt: How do the king and silver-owl comparisons show different sides of Uncle George?
facilitatorNotes: The king image conveys self-command and dignity; the pepper-filled owl conveys irritability when upset. Explain both halves of the comparison.
evidence: very peppery within

questions.prompt: Does Donald finally dismiss Dorry’s concern as a foolish notion?
facilitatorNotes: No. He begins reluctant to blame Uncle, then admits his treatment of her has not been consistently kind. His judgment changes as he reflects.
evidence: secretly sharing it

days.title: Donald and Dorothy: asking Liddy for a story (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track the difference between a requested story and the information a speaker can actually know.
days.focus: Family memory mixes affection, uncertainty, and play.
days.context: The children visit Lydia, called Liddy, who has known the family for years. They hope a familiar storyteller will tell them something new.
days.contentNote: Liddy recalls deceased relatives with affection. The passage also preserves her spoken dialect.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Which Partly Explains Itself; begins “Lydia looked up when Donald and Dorothy entered, with a "Sakes! You've not been fretting again, Miss”; ends “d his growl grew more decided.) "Well, as I was saying--Mercy on us! If there isn't that man again!"”.

questions.prompt: Why do the children reject Liddy’s usual starting point of fourteen years ago?
facilitatorNotes: They already know that part; they want earlier memories and information not previously shared.
evidence: farther back than you ever told us before.

questions.prompt: What do the small benches reveal about the children and this familiar routine?
facilitatorNotes: The seats suited them when younger but are now too small; choosing them recreates an old closeness with Liddy.
evidence: in the days gone by, when the benches had been of exactly the right size

questions.prompt: Why is Liddy cautious about comparing Donald to his mother’s portrait?
facilitatorNotes: She sees a resemblance to the picture but did not meet his mother, so cannot verify the picture’s likeness. That is a useful limit on her evidence.
evidence: I can't say from my own knowledge

days.title: Donald and Dorothy: a change of plans (excerpt)
days.challenge: Infer a feeling that differs from the words a character says aloud.
days.focus: Comfort can be offered through a small sacrifice.
days.context: A man glimpsed at the window has interrupted Liddy’s family story. Donald follows him outside while Dorry still hopes to hear more.
days.contentNote: Dorry grieves parents she cannot remember; the scene moves toward family comfort.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Which Partly Explains Itself; begins “The last part of Lydia's sentence, almost drowned by Nero's barking, was addressed to the empty wind”; ends “"Ay, ay, Capt'n," said Jack, and they were off.”.

questions.prompt: How does Liddy try to move attention away from the man at the window?
facilitatorNotes: She calls him no one in particular and resumes the story. Her assumed carelessness suggests an effort to hide concern.
evidence: with assumed carelessness

questions.prompt: Why does Dorry say “Oh, do!” when Donald offers to leave his pony behind?
facilitatorNotes: She wants him beside her but dislikes depriving him of pleasure. The narrator explicitly reveals that her spoken encouragement conceals another wish.
evidence: in her heart she meant, "Oh, don't!"

questions.prompt: What changes Dorry’s mood by the end even though the mystery remains?
facilitatorNotes: Donald’s companionship, Uncle’s kindness, an invitation for Josie, and the bright outing comfort her. The underlying questions are not answered.
evidence: Her troubles were forgotten

days.title: Donald and Dorothy: one carriage, many thoughts (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track shifts among the narrator’s accounts of several minds.
days.focus: A peaceful appearance can hide conflicting feelings.
days.context: Josie is away, so the family takes its carriage drive without her. Dorry’s uncertainty about her uncle remains beneath the pleasant outing.
days.contentNote: Jack unfairly strikes a horse while angry, and the narrator explicitly says it was undeserved. This is part of the scene’s criticism of displaced anger.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, The Drive; begins “JOSIE MANNING was not at home, when the carriage stopped at her door; and so the party decided to dr”; ends “ear air, the changing roadside, and the glories of the western sky, now ablaze with the setting sun.”.

questions.prompt: Why include the horses and small insects before describing the people’s thoughts?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator playfully widens the scene: many different lives and purposes occupy the same quiet-looking ride.
evidence: how many interests were represented, and how different they were!

questions.prompt: How do Jack’s words show that he still thinks like a sailor?
facilitatorNotes: He calls reins tiller-ropes and the carriage a craft; his familiar sea language recasts a road journey.
evidence: guide the craft as trim

questions.prompt: What does Uncle privately acknowledge after telling Dorry to control herself?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes that his own uneven behavior upset her and resolves to change it. The private reflection complicates the outward instruction.
evidence: I must be more watchful after this

days.title: The Insect Folk — Our Pretty Dragon Flies: Wings and Hands
days.challenge: Hear a teacher’s questions change from an observation to an imagined choice.
days.focus: Admiration that recognizes the different uses of wings and hands.
days.context: The children are watching dragonflies near a pond. Read the questions aloud, pause to imagine each answer, then reread the comparison of flight and human work.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — Our Pretty Dragon Flies: Wings and Hands; source transcription lines 361–391; opens “We all like your pretty wings, little dragon fly; they look like glass and they shine so in the sun.”; closes “They have four wings, all nearly the same size and shape, you see, and they are all stiff and shining.”.

questions.prompt: What explanation does Mollie give for the zigzag flight?
facilitatorNotes: The dragonfly changes direction to pursue insects it sees to one side. The zigzag therefore has a purpose rather than being random decoration.
evidence: it goes zigzagging along after insects.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator interrupt the praise of wings with a question about hands?
facilitatorNotes: The imagined exchange shows that gaining flight would mean losing other abilities. Writing and whittling supply concrete examples of the trade-off.
evidence: We could not whittle a stick nor write a letter

questions.prompt: Does preferring hands make the narrator admire the dragonfly less?
facilitatorNotes: No: the narrator remains glad the insect has swift wings. The passage can value different abilities without choosing one body as best for every task.
evidence: We are glad, too, that the dragon flies have their pretty, swift wings.

days.title: The Insect Folk — Our Pretty Dragon Flies: A Skin Like an Overcoat
days.challenge: Distinguish a helpful clothing comparison from the actual sequence of a moult.
days.focus: Growth explained by anticipating and correcting a reader’s misunderstanding.
days.context: A larva is the young dragonfly living in the pond. Read once for the repeated growth and shedding, then tell the sequence again while checking the author’s exact wording.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — Our Pretty Dragon Flies: A Skin Like an Overcoat; source transcription lines 624–660; opens “When the dragon fly larva first hatches it is very small and its legs are rather long and spidery, but it eats and eats and eats,--my, how it eats!”; closes “It moults several times, and at last little short wings appear. At first it has no wings at all, you know.”.

questions.prompt: What mistaken idea does the narrator expect after saying the insect pulls out of its skin?
facilitatorNotes: A reader might imagine it has no skin left. The next paragraph corrects that by explaining the new soft skin underneath.
evidence: But it is not without a skin.

questions.prompt: In what way is the discarded skin like an old coat, and where does that comparison stop being literal?
facilitatorNotes: Both are outer coverings that can be left behind. The insect grows a covering; it does not choose or sew clothing. The coat makes an unfamiliar process imaginable.
evidence: as though it were an old coat

questions.prompt: Which changes repeat, and which new change appears near the end?
facilitatorNotes: Growth and moulting recur; small wings eventually appear. The ending shows development as well as simple enlargement.
evidence: at last little short wings appear.

days.title: The Insect Folk — Our Pretty Dragon Flies: The First Flight
days.challenge: Track a transformation and then examine how an anecdote supports a proposed conclusion.
days.focus: The same ability that frees a dragonfly complicates a human plan.
days.context: The excerpt begins with the pond-dwelling young dragonfly and ends with a story about raising adults to catch mosquitoes. Reread to separate the reported event from the narrator’s broad conclusion.
days.contentNote: Includes non-graphic descriptions of birds eating insects. The account and its general conclusion come from a 1903 nature book.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — Our Pretty Dragon Flies: The First Flight; source transcription lines 718–774; opens “But now let us return to our funny larva that lives at the bottom of the pond. It stays down there, eating and growing and moulting, for nine or ten months or even longer; then something very wonderful happens.”; closes “They are among the swiftest and strongest of insects.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the newly emerged dragonfly vulnerable before it can fly?
facilitatorNotes: Its wings are soft and small; it stays still while they expand and harden. Birds may find it during that interval.
evidence: with soft and flabby little wings.

questions.prompt: What changes while the insect appears motionless?
facilitatorNotes: The wings stretch and harden and colours develop. Lack of movement is therefore not the same as lack of change.
evidence: it remains motionless an hour or so, but it does not remain unchanged.

questions.prompt: Does the story establish that raising dragonflies could never help anyone?
facilitatorNotes: It reports one attempt in which the adults flew away. That explains why this plan failed but does not supply evidence about every possible setting or plan; distinguish the event from the sweeping last claim.
evidence: They fly so fast and so far there is no use raising them.

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Fairy May Flies: Names and Wings
days.challenge: Separate imaginative descriptions from anatomical details and explanations of names.
days.focus: Delicate adult insects described through both comparison and observation.
days.context: These are adult mayflies; the short life mentioned here refers to that stage, not their whole development. The narrator’s broad descriptions concern the insects being discussed. Read the fairy imagery first, then reread the physical details.
days.contentNote: Mentions the short lives of adult insects and insects fallen to the ground.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Fairy May Flies: Names and Wings; source transcription lines 846–895; opens “Come, children, and see! Hundreds and hundreds of them are dancing about.”; closes “They are called May flies because they often come out in the month of May, though sometimes not until June, and some species are as late as July in appearing.”.

questions.prompt: What do the phrases fairy ships and fine lace help a reader imagine?
facilitatorNotes: The ships suggest delicate movement in air; lace suggests the appearance of the wings. Neither phrase means that the insects are literally made from those things.
evidence: fairy ships sailing in the sea of air.

questions.prompt: Which details could distinguish these wings from the dragonfly wings in the comparison?
facilitatorNotes: The passage calls them more delicate and says the front wings are larger than the hind wings. The answer can be drawn from words without the source illustrations.
evidence: The fore wings, you see, are larger than the hind ones.

questions.prompt: Why might the name May fly mislead someone who treats it as a strict rule?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator explicitly includes insects appearing in June or July. A common name can point to a frequent event without covering every case.
evidence: some species are as late as July in appearing.

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Stone Fly Folk
days.challenge: Follow a life cycle while checking when the narrator is describing young or adult insects.
days.focus: Contrasts between a quiet winged adult and an active hungry young insect.
days.context: John has returned from a fishing trip with stoneflies to show the group. The comparisons with mayflies concern delicate winged insects. This 1903 account gives a general portrait rather than a rule for every species.
days.contentNote: Includes natural predation and a reference to fishing bait. The final sentence urges care for the insects.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Stone Fly Folk; source transcription lines 1066–1125; opens “John has been fishing.”; closes “The stone flies are harmless little people, and we should never kill one needlessly.”.

questions.prompt: How does the adult’s eating differ from that of the young insect in this account?
facilitatorNotes: The adult eats little, whereas the young insect is described as constantly feeding. Track the change in subject rather than assuming every statement applies at every age.
evidence: If the winged stone fly does not eat, its larva does;

questions.prompt: How does the name stone fly connect with the young insect’s shelter?
facilitatorNotes: It lives under stones and quickly slips away when the shelter is lifted. The name recalls this hidden stage as well as the winged adult.
evidence: It lives under stones, which is why it is called the stone fly,

questions.prompt: Why is a cast-off skin evidence of change rather than necessarily of a dead insect?
facilitatorNotes: The adult emerges from that covering and can leave it behind. Connect the discarded skins to the preceding emergence sentence.
evidence: emerges from its larval skin as a perfect winged insect.

days.title: A House Seen Two Ways
days.challenge: Separate the narrator’s teasing opinions from the characters’ observations.
days.focus: Setting and point of view
days.context: Five siblings arrive from London at a country house. The narrator often speaks directly to the reader. A hack is a hired horse-drawn carriage.
days.contentNote: The narrator makes sweeping claims about city children and jokes about a flat, motionless Earth. Treat these as a playful narrator’s claims, not facts. Minor accidental bumps occur.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 1; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 1–12; opens “The house was three miles from the station, but, before the dusty hired hack had rattled a”; closes “of course it knew best, but it was not at all like any fairy you ever saw or heard of or read about.”.

questions.prompt: Why can the same ordinary house feel inconvenient to Mother and like a palace to the children?
facilitatorNotes: Compare storage and household work with space for play. The children’s recent life in London explains the strength of their delight; neither view needs to erase the other.
evidence: the White House seemed to them a sort of Fairy Palace set down in an Earthly Paradise

questions.prompt: Why does the description include a bump and a pinched finger among reasons the children expect to be happy?
facilitatorNotes: Reread the long sentence aloud. Its surprising ending suggests the freedom to explore matters more to them than minor discomfort, while the narrator teases their enthusiasm.
evidence: they had no longer any doubts whatever

questions.prompt: How does the narrator try to make us willing to believe the coming fairy story? Is seeing something enough to explain it?
facilitatorNotes: Notice the direct address and contrast between ordinary stories and astonishing ones. Clarify that Earth is round and orbits the Sun: the narrator humorously describes appearances, not reliable science.
evidence: Grown-up people find it very difficult to believe really wonderful things, unless they have what they call proof

days.title: Something Under the Sand
days.challenge: Track changing guesses as new physical evidence appears.
days.focus: Inference and character choices
days.context: With their parents briefly away and caregivers at home, the siblings take their baby brother, nicknamed the Lamb, to the gravel pit. Anthea is also called Panther and Cyril is called Squirrel.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 1; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 13–50; opens “It was at the gravel-pits. Father had to go away suddenly on business, and mother had gone”; closes “"I believe I must have dropped asleep," it said, stretching itself.”.

questions.prompt: Which details make Anthea reject the guesses that the creature is a rat or snake?
facilitatorNotes: Distinguish observation from guessing: she sees feet and fur and judges its size. Her report of speech gives a further clue, though the others initially doubt it.
evidence: It's got feet; I saw them; and fur

questions.prompt: How does Anthea’s reason for digging change during this scene?
facilitatorNotes: She first persists because she wants to finish the Australia hole; later she digs carefully to uncover and protect a living creature. Invite two details rather than a single character label.
evidence: She always liked to finish a thing when she had once begun it

questions.prompt: At what moment does a private claim become evidence everyone shares? Why does that matter?
facilitatorNotes: Anthea first reports speech alone. When all hear the voice, they check each other’s reactions; the shared experience changes the mystery from an imagined animal to an extraordinary encounter.
evidence: And now everyone heard the voice and looked at the others to see if they had heard it too

days.title: The Sand-Fairy Remembers
days.challenge: Keep track of a comic speaker’s moods and its imaginary history.
days.focus: Dialogue and fantasy worldbuilding
days.context: The children have uncovered a talking creature in the gravel pit. It calls itself a Psammead, or Sand-fairy, and has been asleep for a very long time.
days.contentNote: The fairy describes other fairies dying after getting wet; there is no graphic detail. Its prehistoric menus and account of fossils are fantasy.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 1; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 51–92; opens “The children stood round the hole in a ring, looking at the creature they had found. It wa”; closes “ince. And the sea changed its lodgings afterwards. And now I'm not going to tell you another thing."”.

questions.prompt: Which comparisons help you picture the Psammead? What effect does combining such different animals have?
facilitatorNotes: Collect snail eyes, bat ears, spider-shaped body and monkey-like hands. The mixture makes a vivid creature that resists the children’s familiar idea of a fairy.
evidence: its tubby body was shaped like a spider's and covered with thick soft fur

questions.prompt: What changes the Psammead from offended to willing to talk? Does it promise to be polite itself?
facilitatorNotes: Anthea tries kindness and Robert expresses wonder. Compare its demand for civil speech with its refusal to promise answers; friendliness is uneven rather than instantly achieved.
evidence: If you talk nicely to me, perhaps I'll answer you, and perhaps I won't

questions.prompt: How does the Psammead explain both stone remains and its own survival?
facilitatorNotes: Connect sunset’s magical changes with stone bones, and dangerous water with its move inland. Identify these as invented explanations within a fantasy, not accounts of fossil formation.
evidence: Why, of course at sunset what was left over turned into stone

days.title: A Wish That Hides Familiar Faces
days.challenge: Distinguish getting the exact wish from getting a useful result.
days.focus: Cause, consequence, and recognition
days.context: The newly discovered Sand-fairy can grant wishes. The children have imagined this chance often, but must now choose while the impatient fairy waits.
days.contentNote: The narrator stereotypes girls as easier to persuade; characters compare appearance with nationality and tease hair color. These judgments are historical prejudices, not truths about gender, nationality, or beauty.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 1; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 93–137; opens “"Just one more, please," said the children. "Can you give wishes now?"”; closes “s, but as he refused to hold on to such new acquaintances he was a dead weight, and most exhausting.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the children choose beauty despite having imagined useful wishes before?
facilitatorNotes: Look at the fairy’s pressure and Anthea’s private wish. An available idea wins over group deliberation; the narrator contrasts confident imagining with an actual decision.
evidence: now the chance had suddenly come to them, they could not make up their minds

questions.prompt: How does Cyril discover that the apparent strangers are his siblings?
facilitatorNotes: He uses familiar damaged or dirty clothing, not their transformed faces. Discuss why these ordinary imperfections become reassuring evidence of identity.
evidence: I know the hole in your pinafore

questions.prompt: What does the baby’s response reveal about the value of familiar faces?
facilitatorNotes: He wants the people he knows and cannot connect their voices and actions with their changed appearances. Beauty creates fear and extra care work rather than instant happiness.
evidence: Fancy having to make friends with our own baby!--it's too silly

days.title: Strangers at Their Own Door
days.challenge: Read a statement that can be literally true while still misleading a listener.
days.focus: Reversal and double meanings
days.context: The wish has made the children so beautiful that no one knows them, not even the Lamb at first. Carrying him by turns, they finally reach home.
days.contentNote: Martha empties a jug of water over Robert and calls him a “nasty little Eye-talian monkey,” an insult aimed at Italians in Nesbit’s England; she takes the beautiful strangers for foreign children. The children fear being turned to stone at sunset.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 1; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 138–182; opens “"Thank goodness, we're home!" said Jane, staggering through the iron gate”; closes “And they never have.”.

questions.prompt: What reason does Robert give for believing they will not become stone? Why does it fail to comfort them fully?
facilitatorNotes: He reasons that another promised wish requires living children. Their uncertainty and hunger remain stronger than the argument; the passage distinguishes a reason from an emotion.
evidence: he couldn't if we were stone, could he

questions.prompt: Why is “nice and ugly” a joyful description here?
facilitatorNotes: The children welcome recognizable features after beauty made them strangers. Discuss how the speaker’s priorities have changed.
evidence: how nice and ugly you do look, with your old freckles and your brown hair and your little eyes

questions.prompt: When Anthea says the beautiful children kept them away, what does Martha hear and what does the reader understand?
facilitatorNotes: Martha imagines a separate group; readers know the beautiful children were the siblings themselves. Ask whether literal truth has supplied a fair explanation.
evidence: We couldn't come back till they'd gone

questions.prompt: Why can none of the children’s explanations get them through their own front door?
facilitatorNotes: Martha and cook see only strangers, so every true statement sounds like impudence or a trick; the beauty they wished for has cut them off from the people who know them. Readers may also notice that Martha protects the Lamb and the house as she understands her duty.
evidence: "And who's Us, when you're at home?" asked Martha scornfully.

days.title: Rural Walks
days.challenge: Follow a young speaker’s route through several scales of landscape, from flowers to mountains.
days.focus: A catalogue of beloved places held together by repeated affection.
days.context: The source labels this poem as written at thirteen. “Cambrian” means Welsh. Reread to distinguish the small details the speaker gathers from the large scenes she can only view.

excerpt.locator: Rural Walks; source transcription lines 1328–1364; opens “Oh! may I ever pass my happy hours”; closes “    And every landscape, charms my youthful breast.””.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker do with the flowers rather than merely look at them?
facilitatorNotes: She gathers rosebuds and other blossoms to make a varied festoon. This is a detail in the historical poem, not a request to pick wild plants.
evidence: To form the gay festoon of varied hue.

questions.prompt: How do the village and mountain scenes differ in sound and mood?
facilitatorNotes: The village includes cheerful water and songs, while the mountains and ruins are solemn, grand and old. Both attract the speaker, so admiration need not have one mood.
evidence: Where cliffs in solemn majesty are piled,

questions.prompt: What is gained by repeating the claim that every landscape charms her?
facilitatorNotes: The ending gathers the varied route into a broad declaration of attachment. Readers may notice that the repeated lines return to the opening idea after supplying examples.
evidence: And every landscape, charms my youthful breast.

days.title: The Wandering Wind
days.challenge: Track proposed answers to a question before recognizing the speaker’s final explanation.
days.focus: Memory as the source of the wind’s emotional power.
days.context: Read the opening questions as real possibilities, then reread the later “No” as a turning point. Osiers are willows.

excerpt.locator: The Wandering Wind; source transcription lines 60910–60937; opens “The Wind, the wandering Wind”; closes “      To the Wind, the wandering Wind!”.

questions.prompt: Which possible sources of the wind’s magic does the speaker first test?
facilitatorNotes: Water, grass and hollow rocks are suggested, then combined voices. The questioning form makes the reader search alongside the speaker.
evidence: Or is it from the hollow rocks

questions.prompt: What answer replaces these natural explanations?
facilitatorNotes: Human love and memory make the sound emotionally powerful. The poem distinguishes the physical sound from what it awakens in a listener.
evidence: ’Tis the human love within us

questions.prompt: Why does the last line repeat the title instead of naming a particular memory?
facilitatorNotes: The returning phrase imitates the recurring wind while leaving individual memories open. Accept other explanations that address both repetition and the poem’s refusal to specify one story.
evidence: To the Wind, the wandering Wind!

days.title: The Stream Set Free
days.challenge: Hear how a repeated command changes when the poem makes room for sorrow.
days.focus: Freedom and joy that still offer sympathy to lonely listeners.
days.context: The stream is imagined as returning to woodland freedom. Read for the music vocabulary; then ask why the poem interrupts its celebration to request a pitying tone.

excerpt.locator: The Stream Set Free; source transcription lines 61034–61079; opens “Flow on, rejoice, make music,”; closes “      Be set in thee!”.

questions.prompt: What does the stream regain when it enters the woodland?
facilitatorNotes: It belongs again to a natural home with birds, leaves and winds, away from human care and conflict.
evidence: Thou art all its own again;

questions.prompt: Why call the reeds strings of a forest-lyre?
facilitatorNotes: Their movement and sounds are imagined as part of the stream’s music. This joins several natural objects into one instrument.
evidence: Strings of the forest-lyre,

questions.prompt: Does the request for a pitying tone cancel the poem’s joy?
facilitatorNotes: No: the speaker asks joyful music to include comfort for sad people. The repeated invitation to rejoice remains at the end, so the moods coexist.
evidence: Oh! keep one pitying tone

days.title: Water-Lilies — A Fairy Song
days.challenge: Build a small imagined world from flower parts, water and reeds.
days.focus: A playful transformation made urgent by a flower’s short life.
days.context: This complete fairy song invites imaginary elves into water-lilies. Read twice: first to picture the scene, then to identify the real objects that become boats and flags.

excerpt.locator: Water-Lilies — A Fairy Song; source transcription lines 63347–63370; opens “Come away, elves!--while the dew is sweet,”; closes “    And the life of the lily may not be long.”.

questions.prompt: What becomes the fairies’ boats, oars and streamer?
facilitatorNotes: Lily cups become boats, reeds become oars, and a flag-leaf becomes a streamer. The answers depend on following the precise objects in the imagined voyage.
evidence: Making those urns each a fairy boat;

questions.prompt: Why does the poem compare the flower’s centre to a star looking upward?
facilitatorNotes: The golden centre is imagined as seeking relatives in the sky. The comparison links a tiny pool scene to a much larger world.
evidence: A golden star unto heaven looks up,

questions.prompt: How do the final two lines alter the repeated invitation to come away?
facilitatorNotes: The growing sun and the lily’s limited life add urgency: the beautiful opportunity will not last indefinitely. Accept a tone of excitement, tenderness or both.
evidence: And the life of the lily may not be long.

days.title: The Bird at Sea
days.challenge: Identify the change of speaker and reconsider an earlier judgment after hearing the reply.
days.focus: Attachment to a caring person weighed against a natural home.
days.context: A speaker sees a woodland bird on a ship and urges it away. A “bark” here is a boat. Read the first three stanzas and final reply in different voices.

excerpt.locator: The Bird at Sea; source transcription lines 62365–62401; opens “Bird of the greenwood!”; closes “      Away, away!””.

questions.prompt: Why does the first speaker think the bird does not belong on the ship?
facilitatorNotes: The sea lacks flowers, leaves and sweet water, and storms seem dangerous for a woodland bird. The advice follows the speaker’s view of the bird’s needs.
evidence: How shouldst thou battle

questions.prompt: What does the bird reveal that the first speaker did not know?
facilitatorNotes: A person who cared for it is aboard. This missing relationship changes the meaning of the bird’s decision to linger.
evidence: A hand that hath nursed me

questions.prompt: How does “Away, away!” change meaning in the last stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Initially it means away from the ship toward the woods; at the end it means away from the woods to remain with the carer. The same words mark opposing choices.
evidence: So I turn from the greenwood,

days.title: At Plumfield’s Door
days.challenge: Trace a change in feeling through small gestures and sensory details.
days.focus: Setting and welcome
days.context: Nat Blake, a boy who has no home, arrives at the Plumfield school carrying a letter from Mr. Laurence. He does not yet know whether he may stay.
days.contentNote: Nat has experienced homelessness. A boy falls while sliding down a banister and is unhurt; the narrator exaggerates his toughness for humor, not as a safety claim.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 1; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_1; consecutive transcript paragraphs 8–47; opens “"PLEASE, sir, is this Plumfield?" asked a ragged boy of the man who opened the great gate ”; closes “." And Daisy took him by the hand with a pretty protecting air, which made Nat feel at home at once.”.

questions.prompt: Which details make Plumfield look inviting before anyone promises Nat a place?
facilitatorNotes: Collect light, voices, warmth and food smells. Contrast what he senses with his uncertainty that such comfort could include him.
evidence: felt that it was hardly possible that the light and warmth and comfort within could be for a homeless "little chap" like him

questions.prompt: How do Tommy and Demi offer different kinds of welcome?
facilitatorNotes: Tommy immediately offers play; Demi asks serious questions and expresses trust in Uncle Laurie’s choice. Neither has to give a formal speech to help Nat feel included.
evidence: He is Uncle Laurie; and he always sends nice boys

questions.prompt: Why does Daisy’s taking Nat’s hand matter after the servant has already said he can stay?
facilitatorNotes: Permission settles a practical question, while a child’s warm companionship makes the unfamiliar place feel safer. Notice Nat’s response rather than assuming all welcomes feel alike.
evidence: Daisy took him by the hand with a pretty protecting air, which made Nat feel at home at once

days.title: A Place Beside the Fire
days.challenge: Infer care from actions as well as from words.
days.focus: Characterization and school culture
days.context: Daisy brings Nat to the adults who run Plumfield, Mr. and Mrs. Bhaer, often called Father and Mother Bhaer. Nat is wet, shy, and has a persistent cough.
days.contentNote: Nat’s poverty and illness are described. Historical cough remedies and a shared medicine spoon belong to the story’s setting.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 1; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_1; consecutive transcript paragraphs 48–71; opens “Demi returned to his beloved book, while his sister led the new-comer into a back room, wh”; closes “urished, and manners and morals were insinuated, without the pupils exactly knowing how it was done.”.

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Bhaer notice Nat’s feelings without making him explain them publicly?
facilitatorNotes: She sees his trembling lips, draws him closer, and uses a merry manner while feeling tender. Point to a gesture and a spoken line as different kinds of evidence.
evidence: she said something merry, because she felt so tender

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Bhaer’s “place all ready” communicate beyond the availability of a chair?
facilitatorNotes: It offers belonging rather than reluctant permission. Dry footwear and attention to illness make that welcome concrete.
evidence: There is a place all ready for thee, my son

questions.prompt: How does the supper scene show that Plumfield combines freedom with limits?
facilitatorNotes: The children may make noise and enjoy a holiday, but a word from Father Bhaer can quiet them. Discuss why a few understood rules might work better here than constant correction.
evidence: the lads had learned that liberty must not be abused

days.title: The Music Nat Misses
days.challenge: Read a conversation for information that a listening adult learns indirectly.
days.focus: Revealing backstory through dialogue
days.context: At supper Mrs. Bhaer seats Nat beside friendly Tommy. As they talk about the school’s musicians, Nat begins to explain the life he had before arriving.
days.contentNote: Nat recalls his father’s death, hunger, and loss of his violin. A boy’s nickname mocks his appetite; discuss the person without adopting the insult.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 1; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_1; consecutive transcript paragraphs 72–100; opens “Nat found himself very well off behind the tall pitchers, with Tommy Bangs just round the ”; closes “ Bhaer to herself, as she saw the eager, happy expression on his face when Tommy talked of the band.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Tommy’s idea that street music was fun differ from Nat’s experience?
facilitatorNotes: Tommy imagines the activity; Nat remembers cold, heat, hunger, and tiredness. His love for the violin does not mean the conditions of his work were good.
evidence: No, it was horrid; so cold in winter, and hot in summer

questions.prompt: Why might Mrs. Bhaer learn more by seating Nat with Tommy than by asking all the questions herself?
facilitatorNotes: Tommy’s easy interest helps Nat volunteer confidences. The adult listens quietly and learns what matters to him without turning supper into an interview.
evidence: gave Mrs. Bhaer the key to the new boy's character, better than if she had talked to him herself

questions.prompt: Does Mrs. Bhaer’s decision to care for Nat depend on his becoming a musical genius? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: Mr. Laurence offers to develop his talent later, while she recognizes immediate needs regardless of exceptional ability. Separate worth as a person from future achievement.
evidence: whether he was a genius or not, here was a lonely, sick boy, who needed just what she loved to give

days.title: A Language the Room Understands
days.challenge: Notice changes in the room as attention moves from appearance to ability.
days.focus: Emotional turning point
days.context: Mrs. Bhaer has overheard that Nat misses playing the violin. After supper she offers him an instrument while the other children play noisily nearby.
days.contentNote: The original identifies a kind of melody by a racial term that was the usual name at the time. Nat cries while remembering earlier hardship.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 1; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_1; consecutive transcript paragraphs 101–120; opens “So, after supper, when the lads flocked into the school-room for more "high jinks," Mrs. Jo”; closes “sey and have a bath, and then go to bed, and to-morrow we will lay some nice little plans together."”.

questions.prompt: What changes when Nat begins to play, both in him and in his audience?
facilitatorNotes: He handles the instrument confidently and forgets the room; the boys quiet down and move closer. Track the change through physical actions rather than only saying everyone is happy.
evidence: Gradually they got nearer and nearer

questions.prompt: Why might applause feel better than coins to Nat at this moment?
facilitatorNotes: He gains recognition and a place among peers, not merely payment for work. The text makes this contrast explicit, but allow readers to explain its emotional meaning in their own words.
evidence: rewarded him better than a shower of pennies

questions.prompt: Why does Nat cry after a successful performance, and how does Mrs. Bhaer respond?
facilitatorNotes: Joy, relief and exhaustion can coexist. She moves him to a quieter room, listens, and promises care rather than treating tears as ingratitude.
evidence: You are all so kind—and it's so beautiful—I can't help it

days.title: The Saturday Agreement
days.challenge: Read rules in relation to the reasons and promises behind them.
days.focus: Negotiation and a closing image
days.context: After music and supper, Nat is taken upstairs for a bath and a comfortable bed. He is surprised to discover that Plumfield permits a weekly pillow fight.
days.contentNote: Historical bedtime remedies are mentioned as part of the story.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 1; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_1; consecutive transcript paragraphs 121–142; opens “Nat held her hand fast in his, but had not a word to say, and let his grateful eyes speak ”; closes “night frolic, as Mother Bhaer kissed her new boy, and left him to happy dreams of life at Plumfield.”.

questions.prompt: How do the comparisons with sunshine, whales, ducklings, and snowflakes shape the bedtime scene?
facilitatorNotes: Choose two and explain their different effects: warmth, energetic movement, busy care, or flying pillows. The household is lively rather than perfectly still.
evidence: pillows flew like big snow flakes

questions.prompt: What agreement replaced Mrs. Bhaer’s unsuccessful ban on night-time play?
facilitatorNotes: A fifteen-minute Saturday pillow fight is exchanged for proper bedtime behavior on other nights. Note both permission and the consequence of losing the next frolic.
evidence: I was to allow a fifteen-minute pillow-fight, every Saturday night

questions.prompt: How does the quiet ending answer Nat’s earlier uncertainty about staying?
facilitatorNotes: The children honor the stopping time and Mother Bhaer kisses him goodnight. He can expect both fun and dependable care; compare his happy dreams with his anxious arrival.
evidence: left him to happy dreams of life at Plumfield

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Silver Fish: A Misleading Name
days.challenge: Test several everyday names against the specific evidence offered in the description.
days.focus: Names, appearances and imagined motives that can mislead an observer.
days.context: May has brought an insect in a box with a glass top. Read the narrator’s playful descriptions aloud, then reread for places where the narrator corrects what those words might suggest.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Silver Fish: A Misleading Name; source transcription lines 1135–1174; opens “May has something here for us to look at. She says it is a slippery rascal. Let us see it. Oh, yes, you have it in that little box. See, the box has a glass top. May cut the top off the box herself, and fastened in a little pane of glass so we could see the rascal without danger of its escaping.”; closes “Perhaps it is afraid of us.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the name silver fish seem suitable even though the creature is not a fish?
facilitatorNotes: Its shape, shine, scales and slippery movement resemble a fish. The passage identifies it as an insect with six legs instead.
evidence: But in spite of its name it is no fish.

questions.prompt: What is the reason for calling it a rascal?
facilitatorNotes: It eats starch in wallpaper paste and book bindings, damaging objects people value. The name expresses a human response to its feeding.
evidence: It eats the starch from the paste that fastens on her wall paper,

questions.prompt: How does the narrator revise the idea that it hides because it feels ashamed?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says it dislikes light and offers fear only as a possibility. Ask readers to distinguish observed hiding from guesses about feelings.
evidence: Perhaps it is afraid of us.

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Old Cockroaches: May Objects
days.challenge: Reconstruct a child’s unquoted replies from the teacher’s answers.
days.focus: A humorous attempt to turn dislike into attention and curiosity.
days.context: The teacher speaks to May, whose replies are mostly repeated inside questions. Read as a conversation with pauses for May’s side, then examine the difference between disliking an animal and knowing about it.
days.contentNote: A historical, humorous conversation with broad claims about insect behaviour. Discussion focuses on viewpoint and dialogue; no handling activity is required.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Old Cockroaches: May Objects; source transcription lines 1189–1253; opens “Children, here is a cockroach.”; closes “Perhaps they don't care.”.

questions.prompt: Why might both the person and the cockroach run in the kitchen scene?
facilitatorNotes: Each reacts to the other’s sudden appearance. The narrator denies that the insect deliberately tries to frighten the person.
evidence: It will not frighten you on purpose,

questions.prompt: How can we tell that May resists the lesson even though her own speech is not printed directly?
facilitatorNotes: The teacher repeats or questions her objections about heads, legs and knowing anything about cockroaches. Those responses allow readers to infer May’s position.
evidence: You don't want to know anything about cockroaches?

questions.prompt: What is funny about saying the insects are old enough to know better?
facilitatorNotes: May treats an ancient kind of insect as if each individual were an older person with manners. The joke combines the teacher’s point about ancient origins with May’s dislike.
evidence: They are old enough to know better?

days.title: The Insect Folk — Neighbor Walking Stick: Hidden in Plain Sight
days.challenge: Collect details from several children’s observations and distinguish a question from an explanation.
days.focus: Shape, colour and stillness working together to make an insect hard to notice.
days.context: The group discovers a walking-stick insect while sitting outdoors. Follow its movement from surprise to a twig, and reread each child’s contribution to the description.
days.contentNote: Describes insect defences and potential predators without graphic detail. Colours and sizes refer to the historical examples being discussed.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — Neighbor Walking Stick: Hidden in Plain Sight; source transcription lines 1529–1632; opens “Isn't this a pretty place to sit down and--”; closes “They are gentle little folk, all of them, and move slowly about over the leaves and twigs, not wishing to harm any living thing.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the insect become hard to find even after the group knows it is there?
facilitatorNotes: Its shape and colour match the twig, and it can remain very still. Readers should combine several details rather than rely on colour alone.
evidence: it is not easy to find it.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator admit to not knowing about the long antennae?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator asks whether they improve hearing, feeling and smelling, but does not provide an answer. A question directed at an insect marks curiosity rather than verified explanation.
evidence: I wish you could tell us about them.

questions.prompt: How does the word suppose affect the claim about protection from birds?
facilitatorNotes: It marks an inference from appearance and concealment. The earlier difficulty locating the insect makes the inference plausible, but the group has not watched a bird test it.
evidence: I suppose their queer shape and their color protect them

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Grasshopper Tribes: A Leg Has a Plan
days.challenge: Move between a familiar spring comparison and unfamiliar names for connected parts.
days.focus: Close observation justified by a pattern shared across many insects.
days.context: Locust here names the grasshopper being examined. The children describe and label its leg. The original memory verse is included; the discussion can use the written descriptions without the omitted illustration.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Grasshopper Tribes: A Leg Has a Plan; source transcription lines 1810–1909; opens “Come here, little locust, and let us look at you.”; closes “You see all the legs are made on one common plan, and it is very convenient, as you will soon see, to have the parts named.”.

questions.prompt: Why does John compare the hind legs to a spring?
facilitatorNotes: The insect draws the legs close and then suddenly straightens them, producing a leap. The comparison explains a movement rather than merely a resemblance in shape.
evidence: then suddenly straightens them out

questions.prompt: How does the passage help a beginner keep the five named parts in order?
facilitatorNotes: It gives positions, numbers, descriptions and a short verse. A reader can compare which aid communicates shape and which chiefly supports remembering order.
evidence: The one next the body we will mark I

questions.prompt: How does the teacher answer Charlie’s objection that this is too much trouble?
facilitatorNotes: The names apply to a common plan in insect legs, so one careful study will be useful later. The response offers a reason for detail beyond winning the memory game.
evidence: all the legs are made on one common plan

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Grasshopper Tribes: Watching and Wondering
days.challenge: Follow a conversation that moves from a defence to classification and then to independent observation.
days.focus: The difference between hearing an explanation and looking carefully for oneself.
days.context: The group has called a grasshopper’s unpleasant defensive fluid “molasses”; it is not kitchen syrup. Read the conversation for changes of subject, then reread the closing sound words aloud.
days.contentNote: “Mule-killer” is a historical nickname discussed by the narrator.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Grasshopper Tribes: Watching and Wondering; source transcription lines 2590–2659; opens “John says he hates to touch the grasshopper on account of this molasses.”; closes “And this I am sure of; if you really watch and listen, you can learn to know the different insects by their sounds, just as you can know the birds by their songs. You can even tell whether you are listening to the meadow grasshopper, or the locust.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator mention turkeys after explaining the sticky liquid?
facilitatorNotes: They show that the defence does not deter every predator. The exception prevents a simple claim that the liquid always protects the grasshopper.
evidence: Some birds eat it, however, in spite of its molasses.

questions.prompt: What mistaken category does Ned seem to have in mind?
facilitatorNotes: He appears to separate familiar farm birds from birds generally. The narrator includes turkeys, chickens, ducks and geese in the larger category.
evidence: They are all birds.

questions.prompt: Why end with a long list of chirping, rasping and buzzing sounds?
facilitatorNotes: It invites attention to differences that a reader could overlook under the single word noise. The final claim connects careful listening with identifying insects.
evidence: chirping and shrilling and rasping and kricking

days.title: Heidi: the tower and the kittens (excerpt)
days.challenge: Trace how a goal changes after disappointment.
days.focus: The search for a landscape leads to an unexpected gift.
days.context: Unable to see open countryside from a city window, Heidi asks Sebastian where she could obtain a wide view.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, Miss Rottenmeier Has an Uncomfortable Day; begins “In the afternoon, while Clara was resting, Heidi was left to herself. She planted herself in the hal”; ends “"No. Please send them to Clara; she will like them, I am sure."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Heidi nearly give away Clara’s flower-picture?
facilitatorNotes: She hopes the boy can lead her to a tower with the view she longs for. Its emotional cost is clear because she is reluctant to part with Clara’s gift.
evidence: The temptation to look far down into the valley

questions.prompt: How does the view overturn Heidi’s expectation?
facilitatorNotes: She sees city roofs and chimneys instead of a mountain valley. The tower offers height, but not the kind of scene she imagined.
evidence: a sea of chimneys, roofs and towers

questions.prompt: What changes the tower-keeper from a forbidding figure into a helpful one?
facilitatorNotes: Her distress persuades him to take her up; their shared interest in kittens then leads to an offer and delivery plan. Accept emphasis on either turning point with evidence.
evidence: glad to find a good home for the kittens.

days.title: Heidi: a reason to learn to read (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare competing explanations of a learner’s difficulty.
days.focus: Interest and encouragement challenge a fixed expectation.
days.context: Clara’s grandmother visits Frankfurt and asks why Heidi spends so much time alone.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, A Grandmama; begins “The following evening great expectation reigned in the house. Tinette had put on a new cap, Sebastia”; ends “ long, I can see that. Come now and let us go to Clara." With that they both went over to the study.”.

questions.prompt: How does Grandmama answer the claim that Heidi does nothing useful alone?
facilitatorNotes: She says she would behave similarly if left alone, shifting attention from a supposed defect to the situation.
evidence: if I were left alone like that.

questions.prompt: Why does a beautiful picture make Heidi cry?
facilitatorNotes: Its pasture, flock, and sunset recall her mountain home. Grandmama asks about the reminder instead of merely blaming the tears.
evidence: a peaceful flock grazing on a green pasture.

questions.prompt: What new purpose does Grandmama offer for learning letters?
facilitatorNotes: Reading will unlock the shepherd’s whole story and the book will be hers. Heidi’s wish to read shows a change from expecting failure.
evidence: If I could only read already!

days.title: Heidi: packing for home (excerpt)
days.challenge: Infer priorities from objects a character treasures.
days.focus: Different views of the same journey.
days.context: Heidi has learned to read, but misses home deeply. Mr. Sesemann and the doctor have arranged for her return, with Sebastian escorting her.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, Up the Alp on a Summer Evening; begins “Heidi was dressed in her Sunday frock and stood waiting for further commands.”; ends “n you get there," muttered the baker. "It is strange though, for she must know," he said to himself.”.

questions.prompt: Which gift in the trunk most excites Heidi, and why?
facilitatorNotes: The rolls matter because she can give them to Grandmother. Their value is relational rather than luxurious.
evidence: a little basket with twelve round white rolls

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Sesemann do when the housekeeper throws down Heidi’s old bundle?
facilitatorNotes: He returns it after seeing how she treasures it, respecting a preference the housekeeper dismisses.
evidence: seeing how much she treasured it, gave it back to her.

questions.prompt: How do Sebastian and Heidi view the final mountain journey differently?
facilitatorNotes: Sebastian fears danger and seeks someone else to escort her; Heidi knows the path and longs to return. The same setting carries opposite meanings.
evidence: I can go up alone from the village.

days.title: Heidi: the basket of rolls (excerpt)
days.challenge: Read dialogue and gesture as evidence of reunion and belonging.
days.focus: A gift’s value beside the giver’s presence.
days.context: The baker has brought Heidi from the station to her village. She first climbs to Peter’s house to see Grandmother.
days.contentNote: Grandmother and Heidi express Christian gratitude. The questions examine what their words show about their relationship.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, Up the Alp on a Summer Evening; begins “They conversed no more, and Heidi began to tremble with excitement when she recognized all the trees”; ends “hardly find words to pray. Only when the glow had subsided, was Heidi able to follow the path again.”.

questions.prompt: How does Grandmother recognize Heidi without seeing her?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes the familiar arrival, voice, and hair. The passage supplies several senses rather than relying on sight.
evidence: this is Heidi's hair

questions.prompt: Why is Grandmother’s response larger than thanks for food?
facilitatorNotes: She calls Heidi herself the greatest blessing and asks to hear her voice. The reunion matters even more than the useful rolls.
evidence: you are my greatest blessing yourself, Heidi!

questions.prompt: Why does Heidi change out of her fine dress before going farther?
facilitatorNotes: She fears Grandfather might not know her; Brigida disagrees. This exposes Heidi’s anxiety about preserving their bond, not a proven requirement from him.
evidence: or else he might not know me any more

days.title: Heidi: a bed made ready again (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare emotional responses that are spoken with those shown silently.
days.focus: Familiar routines make a homecoming tangible.
days.context: After visiting Grandmother, Heidi reaches her grandfather’s hut at last.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, Up the Alp on a Summer Evening; begins “She climbed so fast that she could soon discover, first the tree-tops, then the roof, finally the hu”; ends “e. But Heidi slept quietly, for she had seen the flaming mountains and had heard the fir-trees roar.”.

questions.prompt: Why can neither Heidi nor Grandfather say much at first?
facilitatorNotes: Strong emotion limits their words; hugging and moist eyes carry the meaning. Avoid interpreting silence as indifference.
evidence: The old man said nothing either, but his eyes were moist

questions.prompt: How does Grandfather’s advice about the money differ from Heidi’s view?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks her current bed and dresses make money unnecessary; he thinks ahead to later needs. Neither view is simply about wanting possessions.
evidence: you will need it some day.

questions.prompt: What makes the final prepared bed a meaningful response to Heidi’s disappointment?
facilitatorNotes: She earlier discovers her bed gone, but he promises its return and has it ready by night. His repeated listening also shows care after her absence.
evidence: she found a fresh, fragrant bed waiting for her

days.title: Madam How: two walks over the same ground (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow a story inside an essay and identify what it is meant to demonstrate.
days.focus: Reading and direct observation as partners.
days.context: Kingsley introduces a book about learning from nature by retelling a lesson from Evenings at Home. His audience is addressed as boys, though anyone can examine the argument.
days.contentNote: This is nineteenth-century nature writing, with personification and historical scientific explanations. Read it as an argument to examine, not a current science textbook. The borrowed story includes a dead snake and disparaging language about inattentive people; no collecting or harming animals is assigned.

excerpt.locator: Author’s Preface; begins “My dear boys,--When I was your age, there were no such children's books as there are now.  Those whi”; ends “ook; and dupe them, and lead them about--the blind leading the blind, till both fall into the ditch.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer praise an old book he has just called dull?
facilitatorNotes: One story taught him to use his senses. Its useful lesson matters more to him than handsome pictures.
evidence: more grateful to it than if it had been as full of wonderful pictures

questions.prompt: What makes William’s walk richer than Robert’s although they cover the same ground?
facilitatorNotes: William notices birds, plants, landforms, and people and asks questions; the contrast depends on attention rather than a different destination.
evidence: over the very same ground as Master Robert

questions.prompt: Does the opening claim that having more books automatically makes children wiser?
facilitatorNotes: No. The author says reading alone is insufficient and asks readers to use observation and judgment for themselves.
evidence: your eyes, and ears, and common sense.

days.title: Madam How: the difference between how and why (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow a philosophical distinction through an ordinary example.
days.focus: Personification makes an abstract distinction memorable.
days.context: On a foggy walk, an adult speaker tells a child that even a dreary-looking glen can raise interesting questions. Madam How and Lady Why are his imagined figures.
days.contentNote: This is nineteenth-century nature writing, with personification and historical scientific explanations. Read it as an argument to examine, not a current science textbook. The distinction between ultimate purpose and mechanism reflects the author’s religious philosophy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, The Glen; begins “You find it dull walking up here upon Hartford Bridge Flat this sad November day?  Well, I do not de”; ends “ steadily in after life, I should have done you more good than if I had given you a thousand pounds.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the glen worth examining despite its dreary appearance?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker sees ongoing change and a long history in an ordinary place. The apparent lack of flowers is not the absence of anything to learn.
evidence: it is not, I believe, half finished yet.

questions.prompt: How do opening a door and choosing a walk illustrate different questions?
facilitatorNotes: Opening the door describes a means; choosing a walk describes an intention. Explain the distinction in the author’s terms.
evidence: Because we chose to take a walk.

questions.prompt: What limit does the speaker admit when asked for a final reason that fire burns?
facilitatorNotes: He says he does not know, then labels his proposed purpose as a guess. A chemical mechanism and an ultimate purpose are different in his argument.
evidence: If I dare to guess

days.title: Madam How: mud in the pond (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate an unsupported possibility from an inference based on repeated observation.
days.focus: Ordinary evidence can overturn a dramatic guess.
days.context: The speaker asks how a local glen formed. The child proposes explanations; the adult turns to familiar evidence from a pond.
days.contentNote: This is nineteenth-century nature writing, with personification and historical scientific explanations. Read it as an argument to examine, not a current science textbook.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, The Glen; begins “Well--how was the glen made?  You shall guess it if you like, and I will guess too.  You think, perh”; ends “ll show you the mist that fell yesterday, perhaps, coming out of the ground again, and hard at work.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker reject guessing an earthquake first?
facilitatorNotes: He lacks evidence for one here and wants to begin with what is observed. He does not claim earthquakes never happen.
evidence: we must guess from what we do know

questions.prompt: How does the pond’s repeated filling connect to the shape of the glen?
facilitatorNotes: Mud and sand arrive through the stream; the speaker infers that this material came from the surrounding ground.
evidence: the earth which runs down the stream was all once part of the hill

questions.prompt: Why compare water to a spade and mention a builder with a long life?
facilitatorNotes: The images make small repeated actions over great time seem capable of large changes. They explain the argument’s scale rather than proving every detail.
evidence: Madam How has a very long life, and plenty of time

days.title: Madam How: springs along a clay layer (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow spatial relationships in a long explanatory paragraph.
days.focus: A hidden layer helps explain a visible pattern.
days.context: Having linked stream mud to erosion, the speaker looks at the glen’s banks and the layers below them.
days.contentNote: This is nineteenth-century nature writing, with personification and the scientific explanations of its time. The author recalls children playing on dangerous bogs.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, The Glen; begins “You know of what an odd, and indeed of what a pretty form all these glens are.  How the flat moor en”; ends “at the least thing that Madam How does to-day may take effect hundreds and thousands of years hence.”.

questions.prompt: What shape does the speaker ask the child to notice at the top of each glen?
facilitatorNotes: A curved, wave-crest-like edge over the slope. It becomes part of a repeated local pattern.
evidence: like the crest of a wave

questions.prompt: What contrast between sand and gravel does the child know from exploring?
facilitatorNotes: Rabbit holes occur in the sandy banks but not on the gravelly flat above. The familiar distinction introduces different ground materials.
evidence: there are no rabbit-holes on the flat above

questions.prompt: In the explanation, why does water emerge along the slope rather than simply continue downward?
facilitatorNotes: It meets a clay layer it cannot pass through, then runs along the top and out, undermining material. Keep this answer tied to the described local model.
evidence: through that clay the water cannot get

days.title: Madam How: imagining a changed coastline (excerpt)
days.challenge: Hold a hypothetical change and trace its proposed consequences.
days.focus: Using a familiar landscape as a model for the past.
days.context: The speaker compares the inland glen with a narrow coastal chine the child has visited at Bournemouth.
days.contentNote: This is nineteenth-century nature writing, with personification and historical scientific explanations. Read it as an argument to examine, not a current science textbook.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, The Glen; begins “But I must tell you I think there was a time when this glen was of a very different shape from what ”; ends “ Flat a few more feet out of the sea, and leaving the rest to her trusty tool, the water in the sky.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker recall the chine’s miniature cliffs and peaks?
facilitatorNotes: The child has seen water cutting them, so they offer an accessible comparison for a larger or older landscape.
evidence: the rain which wore the sand into furrowed pinnacles and peaks

questions.prompt: What single imagined change begins the chain of effects?
facilitatorNotes: Raising the coast would keep high tide from removing the mud at the mouth. The blocked exit alters what accumulates behind it.
evidence: the high tide would not come up any longer

questions.prompt: How would that change turn a narrow deep chine into a broad shallow glen in his account?
facilitatorNotes: Material accumulates at the entrance and within, while upper slopes continue eroding and rounding. Retell the connected steps, not just the final shape.
evidence: instead of being deep and narrow, would become broad and shallow

days.title: Dream or Yesterday?
days.challenge: Sort dream imagery, remembered events, and corroborating evidence.
days.focus: Evidence and disagreement
days.context: The children are ordinary-looking again after yesterday’s magical beauty wish. They wake uncertain whether the fairy and the wish really happened.
days.contentNote: The children make unfair class-based guesses about servants’ dreams and ambitions. These guesses reveal the children’s limited perspective; they are not reliable descriptions of servants.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 2; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 1–36; opens “Anthea woke in the morning from a very real sort of dream, in which she was walking in the”; closes “mself. Everyone drew a deep breath of satisfaction, for now of course it couldn't have been a dream.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening explain the rain and animal growling in Anthea’s dream?
facilitatorNotes: Match the dream’s sounds and sensations with Jane’s breathing and Robert’s wet towel. The comic explanation prepares the larger question about what was dream and what was real.
evidence: both the growling and the rain went on just the same

questions.prompt: What new rule does Cyril propose for choosing wishes? Which problem from yesterday does it address?
facilitatorNotes: He wants agreement before anyone asks, reducing the chance that one rushed private wish controls everyone’s day. Notice that making a rule does not yet prove they will follow it.
evidence: no one must ask for anything unless the others agree first

questions.prompt: What finally settles the dream question, and how do the children reach that evidence?
facilitatorNotes: They return to their stone marker and dig. Contrast arguing confidently with checking the actual place; the creature’s appearance supplies the clearest shared confirmation.
evidence: Everyone drew a deep breath of satisfaction, for now of course it couldn't have been a dream

days.title: A Quarry Full of Gold
days.challenge: Notice when a triumphant description begins to contain warnings.
days.focus: Imagery and foreshadowing
days.context: The Sand-fairy is real, and the children have agreed to ask for wealth. First they request that household servants not notice magical gifts, hoping to prevent yesterday’s recognition problem.
days.contentNote: A brief game of covering Jane with coins hurts and frightens her; she is freed. Cyril makes a dismissive remark about girls, which can be questioned rather than endorsed.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 2; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 37–67; opens “The Psammead sat up and shook the sand out of its fur.”; closes “"You've no idea what it's like," said she; "it's like stones on you--or like chains."”.

questions.prompt: Why is Jane’s polite request to hear the fairy’s dreams unexpectedly risky?
facilitatorNotes: “I wish” may use the one daily wish. Discuss how ordinary courtesy takes on a literal magical meaning and why the group hesitates to reject her request.
evidence: Is that the day's wish

questions.prompt: How does the description make the gold seem dazzling and overwhelming at once?
facilitatorNotes: Reread the sun, furnace and fairy-hall comparisons; include the birds’ blocked doorways. The huge quantity is spectacular but already interferes with ordinary life.
evidence: all the little bank-martins' little front doors were covered out of sight

questions.prompt: What warning does Jane’s game of being buried in gold give about their wish?
facilitatorNotes: Gold cannot be treated like light sand. Her comparison with chains turns an image of freedom through riches into one of weight and confinement; avoid claiming she has predicted every later event.
evidence: it's like stones on you--or like chains

days.title: Rich Pockets, Difficult Purchases
days.challenge: Follow the difference between possessing valuable objects and being able to spend them.
days.focus: Practical obstacles and social assumptions
days.context: The children have obtained a huge heap of gold that may disappear at sunset. They carry coins toward the village, hoping to hire a cart and shop in Rochester. A guinea is an older gold coin.
days.contentNote: The passage reflects historical gender rules about public houses and adult judgments based on children’s appearance. Discuss those assumptions as part of the setting.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 2; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 68–100; opens “"Look here," Cyril said, "if this is to do us any good, it's no good our staying gasping a”; closes “ey wouldn't think we were so dishonest. It's my hands being so dirty fills their minds with doubts."”.

questions.prompt: How does Cyril’s pride in nine pockets turn into a problem?
facilitatorNotes: Trace his plan to carry more coins, inability to stand comfortably, and need to unload. Robert’s ship-and-cargo comparison makes the physical limit memorable.
evidence: Throw out some of the cargo

questions.prompt: Why does Anthea succeed in hiring a cart when Cyril could not spend the coins at the inn?
facilitatorNotes: She offers one coin for identification and a definite service; the older man recognizes a spade guinea. The contrast concerns recognition and negotiation, not proof that one sibling always succeeds.
evidence: he said it was a spade guinea

questions.prompt: What makes the hat-shop refusal especially surprising to Anthea? What is her explanation afterward?
facilitatorNotes: The hat is priced in guineas, yet her coins are rejected as no longer current. She suspects dirty hands create an impression of dishonesty; distinguish her inference from a confirmed motive.
evidence: I'm glad," she said, "because it says guineas

days.title: A Purchase Turns Into an Accusation
days.challenge: Compare what the reader knows with what suspicious adults infer.
days.focus: Escalation and dramatic irony
days.context: An innkeeper has accepted one old gold guinea for a carriage ride, but Rochester shopkeepers will not generally accept the children’s magical money. The children are tired and hungry.
days.contentNote: Adults accuse and detain the children and threaten to summon police. Historical gender assumptions govern who is expected to buy horses. No physical injury occurs.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 2; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 101–137; opens “So they chose a humble shop, and the girls bought cotton gloves, the kind at a shilling, b”; closes “"Out of the gravel-pit," said truthful Jane.”.

questions.prompt: What desperate plan gets the children food, and what new problem does it create?
facilitatorNotes: They bite into buns before asking the price or gaining agreement. The baker keeps their coin and refuses change. Discuss both the children’s unfair method and the baker’s response.
evidence: each child had seized three new penny buns

questions.prompt: Why does Robert show the horse dealer two handfuls of gold? Why does this fail to persuade him as Robert expects?
facilitatorNotes: Robert wants to disprove the insult that he has no money. The unexpected wealth instead increases suspicion; more evidence of wealth is not evidence of its source.
evidence: And as for tuppence--what do you call this

questions.prompt: What does Jane’s refusal to leave the boys show, and how does the dealer react?
facilitatorNotes: She insists on shared ownership and shared responsibility. The dealer softens slightly, though he still demands an explanation; courage does not instantly resolve the misunderstanding.
evidence: We won't be let go," said Jane heroically; "not without the boys

days.title: What the Adults Can See
days.challenge: Use two earlier rules to explain apparently contradictory testimony.
days.focus: Resolution and responsibility
days.context: The horse dealer has accused the children of possessing stolen gold and sent for a policeman. Jane has truthfully said they found it in the gravel pit, but the magical explanation sounds impossible to the adults.
days.contentNote: Adults use demeaning period language about mental illness and threaten institutional confinement.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 2; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 138–163; opens “"Next article," said the man.”; closes “ at all a nice man, and, besides, penny buns are seven for sixpence in all really respectable shops.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Martha telling the truth when she says there is no gold in the children’s hands?
facilitatorNotes: Recall the extra wish that servants would not notice magical gifts. The children initially think she is bravely lying; understanding the rule changes their interpretation.
evidence: the servants should never notice any of the fairy gifts

questions.prompt: How does sunset change the balance of evidence at the police station?
facilitatorNotes: The gold disappears before it can be produced. The inspector sees empty pockets, while the constable must explain his accusation. This resolves the immediate danger without proving the fairy story to the adults.
evidence: His pockets were empty. So were the pockets of the others

questions.prompt: What do the next day’s visit and Anthea’s posted stamps suggest about responsibility after a bad experience?
facilitatorNotes: They apologize to the waiting driver and check whether his payment lasted. Anthea also pays for the buns despite disliking the baker’s conduct. Consider whether fairness depends on liking the recipient.
evidence: To pay for the buns

days.title: The Crocuses
days.challenge: Identify the sequence of an early spring arrival and interpret the family metaphor.
days.focus: Small flowers personified as brave and affectionate pioneers.
days.context: Read the poem first as the arrival of flowers, then as a story about children greeting a mother. Vernal means belonging to spring.

excerpt.locator: The Crocuses, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 4–5; complete poem; opens “They heard the South wind sighing”; closes “     Were loving her so much.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the crocuses’ arrival different from that of the other flowers?
facilitatorNotes: They rise while snowdrops sleep and daffodils and daisies have not dared to appear. The comparison presents them as first despite lingering cold.
evidence: The crocuses were first.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem mention a tremor of winter even as the flowers rise?
facilitatorNotes: It shows that their arrival is not easy or entirely safe from cold. Their action seems courageous because they grow despite the shiver.
evidence: Though a tremor of the winter

questions.prompt: Who is the white-haired mother at the end, and how do the flowers show love?
facilitatorNotes: The mother is Earth, earlier described as longing for them. Their colour decorates her head and path, so blooming becomes an act of affection.
evidence: Were loving her so much.

days.title: Dandelions
days.challenge: Follow the same flowers through changing comparisons and connect location with meaning.
days.focus: Attention to ordinary beauty near people who are often overlooked.
days.context: The poem welcomes a familiar flower instead of dismissing it as a weed. Reread the stanza about dusty streets and consider why that location matters.
days.contentNote: The poem expresses the historical speaker’s Christian beliefs. Discuss its imagery and reasoning without requiring agreement with those beliefs.

excerpt.locator: Dandelions, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 24–25; complete poem; opens “Welcome children of the Spring,”; closes “     Of our Father's loving care.”.

questions.prompt: Which details make the dandelions resemble children arriving together?
facilitatorNotes: They are called children, wear green and gold, lift heads and arrive as a joyous troop. The personification makes the greeting warm and social.
evidence: As a bright and joyous troop

questions.prompt: Why does placing the flowers in dusty streets affect their importance?
