facilitatorNotes: They brighten places where lowly children play, bringing beauty beyond carefully tended gardens. Avoid assuming an exact city not named in the poem.
evidence: Where the lowly children play,

questions.prompt: What does the question about clearer vision ask the reader to reconsider?
facilitatorNotes: It asks whether familiar flowers are gifts we fail to value. The speaker’s religious gratitude is one response; readers can discuss attentiveness even with different beliefs.
evidence: Were our vision clearer far,

days.title: A Grain of Sand
days.challenge: Track a shift from a human question to an imagined small object’s reply.
days.focus: Human worth considered through an apparently insignificant grain.
days.context: Read this complete poem in two voices. Its speaking grain gives a devotional argument, not a scientific claim that grains cannot change or break.
days.contentNote: The poem expresses the historical speaker’s Christian beliefs. Discuss its imagery and reasoning without requiring agreement with those beliefs. The ocean image is poetic exaggeration, not a geology lesson.

excerpt.locator: A Grain of Sand, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 3–4; complete poem; opens “Do you see this grain of sand”; closes “  Than the brightest sun or star.”.

questions.prompt: Why does looking at the stars lead the speaker to wonder about human importance?
facilitatorNotes: The vast sky makes a life seem short and small. The opening question sets up the grain’s reply about having a place despite smallness.
evidence: Oh how little seems the span

questions.prompt: What does the grain claim that answers the speaker’s worry?
facilitatorNotes: It says that even a tiny thing was made to have a place and remains within divine sight. Explain the argument within the poem rather than testing its ocean image as a scientific experiment.
evidence: I was made to have a place.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker’s final gesture show a change?
facilitatorNotes: Raising the head contrasts with earlier doubt and suggests confidence. The human has learned from an imagined voice much smaller than the stars.
evidence: Trustingly I raised my head

days.title: God Bless Our Native Land
days.challenge: Distinguish praise for a country from hopes and requests about how it should act.
days.focus: Patriotism expressed as a wish for freedom, peace and care.
days.context: Read as a four-stanza prayer for a country, not a claim that the country already fulfils every ideal named. Discuss the repeated wording and the slight change from bless to help.
days.contentNote: A Christian prayer for a country, with a brief reference to graves of the dead. Treat national ideals as the speaker’s hopes.

excerpt.locator: God Bless Our Native Land, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 23; complete poem; opens “God bless our native land,”; closes “     For truth and righteousness.”.

questions.prompt: Which two ideals are paired in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Truth and liberty establish what the speaker hopes the land will stand for. The wording “may” marks a wish rather than a completed achievement.
evidence: For truth and liberty.

questions.prompt: Why does the third stanza ask for help rather than only blessing?
facilitatorNotes: Its reference to strife recognizes a problem and asks for relief and fuller life. The change complicates simple celebration.
evidence: Bring surcease to her strife,

questions.prompt: How does the final stanza make the national wish more personal?
facilitatorNotes: It names homes and children, moving from the country as a whole to the lives within it. Accept answers about protection or shared responsibility grounded in those words.
evidence: Her homes and children bless,

days.title: The Building
days.challenge: Connect several descriptions of a house with the abstract promises it represents.
days.focus: A lasting spiritual home contrasted with an unstable foundation.
days.context: Agates, carbuncles and rubies are precious stones. Read once to picture the imagined house, then reread for what makes it more than a display of wealth.
days.contentNote: The poem expresses the historical speaker’s Christian beliefs. Discuss its imagery and reasoning without requiring agreement with those beliefs.

excerpt.locator: The Building, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 25–26; complete poem; opens “"Build me a house," said the Master,”; closes “     And never again depart."”.

questions.prompt: Why is shifting sand rejected at the start?
facilitatorNotes: It cannot support a house that survives storms. The foundation introduces the contrast between fragility and lasting security.
evidence: But not on the shifting sand,

questions.prompt: Which promised contents matter beyond the expensive stones?
facilitatorNotes: Love, light and peace are the important contents, with Christ as cornerstone. Readers should connect the beautiful materials to the speaker’s spiritual vision.
evidence: Shall be filled with love and light.

questions.prompt: How can a house be bound with links yet promise freedom?
facilitatorNotes: The binding is described as grace and love rather than imprisonment, while freedom means release from sorrow. The apparent contradiction invites interpretation of the metaphor.
evidence: With the links and cords of love.

days.title: A Quiet Day and a Private Record
days.challenge: Consider how routines communicate values without formal lessons.
days.focus: Privacy, routine, and trust
days.context: Nat has spent his first night at Plumfield. This excerpt begins his first Sunday there, after an omitted chapter introducing more pupils. The Bhaers’ household follows Christian practices.
days.contentNote: Christian prayer, hymns, churchgoing and Sunday observance are part of this family’s historical setting. Discuss what the characters value without requiring the reader to share their religious practice.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 3; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_3; consecutive transcript paragraphs 5–26; opens “THE moment the bell rang next morning Nat flew out of bed, and dressed himself with great ”; closes “nuine happiness, learning the sweet old tunes, and forgetting the hard past in the cheerful present.”.

questions.prompt: How does the morning show that even the youngest child contributes to the household?
facilitatorNotes: Follow the different chores, including Teddy’s napkins and chairs. The tasks vary by ability; shared work is part of belonging rather than reserved for older pupils.
evidence: Even baby Teddy had his small job to do

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Bhaer refuse to show Nat Tommy’s record? What kind of relationship is she trying to build?
facilitatorNotes: She makes the record personal to its owner and uses it for improvement rather than public comparison. Discuss privacy and the difference between encouragement and embarrassment.
evidence: I don't show my records to any but the one to whom each belongs

questions.prompt: What makes the Sunday closet different from ordinary schoolwork or play?
facilitatorNotes: The materials support quiet enjoyment, reflection and writing. Mrs. Bhaer wants the day to be loved rather than merely endured, and Nat’s music offers a concrete example of peaceful pleasure.
evidence: rest from common study and play, yet enjoy quiet pleasures

days.title: T. Bangs and Company
days.challenge: Evaluate an exchange from the viewpoints of both participants.
days.focus: Belonging, ownership, and exchange
days.context: While most pupils take a long Sunday walk, Nat stays behind because of his cough. Tommy shows him Plumfield’s animals and the small businesses the children run.
days.contentNote: The tour mentions rescued puppies that someone had intended to drown; the puppies are safe. Historical practices of marking turtles and keeping wild animals are described, not proposed activities.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 3; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_3; consecutive transcript paragraphs 27–53; opens “When the church-goers came back and dinner was over, every one read, wrote letters home, s”; closes “"T. Bangs & Co."”.

questions.prompt: Why does seeing the animals make Nat feel poor even though he is now fed and housed?
facilitatorNotes: The animals represent personal possessions and participation in the children’s projects. His wish is for something of his own, not a rejection of the help he has received.
evidence: Everybody has got something but me

questions.prompt: How does Tommy’s egg proposal benefit each boy? Is it only a gift?
facilitatorNotes: Nat can earn property and money; Tommy avoids a job he dislikes. Explain why the narrator presents the bargain as both useful to Tommy and friendly to Nat.
evidence: having made a good bargain, and done a friendly thing

questions.prompt: What is the effect of writing “T. Bangs & Co.” over their accounts?
facilitatorNotes: The business-like name gives their small arrangement dignity and makes Nat a partner. His delight in a single egg reflects its meaning as a beginning.
evidence: the proud possessor of one egg opened his account with his friend

days.title: A Boost Over the Hard Places
days.challenge: Distinguish lack of opportunity from lack of ability.
days.focus: Reciprocal learning and encouragement
days.context: Tommy has offered Nat a way to earn eggs. Their tour continues to a private seat in a willow tree, where books and nearby garden plots lead to talk about learning.
days.contentNote: Tommy recalls a former teacher hitting pupils on the head; Plumfield’s contrasting teaching approach is supportive. Appetite-based teasing and historical gender expectations also appear.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 3; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_3; consecutive transcript paragraphs 54–83; opens “Poor Nat found them so fascinating that he was with difficulty persuaded to go and deposit”; closes “e Sunday evening talk, he chose a subject which might have been suggested by the walk in the garden.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Nat’s pleasure at being liked turn into embarrassment when reading is mentioned?
facilitatorNotes: He has not had the time or schooling the others assume. His ability to read music then changes Tommy’s response; compare their different strengths.
evidence: I can read music, anyway

questions.prompt: What does Tommy mean by a teacher giving a “boost,” and how does he provide one himself?
facilitatorNotes: He describes explanations that help over difficulty rather than punishment. He then supports Nat through a page, showing the method in action.
evidence: he sort of explains and gives you a boost over the hard places

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Bhaer discuss Nat’s little garden as seriously as if it fed the whole household?
facilitatorNotes: Taking the project seriously tells Nat his effort matters. The rain-and-earth comparison links practical gardening with a mind newly receiving encouragement.
evidence: discussing crops with him as gravely as if the food for the family depended on the harvest

days.title: The Gardens Inside the Story
days.challenge: Follow an extended allegory and test what each image represents.
days.focus: Allegory and shared responsibility
days.context: After Mr. Bhaer gives Nat a garden plot, the household gathers for an evening talk. Mr. Bhaer tells a gardener’s story whose meaning the children gradually recognize.
days.contentNote: The allegory uses Christian beliefs about God. The adult restricts story-reading and food and the narrator uses body-based teasing; these historical choices can be evaluated critically rather than treated as rules for today.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 3; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_3; consecutive transcript paragraphs 84–120; opens “As he looked about him Nat thought it seemed more like a great family than a school, for t”; closes “le Rob, who kept the tip of her nose for his own particular kisses, and then they trooped up to bed.”.

questions.prompt: Which clues help Demi realize that the little gardens stand for the pupils?
facilitatorNotes: The plants fit familiar interests, and the failed melons and “I forgot” point to Tommy. Connect the servant to the teacher and the plots to children without treating them as identical in every detail.
evidence: You are the man, and we are the little gardens

questions.prompt: Why is it significant that Mrs. Bhaer also names a crop she needs?
facilitatorNotes: Her request for patience puts adults within the same work of improvement. The children see that their actions affect others and that being a teacher does not mean being finished with learning.
evidence: the largest crop of patience I can get

questions.prompt: What does the bargain about books, food, and the cricket ground aim to change? Is there another way to reach that aim?
facilitatorNotes: Identify the teacher’s wish for balance, exercise and generosity. Readers may question the restrictions or teasing while showing they understand the text’s purpose; invite a supported alternative, not automatic agreement.
evidence: the other boys want to play, and you can give them the new ground if you choose

days.title: The Picture by Nat’s Bed
days.challenge: Infer why particular details matter to a listener with a different life history.
days.focus: Storytelling, empathy, and religious setting
days.context: After the household’s Sunday talk, Nat notices a picture of Jesus blessing children near his bed. Demi explains the picture and the stories his grandfather told him.
days.contentNote: The passage explicitly presents Christian beliefs through children and narrator, including a brief reference to Jesus’s death. Discuss these as the characters’ religious understanding; no agreement or personal religious disclosure is required.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 3; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_3; consecutive transcript paragraphs 121–151; opens “The light of the shaded lamp that burned in the nursery shone softly on a picture hanging ”; closes “garden, which was already sown with the best of all seed by the little missionary in the night-gown.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Nat ask whether the pictured children were poor and whether Jesus was rich?
facilitatorNotes: His own experience of homelessness and need makes care for poor people especially important to him. Use the questions and his increased attention to support this inference.
evidence: Were they poor children

questions.prompt: How did Demi’s grandfather turn a book from a plaything into something meaningful to him?
facilitatorNotes: He set a boundary, then showed pictures and told stories repeatedly. The gift of the picture continued the connection; compare forbidding alone with offering a new way to engage.
evidence: showed me the pictures, and told me about them

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Bhaer decide not to interrupt or add her own explanation?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes that the children’s peer conversation is reaching Nat. Her restraint is an active choice to support a helpful connection rather than control every lesson.
evidence: I will not spoil it by a single word

days.title: Robin Hood: two guests in the greenwood (excerpt 1 of 5)
days.challenge: Follow a conversation in which apparently apologetic words change meaning at the final line.
days.focus: Robin uses mock ceremony to challenge rank, but his joke has a target who does not enjoy it.
days.context: Robin has met Sir Richard of the Lea in the forest, heard that the knight will lose his lands to Emmet Priory unless a debt is paid, and brought him to the greenwood tree. Meanwhile Little John has stopped the wealthy Bishop of Hereford on the highway and brought him there too.
days.contentNote: The Bishop is detained and mocked with body-based and religious insults, and Friar Tuck answers him with more. These are the characters’ words; readers can question cruelty in a joke as well as abuses of rank.

excerpt.locator: "Robin Hood aideth a Sorrowful Knight", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “The day was well-nigh gone when they came near to the greenwood tree. ”; ends “he feast ready. Meantime we will show our guests our woodland sports."”.

blocks.text: The day was well-nigh gone when they came near to the greenwood tree. Even at a distance they saw by the number of men that Little John had come back with some guest, but when they came near enough, who should they find but the Lord Bishop of Hereford. The good Bishop was in a fine stew, I wot. Up and down he walked beneath the tree like a fox caught in a hencoop. Behind him were three black friars standing close together in a frightened group, like three black sheep in a tempest. Hitched to the branches of the trees close at hand were six horses, one of them a barb with gay trappings upon which the Bishop was wont to ride, and the others laden with packs of divers shapes and kinds, one of which made Robin's eyes glisten, for it was a box not over large, but heavily bound with bands and ribs of iron.

When the Bishop saw Robin and those with him come into the open he made as though he would have run toward the yeoman, but the fellow that guarded the Bishop and the three friars thrust his quarterstaff in front, so that his lordship was fain to stand back, though with frowning brow and angry speech.

"Stay, my Lord Bishop," cried jolly Robin, in a loud voice, when he saw what had passed; "I will come to thee with all speed, for I would rather see thee than any man in merry England." So saying, he quickened his steps, and soon came to where the Bishop stood fuming.

"How now," quoth the Bishop in a loud and angry voice, when Robin had so come to him, "is this the way that thou and thy band treat one so high in the church as I am? I and these brethren were passing peacefully along the high-road with our packhorses, and a half score of men to guard them, when up comes a great strapping fellow full seven feet high, with fourscore or more men back of him, and calls upon me to stop--me, the Lord Bishop of Hereford, mark thou! Whereupon my armed guards--beshrew them for cowards!--straight ran away. But look ye; not only did this fellow stop me, but he threatened me, saying that Robin Hood would strip me as bare as a winter hedge. Then, beside all this, he called me such vile names as 'fat priest,' 'man-eating bishop,' 'money-gorging usurer,' and what not, as though I were no more than a strolling beggar or tinker. Moreover, when I came here I found a great fat man, a mock priest, that slapped me upon the shoulder as though I, God wot, were a pot-house fellow."

"Marry, come up with a wanion!" cried Friar Tuck, bustling forward and thrusting himself in front of the Bishop; "Marry come up, I say!" and he snapped his fingers under the Bishop's nose, whereat the other started back as though the snap were a clap of thunder. "Mock priest! thou callest me, forsooth! Look ye now, Bishop, I wot I am as holy a man as thou art, and might have been a bishop mine own self, had I not been born under a hedge. I am as learned, too, as thou art, albeit I could never master that vile Latin, my tongue being only shaped for good stout English; yet I tell thee, I can say my 'Paters' and 'Aves' with no more a slip o' the tongue than thou, thou fat man!"

At this the Bishop glared upon the stout Friar like an angry cat, whilst even Sir Richard laughed; only Robin kept a grave face. "Stand back, Tuck," said he, "thou shouldst not beard his lordship's reverence in this wise. Alas! my lord, that thou hast been so ill-treated by my band! I tell thee truly that we greatly reverence thy cloth. Little John, stand forth straightway."

At these words Little John came forward, twisting his face into a whimsical look, as though he would say, "Ha' mercy upon me, good master." Then Robin turned to the Bishop of Hereford and said: "Was this the man who spake so boldly to your lordship?"
"Ay, truly it was the same," said the Bishop; "a naughty fellow, I wot."
"And didst thou, Little John," said Robin, in a sad voice, "call his lordship a fat priest?"
"Ay," said Little John, sorrowfully.
"And a man-eating bishop?"
"Ay," said Little John, more sorrowfully than before.
"And a money-gorging usurer?"
"Ay," said Little John, in so sorrowful a voice that it might have drawn tears from the Dragon of Wentley.
"Alas, that these things should be!" said jolly Robin, turning to the Bishop, "for I have ever found Little John a truthful man."

At this a roar of laughter went up, whereat the blood rushed into the Bishop's face till it was cherry red from crown to chin; but he said nothing, and only swallowed his words, though they well-nigh choked him.

"Nay, my Lord Bishop," said Robin, "we are rough fellows, but I trust not such ill men as thou thinkest, after all. There is not a man here that would harm a hair of thy reverence's head. I know thou art galled by our jesting, but we are all equal here in the greenwood, for there are no bishops nor barons nor earls among us, but only men, so thou must share our life with us whilst thou dost abide here. Come, busk ye, my merry men, and get the feast ready. Meantime we will show our guests our woodland sports."

questions.prompt: How do the animal comparisons show the guests’ different kinds of fear?
facilitatorNotes: The Bishop is restless and angry like a trapped fox; the friars stand close like sheep in a storm. Both are afraid, but their behavior differs.
evidence: like a fox caught in a hencoop

questions.prompt: At what point does Robin’s apparent apology become a joke against the Bishop?
facilitatorNotes: He asks Little John to admit each insult, then says he has always found him truthful. This converts the expected reprimand into an endorsement of the insults.
evidence: I have ever found Little John a truthful man

questions.prompt: How could a reader question Robin’s claim that everyone is equal in the forest?
facilitatorNotes: He rejects formal titles as sources of power, but he controls the guests and leads the group. Invite readers to distinguish equal human worth from equal freedom or authority in this scene.
evidence: we are all equal here in the greenwood

days.title: Robin Hood: laughter gives way to a request (excerpt 2 of 5)
days.challenge: Trace a scene’s changing mood from grievance through entertainment to an uncomfortable question.
days.focus: Shared pleasure does not erase the different responsibilities of the two guests.
days.context: The Bishop and Sir Richard are both Robin’s guests. Sir Richard needs money to save his estate, while the Bishop is angry at being stopped and mocked.
days.contentNote: The scene criticizes one fictional church official; it does not establish a claim about all people of a religion.

excerpt.locator: "Robin Hood aideth a Sorrowful Knight", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “So, whilst some went to kindle the fires for roasting meats, others ra”; ends “ot help this needy brother?" But still the Bishop answered not a word.”.

blocks.text: So, whilst some went to kindle the fires for roasting meats, others ran leaping to get their cudgels and long bows. Then Robin brought forward Sir Richard o' the Lea. "My Lord Bishop," said he, "here is another guest that we have with us this day. I wish that thou mightst know him better, for I and all my men will strive to honor you both at this merrymaking."

"Sir Richard," said the Bishop, in a reproachful tone, "methinks thou and I are companions and fellow sufferers in this den of"--He was about to say "thieves," but he stopped suddenly and looked askance at Robin Hood.
"Speak out, Bishop," quoth Robin, laughing. "We of Sherwood check not an easy flow of words. 'Den of thieves' thou wast about to say."

Quoth the Bishop, "Mayhap that was what I meant to say, Sir Richard; but this I will say, that I saw thee just now laugh at the scurrilous jests of these fellows. It would have been more becoming of thee, methinks, to have checked them with frowns instead of spurring them on by laughter."
"I meant no harm to thee," said Sir Richard; "but a merry jest is a merry jest, and I may truly say I would have laughed at it had it been against mine own self."

But now Robin Hood called upon certain ones of his band who spread soft moss upon the ground and laid deer skins thereon. Then Robin bade his guests be seated, and so they all three sat down, some of the chief men, such as Little John, Will Scarlet, Allan a Dale, and others, stretching themselves upon the ground near by. Then a garland was set up at the far end of the glade, and thereat the bowmen shot, and such shooting was done that day as it would have made one's heart leap to see. And all the while Robin talked so quaintly to the Bishop and the Knight that, the one forgetting his vexation and the other his troubles, they both laughed aloud again and again.

Ten men shot three rounds of arrows each, and although the garland was but three palms' breadth wide, and was full sevenscore yards distant, only two arrows went without the ring. "By Our Lady, good friend," said the Bishop to Robin, "never did I see such shooting in all my life as these men of thine do. But I have heard so oft of thy skill, canst thou not show us a touch of it?"

"Why," quoth Robin, "the light groweth somewhat dim, and things begin to glimmer, ne'ertheless I will try what I can do." So saying he arose from where he sat, then, drawing his dagger, he cut a hazel wand a little greater in girth than a man's thumb, and peeling the bark therefrom, he walked with measured steps fourscore yards distance. There he thrust the staff into the ground and came back to where the others sat, and Allan a Dale handed him his good stout yew bow, which Robin forthwith strung. Then emptying his quiver upon the ground, he searched among the arrows carefully till he had chosen one to his liking. Having so done, he nocked the arrow and stood in position, and all around was so hushed that you might have heard the falling of a leaf. Then he drew the string quickly to his ear, and straightened his bow arm, and ere you could draw a breath loosed the string with a twang. So swift flew the arrow that the eye could not follow it, but a great shout went up from the yeomen when it had sped, and Will Scathelock ran leaping and brought the wand, and lo, the arrow was sticking in the wood which it had cleft. Then all the yeomen shouted again till those about the fires came running, for they were proud of their master's skill, which none could hope to match.

But meantime Robin had set him down again between his guests; then, without giving them time for word of praise, he called upon those of his band who were the most deft at quarterstaff. So they sat and watched the game till the shades of evening fell, and there was no light in which to give stroke or parry.

Then Allan a Dale came forth and tuned his harp, and all was hushed around, and he sang in his wondrous voice songs of love, of war, of glory, and of sadness, and all listened without a movement or a sound. So Allan sang till the great round silver moon gleamed with its clear white light amid the upper tangle of the mazy branches of the trees.

At last two fellows came to say that the feast was ready spread, so Robin, leading his guests with either hand, brought them to where great smoking dishes, that sent savory smells far and near, stood along the white linen cloth spread on the grass. All around was a glare of torches that lit everything up with a red light. Then, straightway sitting down, all fell to with noise and hubbub, the rattling of platters blending with the sound of loud talking and laughter. A long time the feast lasted, but at last all was over, and the bright wine and humming ale passed briskly. Then Robin Hood called aloud for silence, and all was hushed till he spoke.

"I have a story to tell you all, so listen to what I have to say," quoth he; whereupon, without more ado, he told them all about Sir Richard, and how his lands were in pawn. But, as he went on, the Bishop's face, that had erst been smiling and ruddy with merriment, waxed serious, and he put aside the horn of wine he held in his hand, for he knew the story of Sir Richard, and his heart sank within him with grim forebodings. Then, when Robin Hood had done, he turned to the Bishop of Hereford. "Now, my Lord Bishop," said he, "dost thou not think this is ill done of any one, much more of a churchman, who should live in humbleness and charity?"
To this the Bishop answered not a word, but looked upon the ground with moody eyes.
Quoth Robin, "Now, thou art the richest bishop in all England; canst thou not help this needy brother?" But still the Bishop answered not a word.

questions.prompt: Why does the Bishop object to Sir Richard’s laughter?
facilitatorNotes: He expected another guest to show solidarity rather than encourage the mockery. Sir Richard answers that he would also laugh at himself; discuss whether that answer addresses the Bishop’s hurt.
evidence: checked them with frowns instead of spurring them on by laughter

questions.prompt: How do the sports and music affect both guests?
facilitatorNotes: One forgets his anger and the other his troubles; the shared entertainment briefly changes their mood without solving the underlying problems.
evidence: the one forgetting his vexation and the other his troubles

questions.prompt: What makes the Bishop’s silence at the end meaningful?
facilitatorNotes: Robin asks directly whether a wealthy religious leader can help someone in need. The absence of an answer contrasts with earlier loud complaints and invites questions about reluctance.
evidence: canst thou not help this needy brother?

questions.prompt: After his remarkable shot, why does Robin sit down and start the quarterstaff game “without giving them time for word of praise”?
facilitatorNotes: He lets the shot speak for itself and moves attention back to the band and his guests. Readers may see modesty, showmanship that knows when to stop, or a host keeping the evening moving toward his real purpose.
evidence: without giving them time for word of praise

days.title: Robin Hood: reading the list of goods (excerpt 3 of 5)
days.challenge: Track categories in an inventory and infer the rule behind different decisions.
days.focus: The inventory makes Robin’s idea of justice visible—and open to challenge.
days.context: After the Bishop gives no answer to a request for help, Robin orders his pack horses brought forward. A written list identifies the goods and their owners.
days.contentNote: The band forcibly opens a box and takes control of property. The narrator’s approval does not require readers to agree that Robin may decide other people’s rights.

excerpt.locator: "Robin Hood aideth a Sorrowful Knight", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “Then Robin turned to Little John, and quoth he, "Go thou and Will Stut”; ends “ forfeits from certain estates belonging to the Bishopric of Hereford.”.

blocks.text: Then Robin turned to Little John, and quoth he, "Go thou and Will Stutely and bring forth those five pack-horses yonder." Whereupon the two yeomen did as they were bidden, those about the cloth making room on the green, where the light was brightest, for the five horses which Little John and Will Stutely presently led forward.
"Who hath the score of the goods?" asked Robin Hood, looking at the Black Friars.
Then up spake the smallest of all, in a trembling voice,--an old man he was, with a gentle, wrinkled face. "That have I; but, I pray thee, harm me not."

"Nay," quoth Robin, "I have never harmed harmless man yet; but give it to me, good father." So the old man did as he was bidden, and handed Robin the tablet on which was marked down the account of the various packages upon the horses. This Robin handed to Will Scarlet, bidding him to read the same. So Will Scarlet, lifting his voice that all might hear, began:--
"Three bales of silk to Quentin, the mercer at Ancaster."
"That we touch not," quoth Robin, "for this Quentin is an honest fellow, who hath risen by his own thrift." So the bales of silk were laid aside without being opened.
"One bale of silk velvet for the Abbey of Beaumont."

"What do these priests want of silk velvet?" quoth Robin. "Nevertheless, though they need it not, I will not take all from them. Measure it off into three lots, one to be sold for charity, one for us, and one for the abbey." So this, too, was done as Robin Hood bade.
"Twoscore of great wax candles for the Chapel of Saint Thomas."

"That belongeth fairly to the chapel," quoth Robin, "so lay it to one side. Far be it from us to take from the blessed Saint Thomas that which belongeth to him." So this, also, was done according to Robin's bidding, and the candles were laid to one side, along with honest Quentin's unopened bales of silk. So the list was gone through with, and the goods adjudged according to what Robin thought most fit. Some things were laid aside untouched, and many were opened and divided into three equal parts, for charity, for themselves, and for the owners. And now all the ground in the torchlight was covered over with silks and velvets and cloths of gold and cases of rich wines, and so they came to the last line upon the tablet,--"A box belonging to the Lord Bishop of Hereford."
At these words the Bishop shook as with a chill, and the box was set upon the ground.
"My Lord Bishop, hast thou the key of this box?" asked Robin.
The Bishop shook his head.

"Go, Will Scarlet," said Robin, "thou art the strongest man here--bring a sword straightway, and cut this box open, if thou canst." Then up rose Will Scarlet and left them, coming back in a short time, bearing a great two-handed sword. Thrice he smote that strong, iron-bound box, and at the third blow it burst open and a great heap of gold came rolling forth, gleaming red in the light of the torches. At this sight a murmur went all around among the band, like the sound of the wind in distant trees; but no man came forward nor touched the money.
Quoth Robin, "Thou, Will Scarlet, thou, Allan a Dale, and thou, Little John, count it over."

A long time it took to count all the money, and when it had been duly scored up, Will Scarlet called out that there were fifteen hundred golden pounds in all. But in among the gold they found a paper, and this Will Scarlet read in a loud voice, and all heard that this money was the rental and fines and forfeits from certain estates belonging to the Bishopric of Hereford.

questions.prompt: Why does Robin leave Quentin’s silk untouched?
facilitatorNotes: He calls Quentin honest and credits his thrift. The decision depends on Robin’s judgment of the owner, not simply on the luxury or value of the item.
evidence: an honest fellow, who hath risen by his own thrift

questions.prompt: What three destinations does Robin choose for some of the goods?
facilitatorNotes: One part goes to charity, one to the band, and one stays with the owner. Ask students to notice that his group benefits too, rather than describing the action as only giving to the poor.
evidence: divided into three equal parts, for charity, for themselves, and for the owners

questions.prompt: What new information does the paper inside the box supply beyond the sight of gold?
facilitatorNotes: It identifies the money as estate rents, fines, and forfeits. A record can explain origin in a way glittering coins alone cannot.
evidence: the rental and fines and forfeits from certain estates belonging to the Bishopric of Hereford

days.title: Robin Hood: a gift or a loan? (excerpt 4 of 5)
days.challenge: Read a short moral disagreement closely, distinguishing gratitude from agreement.
days.focus: Sir Richard accepts help on terms that preserve his promise and responsibility.
days.context: The box contains fifteen hundred pounds. Robin proposes three equal portions and wants the charitable portion to help Sir Richard save his home.
days.contentNote: This passage discusses money obtained under pressure from another character. Distinguish the generosity of helping from questions about where the help comes from.

excerpt.locator: "Robin Hood aideth a Sorrowful Knight", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “"My Lord Bishop," said Robin Hood, "I will not strip thee, as Little J”; ends “lady will wax anxious if I come not home; so I crave leave to depart."”.

blocks.text: "My Lord Bishop," said Robin Hood, "I will not strip thee, as Little John said, like a winter hedge, for thou shalt take back one third of thy money. One third of it thou canst well spare to us for thy entertainment and that of thy train, for thou art very rich; one third of it thou canst better spare for charity, for Bishop, I hear that thou art a hard master to those beneath thee and a close hoarder of gains that thou couldst better and with more credit to thyself give to charity than spend upon thy own likings."
At this the Bishop looked up, but he could say never a word; yet he was thankful to keep some of his wealth.

Then Robin turned to Sir Richard of the Lea, and quoth he, "Now, Sir Richard, the church seemed like to despoil thee, therefore some of the overplus ot church gains may well be used in aiding thee. Thou shalt take that five hundred pounds laid aside for people more in need than the Bishop is, and shalt pay thy debts to Emmet therewith."

Sir Richard looked at Robin until something arose in his eyes that made all the lights and the faces blur together. At last he said, "I thank thee, friend, from my heart, for what thou doest for me; yet, think not ill if I cannot take thy gift freely. But this I will do: I will take the money and pay my debts, and in a year and a day hence will return it safe either to thee or to the Lord Bishop of Hereford. For this I pledge my most solemn knightly word. I feel free to borrow, for I know no man that should be more bound to aid me than one so high in that church that hath driven such a hard bargain with me."

"Truly, Sir Knight," quoth Robin, "I do not understand those fine scruples that weigh with those of thy kind; but, nevertheless, it shall all be as thou dost wish. But thou hadst best bring the money to me at the end of the year, for mayhap I may make better use of it than the Bishop." Thereupon, turning to those near him, he gave his orders, and five hundred pounds were counted out and tied up in a leathern bag for Sir Richard. The rest of the treasure was divided, and part taken to the treasure-house of the band, and part put by with the other things for the Bishop.
Then Sir Richard arose. "I cannot stay later, good friends," said he, "for my lady will wax anxious if I come not home; so I crave leave to depart."

questions.prompt: How does Robin justify the three-way division of the money?
facilitatorNotes: He says the Bishop is wealthy, can spare a share for hospitality, and should give another to charity. Invite readers to examine those reasons rather than treating them as proof that taking the money is fair.
evidence: thou shalt take back one third of thy money

questions.prompt: Why does Sir Richard promise repayment when Robin offers the money freely?
facilitatorNotes: He is grateful but does not feel able to accept it as an outright gift. His stated willingness to borrow lets him receive aid while keeping an obligation to repay.
evidence: I feel free to borrow

questions.prompt: How does Robin respond to a value he does not fully understand?
facilitatorNotes: He admits he does not understand the knight’s scruples but agrees to the requested terms. That response can be read as respectful accommodation even amid disagreement.
evidence: it shall all be as thou dost wish

days.title: Robin Hood: kindness beyond coins (excerpt 5 of 5)
days.challenge: Notice a repeated speaking pattern and contrast visible gratitude with concealed resentment.
days.focus: Different kinds of help create different kinds of obligation.
days.context: Sir Richard has accepted a loan and is ready to return home. Robin’s companions consider what else might help him regain security and dignity.
days.contentNote: The Bishop is kept in the forest for three days against his will. The passage’s cheerful account of his stay does not make that loss of freedom disappear.

excerpt.locator: "Robin Hood aideth a Sorrowful Knight", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “Then Robin Hood and all his merry men arose, and Robin said, "We canno”; ends “d his debts at Emmet Priory, and likewise in due season to Robin Hood.”.

blocks.text: Then Robin Hood and all his merry men arose, and Robin said, "We cannot let thee go hence unattended, Sir Richard."

Then up spake Little John: "Good master, let me choose a score of stout fellows from the band, and let us arm ourselves in a seemly manner and so serve as retainers to Sir Richard till he can get others in our stead."
"Thou hast spoken well, Little John, and it shall be done," said Robin.
Then up spake Will Scarlet: "Let us give him a golden chain to hang about his neck, such as befits one of his blood, and also golden spurs to wear at his heels."
Then Robin Hood said, "Thou hast spoken well, Will Scarlet, and it shall be done."
Then up spake Will Stutely: "Let us give him yon bale of rich velvet and yon roll of cloth of gold to take home to his noble lady wife as a present from Robin Hood and his merry men all."
At this all clapped their hands for joy, and Robin said: "Thou hast well spoken, Will Stutely, and it shall be done."

Then Sir Richard o' the Lea looked all around and strove to speak, but could scarcely do so for the feelings that choked him; at last he said in a husky, trembling voice, "Ye shall all see, good friends, that Sir Richard o' the Lea will ever remember your kindness this day. And if ye be at any time in dire need or trouble, come to me and my lady, and the walls of Castle Lea shall be battered down ere harm shall befall you. I"--He could say nothing further, but turned hastily away.

But now Little John and nineteen stout fellows, whom he had chosen for his band, came forth all ready for the journey. Each man wore upon his breast a coat of linked mail, and on his head a cap of steel, and at his side a good stout sword. A gallant show they made as they stood all in a row. Then Robin came and threw a chain of gold about Sir Richard's neck, and Will Scarlet knelt and buckled the golden spurs upon his heel; and now Little John led forward Sir Richard's horse, and the Knight mounted. He looked down at Robin for a little time, then of a sudden stooped and kissed his cheek. All the forest glades rang with the shout that went up as the Knight and the yeomen marched off through the woodland with glare of torches and gleam of steel, and so were gone.
Then up spake the Bishop of Hereford in a mournful voice: "I, too, must be jogging, good fellow, for the night waxes late."

But Robin laid his hand upon the Bishop's arm and stayed him. "Be not so hasty, Lord Bishop," said he. "Three days hence Sir Richard must pay his debts to Emmet; until that time thou must be content to abide with me lest thou breed trouble for the Knight. I promise thee that thou shalt have great sport, for I know that thou art fond of hunting the dun deer. Lay by thy mantle of melancholy, and strive to lead a joyous yeoman life for three stout days. I promise thee thou shalt be sorry to go when the time has come."

So the Bishop and his train abided with Robin for three days, and much sport his lordship had in that time, so that, as Robin had said, when the time had come for him to go he was sorry to leave the greenwood. At the end of three days Robin set him free, and sent him forth from the forest with a guard of yeomen to keep freebooters from taking what was left of the packs and bundles.
But, as the Bishop rode away, he vowed within himself that he would sometime make Robin rue the day that he stopped him in Sherwood.
But now we shall follow Sir Richard; so listen, and you shall hear what befell him, and how he paid his debts at Emmet Priory, and likewise in due season to Robin Hood.

questions.prompt: What do Little John, Will Scarlet, and Will Stutely each add to the plan?
facilitatorNotes: Little John offers a temporary escort, Scarlet suggests a chain and spurs, and Stutely proposes gifts for the knight’s wife. Their ideas address safety, social standing, and family.
evidence: Let us give him yon bale of rich velvet and yon roll of cloth of gold

questions.prompt: How does the repeated “it shall be done” affect the scene?
facilitatorNotes: Robin turns each companion’s suggestion into shared action. The repetition lets generosity build through several voices rather than making him the only giver.
evidence: it shall be done

questions.prompt: Why does the ending prevent a completely happy conclusion?
facilitatorNotes: The knight expresses lasting gratitude, but the Bishop privately plans revenge after being released. The same event has produced friendship and a new grievance.
evidence: he vowed within himself that he would sometime make Robin rue the day

evidence: Money, money, money!

facilitatorNotes: The narrator reveals he is reminded of Aunt Kate and is troubled by the resemblance; he also recognizes that many people feel this way. His private reason differs from Dorry’s guess.

days.focus: An invented celebration becomes a shared plan.
days.context: Their tutor has departed and a new one has not yet arrived. Uncle George proposes an indoor celebration while stormy weather keeps the family close to home.

questions.prompt: What does Uncle mean by having fun “between times”?
facilitatorNotes: He means the interval between the tutors’ departure and arrival, not a time on the clock. Don’s question prompts the explanation.
evidence: between the going of our good friend Dr. Lane and the coming

questions.prompt: How does the list of activities explain a “house-picnic”?
facilitatorNotes: The whole house becomes a place for games, stories, music, candy-pulling, and performance. It keeps the variety of a picnic while moving indoors.
evidence: story-telling in odd corners

questions.prompt: Why does Dorry especially want to invite the Danbys?
facilitatorNotes: They seldom have a chance to attend a party. She considers who would benefit from being included, even though the family is a large part of the guest list.

questions.prompt: Why is Fandy’s defeat different from the others’?
facilitatorNotes: Deliberate jokes fail, but his little sister’s worried cry makes him laugh. He then goes to comfort her, mixing the game with a real relationship.

days.title: Donald and Dorothy: the thank-you game (excerpt)
days.challenge: Test a set of rules against several outcomes.
days.focus: Suspense and fairness in a playful exchange.
days.context: Later at the party, two disguised performers bring a bag of gifts. Even Donald and Dorothy have not been told how this game will work.
days.contentNote: The narrator assumes certain gifts suit boys and others girls. Readers need not adopt those expectations; the children trade according to what they want.

questions.prompt: Why do players disguise their voices when they say thank you?
facilitatorNotes: If the blindfolded gnome identifies them correctly, they must return the unopened gift; a wrong guess lets them keep it.
evidence: if he guesses your name you must put the gift back

questions.prompt: What rule eventually allows everyone to receive a parcel?
facilitatorNotes: Children who already have a gift cannot try again, so unsuccessful players get more chances. It balances the initial uneven results.
evidence: would not suffer those who had parcels to try again

questions.prompt: What makes the guests’ claim after Uncle’s disguise comes off funny?
facilitatorNotes: They all immediately claim they knew his identity, although they had eagerly treated it as a mystery. Accept recognition of exaggeration or hindsight.
evidence: Instantly one and all discovered that they had known all along it was he.

days.title: The Insect Folk — Pretty Katydids: A Make-Believe Argument
days.challenge: Separate a playful invented conversation from the explanation of the sound producing it.
days.focus: A memorable name built from the way people interpret an insect’s call.
days.context: Read the opening “did” and “didn’t” lines as an argument, then reread the narrator’s correction. Morley uses larvae broadly for young insects; in current terminology a young katydid is a nymph.
days.contentNote: This historical account makes broad claims about which katydids sing; treat its portrait as the narrator’s example rather than a rule for every species.
