questions.prompt: What does little Nell need clarified after the opening joke?
facilitatorNotes: The insect does not speak those words; people hear a resemblance and pretend. The correction makes the boundary between observation and imagination explicit.
evidence: we make believe she says it.

questions.prompt: Where does the narrator locate the sound-making parts?
facilitatorNotes: On the male’s wings, where small membranes vibrate. The explanation shifts attention from an imagined speaking mouth to wing movement.
evidence: little membranes that vibrate

questions.prompt: Why can the group hear a katydid but still have trouble seeing it?
facilitatorNotes: Green colour among green leaves makes it difficult to pick out, although the call can be noticeable. Different senses supply different kinds of evidence.
evidence: It is not easy to find a katydid among the green leaves.

days.title: The Insect Folk — Pretty Katydids: Delicate but Useful
days.challenge: Connect apparently fragile body parts with the actions they make possible.
days.focus: The limits of judging usefulness from appearance alone.
days.context: Charlie has brought a katydid for the group to observe before releasing it. Isinglass was a name for thin, translucent material. Read once to picture the insect, then reread for the jobs its parts perform.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — Pretty Katydids: Delicate but Useful; source transcription lines 2919–2984; opens “See this dainty katydid that Charlie has caught for us.”; closes “Happy katydids.”.

questions.prompt: Which observation supports calling the feelers sensitive?
facilitatorNotes: The insect starts away quickly when one is touched. The passage provides an observed response after making the description.
evidence: It quickly starts away when we touch one of the feelers.

questions.prompt: What assumption about the inner wings does the passage correct?
facilitatorNotes: They look too delicate to work, yet the katydid flies well. Appearance alone would give the wrong impression of function.
evidence: They look too delicate for use

questions.prompt: What does the narrator’s farewell show about the group’s relation to the insect?
facilitatorNotes: Thanks and concern about troubling it treat the insect as a temporary guest. The farewell also shifts from close examination to allowing it to depart.
evidence: we hope we have not troubled you too much.

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Cheery Cricket People: A Fireside Friend
days.challenge: Notice how affectionate language frames physical descriptions and movements.
days.focus: An animal made familiar through sound, setting and personification.
days.context: The opening cricket is near a fireplace, called a hearth. Dickens’s story is mentioned as part of the author’s enthusiasm; no other book is needed to understand this excerpt. Reread for the movement from indoors to outdoors.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Cheery Cricket People: A Fireside Friend; source transcription lines 3048–3125; opens “Chirp! chirp!”; closes “When we stir,--pop! they are back out of sight.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator feel closer to crickets than to grasshoppers?
facilitatorNotes: An occasional cricket shares the house and its familiar sound, whereas the other insects are associated with outdoors. The narrator also acknowledges that crickets live outdoors.
evidence: our very own little friends

questions.prompt: How does the box-cover comparison help distinguish the cricket’s back?
facilitatorNotes: It is flat above and bends down at the sides, rather than forming a peaked roof. Readers can picture the difference using the verbal description.
evidence: flat on top and bent down at the sides like a box cover.

questions.prompt: What do peeping, inquisitive and rascals add beyond facts about movement?
facilitatorNotes: They suggest curious personalities and affectionate amusement. These are the narrator’s interpretations; the visible actions are emerging, running and disappearing.
evidence: an inquisitive little head looking around a corner.

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Water Boatman: A Silver Dress of Air
days.challenge: Follow a causal explanation that uses a plant comparison to explain an insect’s appearance.
days.focus: A changed appearance explained without assuming a changed body colour.
days.context: A water boatman has just come to the surface after looking silvery underwater. Read slowly twice: first trace what Nell notices, then explain what the hairs and air contribute.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Water Boatman: A Silver Dress of Air; source transcription lines 3520–3540; opens “Now, Mr. Water Boatman, we are going to have a good look at you.”; closes “Our water boatman breathes this air that surrounds him.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Nell think the insect has stopped looking silver?
facilitatorNotes: It is now above the water, where she sees the black and grey body rather than the silvery appearance associated with the underwater air layer.
evidence: it is now on top of the water.

questions.prompt: How does the leaf comparison help explain the insect’s underwater covering?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says fine hairs on both surfaces hold air. A familiar shining leaf is used as an analogy for a less familiar insect surface.
evidence: the hairs on the bugs serve the same purpose as those on the leaves;

questions.prompt: Why is calling the air layer a silver dress helpful but incomplete?
facilitatorNotes: Dress suggests a surrounding covering and shiny appearance, but the final sentence gives a function beyond decoration: the insect breathes the air.
evidence: Our water boatman breathes this air that surrounds him.

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Airy Water Striders: Meeting the Water Striders
days.challenge: Examine a short scene twice, shifting between human and imagined insect viewpoints.
days.focus: Quiet observation and the playful reversal of who seems strange.
days.context: Water striders move across the surface of a pond. Read the scene aloud, then pause over its dimples, quick movements and final reversal; the questions invite careful rereading of this short excerpt.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Airy Water Striders: Meeting the Water Striders; source transcription lines 3832–3861; opens “Then there are the water striders.”; closes “Eat? Why, insects, of course. And as to behavior, they may well wonder more at ours than we at theirs.”.

questions.prompt: Which details make the feet seem fairy-like even though the scene describes a real pond?
facilitatorNotes: The insects move over water as though on land and make small dimples when still. The language expresses wonder at the movement rather than claiming actual magic.
evidence: as though you were on dry land.

questions.prompt: What change in the observers’ behaviour may make the insects easier to see?
facilitatorNotes: Remaining quiet may reduce the insects’ darting. The passage suggests that observing involves adjusting the observer, not only describing the subject.
evidence: If we keep very quiet,

questions.prompt: How does the final sentence reverse the group’s question about strange behaviour?
facilitatorNotes: It imagines insects wondering about humans in return. Readers can discuss how people approaching and trying to catch them might seem from that imagined viewpoint.
evidence: they may well wonder more at ours than we at theirs.

days.title: Letters That Almost Tell
days.challenge: Trace several different causes leading to the same missed communication.
days.focus: Cause and narrator’s humor
days.context: Several magical wishes have caused trouble. A rainy day keeps the children indoors; all mean to tell their absent mother about the Sand-fairy. This begins a new episode after omitted adventures.
days.contentNote: The baby accidentally pokes Robert’s leg with a toy wire. The characters’ spelling and grammar are retained as part of their letters.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 4; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 1–17; opens “The next day was very wet--too wet to go out, and far too wet to think of disturbing a San”; closes “ything about the Psammead. I do not know why. And they do not know why. But I daresay you can guess.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the ink accident more complicated than saying Robert chose to spoil Anthea’s work?
facilitatorNotes: Follow the timing: open desk, lifted ink, the baby’s toy wire, startled movement. Separate responsibility for repair from an intention to cause harm.
evidence: without anyone's meaning to do it the secret drawer was flooded with ink

questions.prompt: Why does the one letter actually sent still fail to tell Mother what happened?
facilitatorNotes: Jane spends her time on spelling Psammead instead of explaining it in other words. Her postscript hints at wishes but lacks the information Mother would need.
evidence: We found a strange thing, but it is nearly post-time

questions.prompt: How does Robert’s chosen present undermine what he expected from choosing freely?
facilitatorNotes: He expects the animals pictured on the box and receives an educational puzzle. Explain the narrator’s joke about children accidentally choosing something instructive.
evidence: When he got it home it was a Sunday puzzle about ancient Nineveh

days.title: Anthea Asks for Advice
days.challenge: Hear what a character says while noticing qualifications and contradictions.
days.focus: Advice, kindness, and limits
days.context: After rain and an outing have interrupted wishing, Anthea rises early to speak privately with the Psammead. She wants their next wish to work out better.
days.contentNote: A brief cautionary tale implies a boy’s fatal fall when magical wings become stone.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 4; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 18–52; opens “The day after Uncle Richard had behaved so handsomely was a very hot day indeed. The peopl”; closes “It jumped off her lap--dug frantically, and vanished.”.

questions.prompt: What does the unusual clock comparison tell us about Anthea’s familiarity with her home?
facilitatorNotes: The clock strikes incorrectly, but she knows how to interpret it, like a known language. It is useful to her because of learned knowledge, not because eleven actually means five on clocks generally.
evidence: And Anthea knew the clock language

questions.prompt: Why does Anthea choose to admit the children’s mistakes privately? How does she also show care for the fairy?
facilitatorNotes: She can call herself silly without embarrassing the others. She covers the cold fairy and offers her lap; humility and practical kindness accompany the request.
evidence: It's one thing to say you're silly, and quite another to say that other people are

questions.prompt: Does the Psammead keep its rule that it never gives advice? What useful caution nevertheless emerges?
facilitatorNotes: It offers “think before you speak” and warns against being aloft at sunset, then dismisses its own general advice as unoriginal. Let readers explain the contradiction and identify the concrete risk.
evidence: Only, take care you aren't flying high at sunset

days.title: A Living Map Below
days.challenge: Track how a new power changes a familiar ethical question.
days.focus: Sensory description and reasoning
days.context: Anthea has privately learned to avoid being high in the air at sunset. The siblings now agree to take turns suggesting wishes, with the others allowed to object.
days.contentNote: The children take fruit without permission and a farmer approaches carrying a stick. The text also alludes to alcohol-related frightening visions; no assault occurs.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 4; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 53–80; opens “Anthea was late for breakfast. It was Robert who quietly poured a spoonful of molasses dow”; closes “ut, on the other hand, if you are in trouble, there is nothing like wings for getting you out of it.”.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison with a “beautiful live map” convey that simply saying they fly high would miss?
facilitatorNotes: Identify the moving woods and real fields seen from above. The narrator admits the experience is hard to describe, then uses a familiar object to help the reader imagine it.
evidence: a beautiful live map

questions.prompt: How does Jane try to justify eating the plums? Is having wings enough to make her reasoning convincing?
facilitatorNotes: She argues that winged children count as birds and birds break rules without punishment. Ask whether changed ability removes responsibility; readers may challenge the comparison with details from the scene.
evidence: If you've got wings you're a bird

questions.prompt: What does Anthea do when she becomes uncertain that the plums were theirs to take?
facilitatorNotes: She acknowledges doubt, pays with her keepsake coin and tries to reassure the frightened grower. Her action differs from merely finding a clever justification after taking food.
evidence: we thought it wasn't stealing, but now I am not so sure

days.title: The Necessaries of Life
days.challenge: Distinguish reasons, excuses, and incomplete information.
days.focus: Argument and narrator commentary
days.context: The children’s wings frighten people who might otherwise sell them food. Hungry and tired, they settle on a church tower and see food through the nearby clergyman’s window.
days.contentNote: The children take food without permission, and a dog threatens them. Cyril misquotes a historical saying to suit himself.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 4; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 81–107; opens “This was the case in the matter of the fierce dog who sprang out at them when they had fol”; closes “ck themselves. The man appeared to live in Rochester, which would not be much out of their way home.”.

questions.prompt: How does Cyril use war and storybook heroes to defend taking food? What is missing from those comparisons?
facilitatorNotes: He treats their difficulty as wartime necessity and himself as a protective hero. They have not asked this owner; being hungry does not establish that the owner would refuse.
evidence: if the country you're in won't sell provisions, you take them

questions.prompt: What does Anthea’s letter reveal about both her conscience and her fear?
facilitatorNotes: She wants to explain, pay, and limit the food, yet avoids asking permission because refusal is possible. Reread the letter for both concerns rather than labeling her wholly honest or dishonest.
evidence: We are afraid to ask you for fear you should say 'No

questions.prompt: What information does the narrator supply that the children do not have? How does it affect their claim of a fair exchange?
facilitatorNotes: They underestimate the food’s value. Leaving money shows intention, but does not establish sufficient payment or consent; the narrator complicates their confident explanation.
evidence: cannot be bought in the stores for half-a-crown

days.title: The Door They Never Tried
days.challenge: Notice how comfort delays attention to an already established deadline.
days.focus: Suspense and consequences
days.context: The winged children have taken food and a soda-water syphon from a clergyman’s larder, leaving a letter and money. They eat on the church tower, still needing to get home before their wings vanish.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 4; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 108–123; opens “Everything was carried up to the top of the tower, and laid down on a sheet of kitchen pap”; closes “ be better employed in making up your minds what you would have done if you had been in their place.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Cyril insist the paper is necessary, and what does his word “germans” reveal?
facilitatorNotes: He tries to apply something overheard about germs, but confuses the word and overstates his knowledge. Separate a sensible concern for clean food from an imperfect explanation.
evidence: people got diseases from germans in rain-water

questions.prompt: How does the sunset paragraph change the wings from a comfort into a source of danger?
facilitatorNotes: Soft wings help them sleep through the deadline, then vanish like removed blankets. Trace the falling shadows and increasing chill to show how setting supplies the turning point.
evidence: the sun had set, and the wings were gone

questions.prompt: Why had they ignored the tower door earlier? How does the last discovery change what they must do next?
facilitatorNotes: Flight made an ordinary exit seem unimportant. The locked door removes their assumed route home; ask for a grounded prediction using their location, darkness and the syphon.
evidence: when you have wings and can explore the whole sky, doors seem hardly worth exploring

days.title: The Wanderer and the Night-Flowers
days.challenge: Compare two voices with different ideas of what makes beauty useful or worthwhile.
days.focus: A reply that challenges the assumption that unseen beauty is wasted.
days.context: The wanderer speaks for five stanzas, and the flowers answer. Read in two voices and pause at the beginning of their reply.
days.contentNote: The flowers’ reply uses religious images of gratitude and hope directed toward heaven.

excerpt.locator: The Wanderer and the Night-Flowers; source transcription lines 61845–61885; opens ““Call back your odours, lovely flowers!”; closes “      Looking alone to heaven!””.

questions.prompt: Why does the wanderer tell the flowers to close?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker assumes they are lonely and deprived of the daylight’s birds, bees and children. The questions reveal those assumptions before the flowers answer.
evidence: Why watch ye here alone?

questions.prompt: How do the flowers redefine the value of their perfume?
facilitatorNotes: They offer it even when no person is nearby. Their value does not depend only on being watched or praised.
evidence: Call it not wasted, the scent we lend

questions.prompt: What kind of hope do the flowers represent in the final stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Hope that can grow in sorrow or darkness rather than only in easy times. The night-blooming pattern supports that comparison.
evidence: That spring through the gloom of the darkest hours

days.title: Night-Blowing Flowers
days.challenge: Follow shifts from a description of flowers to comparisons with private thoughts and prayer.
days.focus: Quiet beauty and feeling that appear away from crowds.
days.context: Some flowers open or become fragrant at night. The poem uses that natural pattern to imagine inward experiences.
days.contentNote: The last stanza includes grief and private prayer as part of the speaker’s comparison.

excerpt.locator: Night-Blowing Flowers; source transcription lines 61812–61842; opens “Children of night! unfolding meekly, slowly,”; closes “            In silent hours to fill.”.

questions.prompt: How do the opening verbs affect the pace of reading?
facilitatorNotes: Unfolding meekly and slowly invites a gentle, deliberate voice. It contrasts with dramatic or sudden blooming.
evidence: Children of night! unfolding meekly, slowly,

questions.prompt: What does the poem compare with flowers that keep their sweetness hidden?
facilitatorNotes: A loving heart keeps private thoughts away from a crowd and discloses them in quiet. Encourage readers to identify the comparison rather than assume all private feelings are identical.
evidence: So doth love’s dreaming heart

questions.prompt: Why are hidden streams a suitable sound near these flowers?
facilitatorNotes: Their faint sounds match the flowers’ subtle fragrance and the poem’s private prayer image. Neither demands the attention of a loud daytime celebration.
evidence: Rising from hidden streams, when all is still.

days.title: Fairy Song
days.challenge: Notice how unanswered questions become a firm answer through repeated ending words.
days.focus: An imagined departure from a woodland once filled with wonder.
days.context: Two stanzas ask whether the fairies will return; two give their reply. Read in two voices and listen for how “Never more” changes from question to answer.

excerpt.locator: Fairy Song; source transcription lines 63089–63117; opens “Have ye left the greenwood lone,”; closes “              Never more!””.

questions.prompt: Which sounds does the questioner hope to hear again?
facilitatorNotes: Voices from flowers and faint flute-like notes in moonlight stand for the lost fairy presence.
evidence: Voices from the folded flowers,

questions.prompt: What reason do the fairies give for leaving?
facilitatorNotes: They say unhallowed steps have entered their green places. The text does not name the intruders, so avoid inventing a specific event.
evidence: Since unhallow’d steps have been,

questions.prompt: How does the recurring “Never more” shape the mood?
facilitatorNotes: It turns longing into finality as the answer confirms the questioner’s fear. Accept readings of sorrow, mystery or warning grounded in that repeated closure.
evidence: Never more!

days.title: Echo-Song
days.challenge: Connect an audible echo to a chain of remembered thoughts, while hearing repeated lines.
days.focus: How one small sound can awaken many inward responses.
days.context: Read the refrain lines together after one reader speaks the longer lines. The footnote reference number after the last line is edition apparatus and is omitted; the full poem remains.

excerpt.locator: Echo-Song; source transcription lines 61888–61913; opens “In thy cavern-hall,”; closes “    --Strange, sweet Echo! even like thee replying.”.

questions.prompt: What first wakes Echo from silence?
facilitatorNotes: One soft note from a shepherd’s horn starts the response. The contrast between a single note and the many replies prepares the later thought comparison.
evidence: From the shepherd’s horn,

questions.prompt: Why are the hills’ sounds described as many notes of one life?
facilitatorNotes: The echoes seem like separate sister-voices but grow from a common original sound. Readers can connect repetition with unity.
evidence: With a thousand notes, of _one_ life telling!

questions.prompt: What changes when the final stanza addresses Echo in the speaker’s heart?
facilitatorNotes: The poem moves from a landscape’s sound to memories or thoughts stirred by a gentle tone. The echo becomes a model for inward association.
evidence: Calls a thousand forth, like thee replying!

days.title: The Summer’s Call
days.challenge: Use recurring invitations to organize a dense sequence of sights, sounds and scents.
days.focus: Remembered natural richness gathered into a persuasive invitation.
days.context: Read each repeated “Come away” as an invitation with a new reason. The source’s footnote call after the final line is omitted as apparatus; none of the poem’s wording is omitted.

excerpt.locator: The Summer’s Call; source transcription lines 61082–61130; opens “Come away! The sunny hours”; closes “                Come away--away!”.

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza make summer audible even when the scene seems quiet?
facilitatorNotes: Murmurs, faint winds and the bee’s deep music fill the air. The sounds differ in volume but together suggest a living scene.
evidence: Where the bee’s deep music swells

questions.prompt: How does the poem show both brightness and shade?
facilitatorNotes: Sapphire sky, glowing flowers and bright wings contrast with dewy gloom and trees’ private twilight. Summer is not presented as unbroken glare.
evidence: Sheds its own rich twilight round;

questions.prompt: Why repeat “Come away” instead of describing the landscape only once?
facilitatorNotes: Each return renews the invitation and gives the listener another detail to imagine. A performance can emphasize insistence, delight or both with textual support.
evidence: Come away--away!

days.title: Heidi: reading to Grandmother (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish practical change from figurative brightness.
days.focus: A learned skill becomes a gift to someone else.
days.context: Home again, Heidi brings a new ability—reading—and wants Grandmother to have softer bread.
days.contentNote: The scene contains a Christian hymn and a child’s mistaken hope about curing blindness. Emotional comfort is not a claim that disability disappears.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, On Sunday When the Church Bells Ring; begins “Heidi was standing under the swaying fir-trees, waiting for her grandfather to join her. He had prom”; ends “ong, and with it on her arm the child joined the old man and immediately told him what had happened.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Brigida question sending a large new supply of rolls from Frankfurt?
facilitatorNotes: They become hard quickly. Heidi’s money suggests a local daily purchase instead.
evidence: they get hard so soon.

questions.prompt: What details show care in the way Heidi begins reading?
facilitatorNotes: She fetches and dusts the book, asks what to read, and chooses a song. These small actions prepare a shared experience.
evidence: After she had carefully wiped it off

questions.prompt: Does “everything seems bright” mean Grandmother’s sight is restored?
facilitatorNotes: No. Her lightened heart and changed expression describe joy from hearing the song. Contrast this with Heidi’s earlier mistaken hope about physical sight.
evidence: everything seems bright to me again and my heart is light.

days.title: Heidi: an unexpected guest (excerpt)
days.challenge: Trace a reversal in who offers comfort to whom.
days.focus: Gratitude and disappointment can coexist.
days.context: Heidi expects Clara and Grandmama to visit from Frankfurt. One morning she sees their doctor climbing toward the hut.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, A Guest on the Alp; begins “The early dawn was tinging the mountains and a fresh morning-breeze rocked the old fir-trees to and ”; ends “"They are not here yet, but it won't be very long before they are coming!"”.

questions.prompt: Why does Heidi stay home instead of going to the pasture with Peter?
facilitatorNotes: She does not want to miss the anticipated visitors. Her repeated expectation explains her choice even when Peter complains.
evidence: I must be home when they come.

questions.prompt: Why does Heidi’s thanks surprise the doctor?
facilitatorNotes: He expects to be forgotten and to disappoint her with news that Clara cannot come. She remembers his help in sending her home.
evidence: Because you let me come home again

questions.prompt: How does Heidi’s response change after the disappointing news?
facilitatorNotes: She is first stunned, then notices his sadness and comforts him with the prospect of spring. Show both stages rather than calling her instantly cheerful.
evidence: All the way she tried to cheer him up

days.title: Heidi: a winter room in the village (excerpt)
days.challenge: Hold a building’s history alongside its present uses.
days.focus: A damaged house becomes a carefully adapted home.
days.context: Grandfather has arranged a winter home in the village so Heidi can attend school. Snow still surrounds Peter’s mountain hut.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVIII, Winter in the Village; begins “The snow lay so deep around the Alm-hut that the windows seemed to stand level with the ground and t”; ends “or school, so the boy took his time and only arrived in the village when Heidi came home for dinner.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator describe the house’s former owner and decay?
facilitatorNotes: Its history explains the present ruin and low rent, making Grandfather’s repairs more significant.
evidence: the house, which was gradually crumbling and falling to pieces.

questions.prompt: Which choices make Heidi’s particular sleeping place suitable for winter?
facilitatorNotes: Grandfather places her bed beside the stove; she also enjoys the painted tiles and protected room. Separate warmth from decoration.
evidence: Your bed must be near the stove, to keep you warm

questions.prompt: What changes in the snow permit travel but still do not get Peter to school on time?
facilitatorNotes: It freezes hard enough for his sled, but he overshoots the village and delays returning. Conditions and choices both affect the outcome.
evidence: he coasted down further and further

days.title: Heidi: a letter from Clara (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate reported information, a plan, and a guess within a letter.
days.focus: A friend’s voice travels through writing.
days.context: Spring has returned, and Heidi is back in the mountain hut. Grandfather is preparing for the hoped-for guests.
days.contentNote: The letter repeats period beliefs about mountain air and health.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XX, News from Distant Friends; begins “May had come. Warm sunshine was bathing the whole Alp in glorious light, and having melted the last ”; ends “I am your true friend, CLARA.”.

questions.prompt: How do the new chairs show that the visit already matters before a letter arrives?
facilitatorNotes: Grandfather is doing practical preparation; Heidi immediately identifies their intended guests.
evidence: You are making them for Clara and grandmama.

questions.prompt: Why is Peter’s answer that the letter came “From my bag” incomplete?
facilitatorNotes: It names its recent location but not sender or delivery history. The narrator supplies what Heidi needs to understand.
evidence: putting it in his lunch-bag, the boy had forgotten it there

questions.prompt: Which part of Clara’s account of Miss Rottenmeier is a guess rather than direct knowledge?
facilitatorNotes: Clara thinks Sebastian frightened her with descriptions of heights. Her repeated “I think” signals inference; the travel plans are stated more directly.
evidence: I think Sebastian must have given her such a terrible description

days.title: Heidi: Clara reaches the mountain (excerpt)
days.challenge: Infer how physical arrangements affect a character’s freedom to participate.
days.focus: Hospitality made visible through actions.
days.context: Clara and Grandmama’s planned visit finally begins. Clara uses a rolling-chair, so the journey requires several people and careful preparation.
days.contentNote: This translation uses “lame” for a person with limited mobility, and the scene briefly recalls a soldier’s death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XX, News from Distant Friends; begins “The blossom month had passed, and June, with the long, long days, had come. Quantities of flowers we”; ends “on't stop, our mountain wind helps along where the cooking is faulty!" contentedly said the old man.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the arriving procession different from Heidi’s usual climb?
facilitatorNotes: People carry Clara, a separate rolling-chair, and many wraps while Grandmama rides. The detailed list shows the work of making the visit possible.
evidence: Then an empty rolling-chair, carried by a young fellow

questions.prompt: How does Grandfather answer praise for his skill in caring for Clara?
facilitatorNotes: He emphasizes care more than study; the narrator then connects it with his earlier experience nursing a wounded captain.
evidence: It comes more from care than study.

questions.prompt: How does the scene show both the value and the limit of Heidi’s eagerness to help?
facilitatorNotes: She pushes Clara to see the trees and brings flowers, but later pushes too fast and Grandfather must stop the chair. Good intentions still require attention.
evidence: if the grandfather had not stopped it at the last moment.

days.title: Madam How: a model and a test (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare a small experiment with a broad generalization.
days.focus: A good explanation invites scrutiny.
days.context: The speaker has proposed that water shaped a local glen. Now he asks how the child could test that proposal rather than merely accept it.
days.contentNote: This is nineteenth-century nature writing, with personification and historical scientific explanations. Read it as an argument to examine, not a current science textbook. Water and ice erode land, but the claim that they alone account for mountain forms is incomplete: tectonic uplift also matters. Modern context: US Geological Survey, Understanding plate motions (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/understanding.html).

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, The Glen; begins “That is my guess: and I think it is a good guess, because I have asked Madam How a hundred different”; ends “Madam How at work on little things.  For that is the way to see her at work upon all space and time.”.

questions.prompt: What two soil arrangements does the proposed model compare?
facilitatorNotes: Clay below sand, then sand below clay. Reversing the layers tests whether their order changes the gullies made by water.
evidence: a cake of sand with a cap of clay on the top

questions.prompt: Why examine other valleys as well as the model?
facilitatorNotes: The model alone concerns one arrangement. Comparing different materials and shapes tests how widely the explanation fits.
evidence: seeing if my guess holds good

questions.prompt: Where does the author’s certainty become broader than the small experiment can establish?
facilitatorNotes: He says water and nothing else has shaped great mountain peaks and valleys. A tabletop model supports a process but cannot establish that no other geological processes matter.
evidence: Water, and nothing else

days.title: Madam How: reading scratches on stone (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish an observed trace from a proposed cause and from secondhand information.
days.focus: A small object can preserve evidence of a large process.
days.context: The speaker shows a small stone brought from beside a Swiss glacier. He asks the child to reason from its surface marks.
days.contentNote: This is nineteenth-century nature writing, with personification and historical scientific explanations. Read it as an argument to examine, not a current science textbook.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, The Ice-Plough; begins “You want to know why I am so fond of that little bit of limestone, no bigger than my hand, which lie”; ends “what is going on slowly and surely in the Alps in Switzerland was going on once here where we stand.”.

questions.prompt: Which features make ordinary flat polishing an inadequate explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The rubbed edge is curved, fluted, and finely scratched in the same direction rather than simply flat.
evidence: it is not flat.  It is rolled, fluted, channelled

questions.prompt: How does calling ice a hand make its action understandable?
facilitatorNotes: The imagined hand grips tools of different sizes, like rock and sand, explaining how ice can scrape and scratch.
evidence: its own carving tools

questions.prompt: What does the speaker know firsthand, and what has been brought to him?
facilitatorNotes: He has seen similar marks elsewhere but admits never seeing a glacier himself. The Swiss specimen lets him compare traces without pretending to eyewitness its formation.
evidence: who never saw a glacier myself

days.title: Madam How: why cart chalk to a field? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Notice how questions turn a commonplace object into an investigation.
days.focus: Practical knowledge gives an inquiry a starting point.
days.context: The child wants to learn about caves, but passing carts lead the speaker to an ordinary farming question first.

facilitatorNotes: Burdock balls become furniture, ledges become castle stairs, and leaves become doll blankets. Specific transformations show active invention.

days.title: Sir Richard: approaching the Priory (excerpt 1 of 5)
days.challenge: Compare simultaneous scenes and notice how a minor character disrupts apparent agreement.
days.focus: The setting and conversation expose the difference between abundance and mercy.
days.context: Robin has provided money and an escort so Sir Richard can repay the debt threatening his estate. The Prior expects the knight to arrive without enough money.
days.contentNote: This fictional scene portrays abuse of financial and religious authority. One member of the religious household objects, and readers should preserve that distinction.

excerpt.locator: "How Sir Richard of the Lea paid his Debts to Emmet", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “THE long highway stretched straight on, gray and dusty in the sun. On ”; ends “was below, albeit he knew right well it could be none but Sir Richard.”.

blocks.text: THE long highway stretched straight on, gray and dusty in the sun. On either side were dykes full of water bordered by osiers, and far away in the distance stood the towers of Emmet Priory with tall poplar trees around.

Along the causeway rode a knight with a score of stout men-at-arms behind him. The Knight was clad in a plain long robe of gray serge, gathered in at the waist with a broad leathern belt, from which hung a long dagger and a stout sword. But though he was so plainly dressed himself, the horse he rode was a noble barb, and its trappings were rich with silk and silver bells.

So thus the band journeyed along the causeway between the dykes, till at last they reached the great gate of Emmet Priory. There the Knight called to one of his men and bade him knock at the porter's lodge with the haft of his sword.

The porter was drowsing on his bench within the lodge, but at the knock he roused himself and, opening the wicket, came hobbling forth and greeted the Knight, whilst a tame starling that hung in a wicker cage within piped out, "In cœlo quies! In cœlo quies!" such being the words that the poor old lame porter had taught him to speak.
"Where is thy prior?" asked the Knight of the old porter.
"He is at meat, good knight, and he looketh for thy coming," quoth the porter, "for, if I mistake not, thou art Sir Richard o' the Lea."
"I am Sir Richard of the Lea; then I will go seek him forthwith," said the Knight.

"But shall I not send thy horse to stable?" said the porter. "By Our Lady, it is the noblest nag, and the best harnessed, that e'er I saw in all my life before." And he stroked the horse's flank with his palm.

"Nay," quoth Sir Richard, "the stables of this place are not for me, so make way, I prythee." So saying he pushed forward, and, the gates being opened, he entered the stony courtyard of the Priory, his men behind him. In they came with rattle of steel and clashing of swords, and ring of horses' feet on cobble-stones, whereat a flock of pigeons that strutted in the sun flew with flapping wings to the high eaves of the round towers.

Whilst the Knight was riding along the causeway to Emmet, a merry feast was toward in the refectory there. The afternoon sun streamed in through the great arched windows, and lay in broad squares of light upon the stone floor and across the board covered with a snowy linen cloth, whereon was spread a princely feast. At the head of the table sat Prior Vincent of Emmet all clad in soft robes of fine cloth and silk; on his head was a black velvet cap picked out with gold, and around his neck hung a heavy chain of gold, with a great locket pendant therefrom. Beside him, on the arm of his great chair, roosted his favorite falcon, for the Prior was fond of the gentle craft of hawking. On his right hand sat the Sheriff of Nottingham in rich robes of purple all trimmed about with fur, and on his left a famous doctor of law in dark and sober garb. Below these sat the high cellarer of Emmet, and others chief among the brethren.

Jest and laughter passed around, and all was as merry as merry could be. The weazened face of the man of law was twisted into a wrinkled smile, for in his pouch were fourscore golden angels that the Prior had paid him in fee for the case betwixt him and Sir Richard of the Lea. The learned doctor had been paid beforehand, for he had not overmuch trust in the holy Vincent of Emmet.
Quoth the Sheriff of Nottingham, "But art thou sure, Sir Prior, that thou hast the lands so safe?"

"Ay, marry," said Prior Vincent, smacking his lips after a deep draught of wine; "I have kept a close watch upon him, albeit he was unawares of the same, and I know right well that he hath no money to pay me withal."

"Ay, true," said the man of law in a dry, husky voice, "his land is surely forfeit if he cometh not to pay; but, Sir Prior, thou must get a release beneath his sign manual, or else thou canst not hope to hold the land without trouble from him."
"Yea," said the Prior, "so thou hast told me ere now, but I know that this knight is so poor that he will gladly sign away his lands for two hundred pounds of hard money."

Then up spake the high cellarer: "Methinks it is a shame to so drive a misfortunate knight to the ditch. I think it sorrow that the noblest estate in Derbyshire should so pass away from him for a paltry five hundred pounds. Truly, I"--

"How now," broke in the Prior, in a quivering voice, his eyes glistening and his cheeks red with anger, "dost thou prate to my very beard, sirrah? By Saint Hubert, thou hadst best save thy breath to cool thy pottage, else it may scald thy mouth."

"Nay," said the man of law, smoothly, "I dare swear this same knight will never come to settlement this day, but will prove recreant. Nevertheless, we will seek some means to gain his lands from him, so never fear."

But even as the doctor spoke there came a sudden clatter of horses' hoofs and a jingle of iron mail in the courtyard below. Then up spake the Prior, and called upon one of the brethren that sat below the salt, and bade him look out of the window and see who was below, albeit he knew right well it could be none but Sir Richard.

questions.prompt: What contrast is created between the knight’s simple clothes and the Prior’s feast?
facilitatorNotes: Sir Richard wears plain gray cloth while the Prior sits amid silk, gold, and plentiful food. The contrast prepares readers to judge how power and wealth are used.
evidence: a plain long robe of gray serge

questions.prompt: What does the lawyer’s demand for a signed release tell us about the plan?
facilitatorNotes: Possessing the land is not automatic or uncomplicated; the Prior wants the knight’s signature to avoid future trouble. The lawyer’s details reveal a calculated transaction.

questions.prompt: Why is the high cellarer’s objection important even though the Prior interrupts him?
facilitatorNotes: It shows that not everyone at the table approves. His dissent also prevents treating all the religious characters as sharing the Prior’s greed.
evidence: Methinks it is a shame to so drive a misfortunate knight to the ditch.

blocks.text: So the brother arose and went and looked, and he said, "I see below a score of stout men-at-arms and a knight just dismounting from his horse. He is dressed in long robes of gray which, methinks, are of poor seeming; but the horse he rideth upon hath the richest coursing that ever I saw. The Knight dismounts and they come this way, and are even now below in the great hall."

"Lo, see ye there now," quoth Prior Vincent. "Here ye have a knight with so lean a purse as scarce to buy him a crust of bread to munch, yet he keeps a band of retainers, and puts rich trappings upon his horse's hide, whilst his own back goeth bare. Is it not well that such men should be brought low?"

"But art thou sure," said the little doctor, tremulously, "that this knight will do us no harm? Such as he are fierce when crossed, and he hath a band of naughty men at his heels. Mayhap thou hadst better give an extension of his debt." Thus he spake, for he was afraid Sir Richard might do him a harm.
"Thou needst not fear," said the Prior, looking down at the little man beside him. "This knight is gentle, and would as soon think of harming an old woman as thee."

As the Prior finished, a door at the lower end of the refectory swung open, and in came Sir Richard, with folded hands and head bowed upon his breast. Thus humbly he walked slowly up the hall, whilst his men-at-arms stood about the door. When he had come to where the Prior sat, he knelt upon one knee. "Save and keep thee, Sir Prior" said he; "I am come to keep my day."
Then the first word that the Prior said to him was, "Hast thou brought my money?"
"Alas! I have not so much as one penny upon my body," said the Knight; whereat the Prior's eyes sparkled.
"Now, thou art a shrewd debtor, I wot," said he. Then, "Sir Sheriff, I drink to thee."
But still the Knight kneeled upon the hard stones, so the Prior turned to him again. "What wouldst thou have?" quoth he, sharply.

At these words, a slow red mounted into the Knight's cheeks; but still he knelt. "I would crave thy mercy," said he. "As thou hopest for Heaven's mercy, show mercy to me. Strip me not of my lands, and so reduce a true knight to poverty."
"Thy day is broken and thy lands forfeit," said the man of law, plucking up his spirits at the Knight's humble speech.
Quoth Sir Richard, "Thou man of law, wilt thou not befriend me in mine hour of need?"
"Nay," said the other, "I hold with this holy Prior, who hath paid me my fees in hard gold, so that I am bounden to him."
"Wilt thou not be my friend, Sir Sheriff?" said Sir Richard.

"Nay, 'fore Heaven," quoth the Sheriff of Nottingham, "this is no business of mine, yet I will do what I may," and he nudged the Prior beneath the cloth with his knee. "Wilt thou not ease him of some of his debts, Sir Prior?"
At this the Prior smiled grimly. "Pay me three hundred pounds, Sir Richard," said he, "and I will give thee quittance of thy debt."
"Thou knowest, Sir Prior, that it is as easy for me to pay four hundred pounds as three hundred," said Sir Richard. "But wilt thou not give me another twelvemonth to pay my debt?"
"Not another day," said the Prior, sternly.
"And is this all thou wilt do for me?" asked the Knight.
"Now, out upon thee, false Knight!" cried the Prior, bursting forth in anger. "Either pay thy debt as I have said or release thy land, and get thee gone from out my hall."

Then Sir Richard arose to his feet. "Thou false, lying priest!" said he, in so stern a voice that the man of law shrunk affrighted, "I am no false knight, as thou knowest full well, but have ever held my place in the press and the tourney. Hast thou so little courtesy that thou wouldst see a true knight kneel for all this time, or see him come into thy hall and never offer him meat or drink?"

Then quoth the man of law, in a trembling voice, "This is surely an ill way to talk of matters appertaining to business; let us be mild in speech. What wilt thou pay this knight, Sir Prior, to give thee release of his land?"
"I would have given him two hundred pounds," quoth the Prior, "but since he hath spoken so vilely to my teeth, not one groat over one hundred pounds will he get."

"Hadst thou offered me a thousand pounds, false Prior," said the Knight, "thou wouldst not have got an inch of my land." Then, turning to where his men-at-arms stood near the door, he called, "Come hither," and beckoned with his finger; whereupon the tallest of them all came forward and handed him a long leathern bag. Sir Richard took the bag and shot from it upon the table a glittering stream of golden money. "Bear in mind, Sir Prior," said he, "that thou hast promised me quittance for three hundred pounds. Not one farthing above that shalt thou get." So saying, he counted out three hundred pounds and pushed it toward the Prior.

But now the Prior's hands dropped at his sides and the Prior's head hung upon his shoulder, for not only had he lost all hopes of the land, but he had forgiven the Knight one hundred pounds of his debt and had needlessly paid the man of law fourscore angels. To him he turned, and quoth he, "Give me back my money that thou hast."
"Nay," cried the other, shrilly, "it is but my fee that thou didst pay me, and thou gettest it not back again." And he hugged his gown about him.

"Now, Sir Prior," quoth Sir Richard, "I have held my day and paid all the dues demanded of me; so, as there is no more betwixt us, I leave this vile place straightway." So saying, he turned upon his heel and strode away.
All this time the Sheriff had been staring with wide-open eyes and mouth agape at the tall man-at-arms, who stood as though carved out of stone. At last he gasped out, "Reynold Greenleaf!"

At this, the tall man-at-arms, who was no other than Little John, turned, grinning, to the Sheriff. "I give thee good den, fair gossip," quoth he. "I would say, sweet Sheriff, that I have heard all thy pretty talk this day, and it shall be duly told unto Robin Hood. So, farewell for the nonce, till we meet again in Sherwood Forest." Then he, also, turned and followed Sir Richard down the hall, leaving the Sheriff, all pale and amazed, shrunk together upon his chair.

A merry feast it was to which Sir Richard came, but a sorry lot he left behind him, and little hunger had they for the princely food spread before them. Only the learned doctor was happy, for he had his fee.

days.title: Sir Richard: a year later at the fair (excerpt 3 of 5)
days.challenge: Distinguish evidence of fair play from the crowd’s loyalty to a local favorite.
days.focus: A stranger’s victory tests whether spectators value fairness more than belonging.
days.context: A year has passed. Sir Richard’s land has recovered, and he travels to repay Robin. On the way, he stops at a fair and is asked to help judge a wrestling contest.
days.contentNote: The wrestling includes a hard fall and concern that a contestant might have died, followed by confirmation that he has not. The crowd’s anger continues into the next reading.

excerpt.locator: "How Sir Richard of the Lea paid his Debts to Emmet", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “But now a twelvemonth and a day has passed since Prior Vincent of Emme”; ends “d tightening the girths of his saddle, he mounted his horse once more.”.

blocks.text: But now a twelvemonth and a day has passed since Prior Vincent of Emmet sat at feast, as has just been told, and once more the mellow fall of another year has come. But the year had brought great change, I wot, to the lands of Sir Richard of the Lea; for, where before shaggy wild grasses grew upon the meadow lands, now all stretch away in golden stubble, betokening that a rich and plentiful crop had been gathered therefrom. A year had made a great change in the castle, also, for, where were empty moats and the crumbling of neglect, all was now orderly and well kept.

Bright shone the sun on battlement and tower, and in the blue air overhead a flock of clattering jackdaws flew around the gilded weathervane and spire. Then, in the brightness of the morning, the drawbridge fell across the moat with a rattle and clank of chains, the gate of the castle swung slowly open, and a goodly array of steel-clad men-at-arms, with a knight all clothed in chain-mail, as white as frost on briar and thorn of a winter morning, came flashing out from the castle courtyard. In his hand the Knight held a great spear, from the point of which fluttered a blood-red pennant as broad as the palm of one's hand. So this troop came forth from the castle, and in the midst of them walked three packhorses laden with parcels of divers shapes and kinds.

Thus rode forth good Sir Richard of the Lea to pay his debt to Robin Hood this bright and merry morn. Along the highway they wended their way, with measured tramp of feet and rattle and jingle of sword and harness. Onward they marched till they came nigh to Denby, where, from the top of a hill, they saw, over beyond the town, many gay flags and streamers floating in the bright air. Then Sir Richard turned to the man-at-arms nearest to him. "What is toward yonder at Denby to-day?" quoth he.

"Please your worship," answered the man-at-arms, "a merry fair is held there to-day, and a great wrestling-match, to which many folk have come, for a prize hath been offered of a pipe of red wine, a fair golden ring, and a pair of gloves, all of which go to the best wrestler."

"Now, by my faith," quoth Sir Richard, who loved good manly sports right well, "this will be a goodly thing to see. Methinks we have to stay a little while on our journey, and see this merry sport." So he turned his horse's head aside toward Denby and the fair, and thither he and his men made their way.

There they found a great hubbub of merriment. Flags and streamers were floating, tumblers were tumbling on the green, bag-pipes were playing, and lads and lasses were dancing to the music. But the crowd were gathered most of all around a ring where the wrestling was going forward, and thither Sir Richard and his men turned their steps.

Now when the judges of the wrestling saw Sir Richard coming and knew who he was, the chief of them came down from the bench where he and the others sat, and went to the Knight and took him by the hand, beseeching him to come and sit with them and judge the sport. So Sir Richard got down from his horse, and went with the others to the bench raised beside the ring.

Now there had been great doings that morning, for a certain yeoman named Egbert, who came from Stoke over in Staffordshire, had thrown with ease all those that came against him; but a man of Denby, well known through all the countryside as William with the Scar, had been biding his time with the Stoke man; so, when Egbert had thrown every one else, stout William leaped into the ring. Then a tough bout followed, and at last he threw Egbert heavily, whereat there was a great shouting and shaking of hands, for all the Denby men were proud of their wrestler.

When Sir Richard came, he found stout William, puffed up by the shouts of his friends, walking up and down the ring, daring any one to come and try a throw with him. "Come one, come all!" quoth he. "Here stand I, William of the Scar, against any man. If there is none in Derbyshire to come against me, come all who will, from Nottingham, Stafford, or York, and if I do not make them one and all root the ground with their noses like swine in the forests, call me no more brave William the wrestler."

At this all laughed; but above all the laughter a loud voice was heard to cry out, "Sin' thou talkest so big, here cometh one from Nottinghamshire to try a fall with thee, fellow;" and straightway a tall youth with a tough quarterstaff in his hand came pushing his way through the crowd, and at last leaped lightly over the rope into the ring. He was not as heavy as stout William, but he was taller and broader in the shoulders, and all his joints were well knit. Sir Richard looked upon him keenly, then, turning to one of the judges, he said, "Knowest thou who this youth is? Methinks I have seen him before."
"Nay," said the judge, "he is a stranger to me."

Meantime, without a word, the young man, laying aside his quarterstaff, began to take off his jerkin and body clothing until he presently stood with naked arms and body; and a comely sight he was when so bared to the view, for his muscles were cut round and smooth and sharp like swift-running water.

And now each man spat upon his hands, and, clapping them upon his knees, squatted down, watching the other keenly, so as to take the vantage of him in the grip. Then like a flash they leaped together, and a great shout went up, for William had gotten the better hold of the two. For a short time they strained and struggled and writhed, and then stout William gave his most cunning trip and throw, but the stranger met it with greater skill than his, and so the trip came to nought. Then, of a sudden, with a twist and a wrench, the stranger loosed himself, and he of the scar found himself locked in a pair of arms that fairly made his ribs crack. So, with heavy, hot breathing, they stood for a while straining, their bodies all glistening with sweat, and great drops of sweat trickling down their faces. But the stranger's hug was so close that at last stout William's muscles softened under his grip, and he gave a sob. Then the youth put forth all his strength, and gave a sudden trip with his heel, and a cast over his right hip, and down stout William went, with a sickening thud, and lay as though he would never move hand nor foot again.

But now no shout went up for the stranger, but an angry murmur was heard among the crowd, so easily had he won the match. Then one of the judges, who was a kinsman to William of the Scar, rose with trembling lip and baleful look. Quoth he, "If thou hast slain that man it will go ill with thee, let me tell thee, fellow."
But the stranger answered boldly, "He took his chance with me as I took mine with him. No law can touch me to harm me, even if I slew him, so that it was fairly done in the wrestling ring."
"That we shall see," said the judge, scowling upon the youth, whilst once more an angry murmur ran around the crowd; for, as I have said, the men of Denby were proud of stout William of the Scar.
Then up spoke Sir Richard, gently. "Nay," said he, "the youth is right; if the other dieth, he dieth in the wrestling ring, where he took his chance, and was cast fairly enow."

But in the mean time three men had come forward and lifted stout William from the ground, and found that he was not dead, though badly shaken by his heavy fall. Then the chief judge rose and said, "Young man, the prize is duly thine. Here is the red gold ring, and here the gloves, and yonder stands the pipe of wine to do with whatsoever thou dost list."

At this the youth, who had donned his clothes and taken up his staff again, bowed, without a word, then, taking the gloves and the ring, and thrusting the one into his girdle and slipping the other upon his thumb, he turned and, leaping lightly over the ropes again, made his way through the crowd, and was gone.

"Now, I wonder who yon youth may be," said the judge, turning to Sir Richard; "he seemeth like a stout Saxon from his red cheeks and fair hair. This William of ours is a stout man, too, and never have I seen him cast in the ring before, albeit he hath not yet striven with such great wrestlers as Thomas of Cornwall, Diccon of York, and young David of Doncaster. Hath he not a firm foot in the ring, thinkest thou, Sir Richard?"
"Ay, truly; and yet this youth threw him fairly, and with wondrous ease. I much wonder who he can be." Thus said Sir Richard in a thoughtful voice.

For a time the Knight stood talking to those about him, but at last he arose and made ready to depart, so he called his men about him, and tightening the girths of his saddle, he mounted his horse once more.

days.title: Sir Richard: a rescue at the fair and a debt repaid (excerpt 4 of 5)
days.challenge: Distinguish financial debt from a figurative debt of gratitude.
days.focus: Robin and Sir Richard each see himself as owing something to the other.
days.context: The stranger who threw William of the Scar has just left the wrestling ring. The Denby crowd is angry at its champion’s defeat. Sir Richard is still at the fair with his men before riding on to Sherwood.
days.contentNote: An angry crowd throws stones at the stranger, a blacksmith attacks him with a club, and he is cut and knocked down before Sir Richard drives the crowd off with the flat of swords. The narrator criticizes the crowd’s fickleness. Robin later uses an extreme figurative statement about his hand to express concern for his friend.

excerpt.locator: "How Sir Richard of the Lea paid his Debts to Emmet", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “Meanwhile the young stranger had made his way through the crowd, but, ”; ends “itterness like gifts forced upon one that cannot choose but take them.”.

blocks.text: Meanwhile the young stranger had made his way through the crowd, but, as he passed, he heard all around him such words muttered as, "Look at the cockeril!" "Behold how he plumeth himself!" "I dare swear he cast good William unfairly!" "Yea, truly, saw ye not bird-lime upon his hands?" "It would be well to cut his cock's comb!" To all this the stranger paid no heed, but strode proudly about as though he heard it not. So he walked slowly across the green to where the booth stood wherein was dancing, and standing at the door he looked in on the sport. As he stood thus a stone struck his arm of a sudden with a sharp jar, and, turning, he saw that an angry crowd of men had followed him from the wrestling ring. Then, when they saw him turn so, a great hooting and yelling arose from all, so that the folk came running out from the dancing booth to see what was to do. At last a tall, broad-shouldered, burly blacksmith strode forward from the crowd swinging a mighty blackthorn club in his hand.

"Wouldst thou come here to our fair town of Denby, thou Jack in the Box, to overcome a good honest lad with vile, juggling tricks?" growled he in a deep voice like the bellow of an angry bull. "Take that, then!" And of a sudden he struck a blow at the youth that might have felled an ox. But the other turned the blow deftly aside, and gave back another so terrible that the Denby man went down with a groan, as though he had been smitten by lightning. When they saw their leader fall the crowd gave another angry shout; but the stranger placed his back against the tent near which he stood, swinging his terrible staff, and so fell had been the blow that he struck the stout smith, that none dared to come within the measure of his cudgel, so the press crowded back, like a pack of dogs from a bear at bay. But now some coward hand from behind threw a sharp jagged stone that smote the stranger on the crown, so that he staggered back, and the red blood gushed from the cut and ran down his face and over his jerkin. Then, seeing him dazed with this vile blow, the crowd rushed upon him, so that they overbore him and he fell beneath their feet.

Now it might have gone ill with the youth, even to the losing of his young life, had not Sir Richard come to this fair; for of a sudden shouts were heard, and steel flashed in the air, and blows were given with the flat of swords, whilst through the midst of the crowd Sir Richard of the Lea came spurring on his white horse. Then the crowd, seeing the steel-clad knight and the armed men, melted away like snow on the warm hearth, leaving the young man all bloody and dusty upon the ground.
Finding himself free, the youth arose, and, wiping the blood from his face, looked up. Quoth he, "Sir Richard of the Lea, mayhap thou hast saved my life this day."
"Who art thou that knowest Sir Richard of the Lea so well?" quoth the Knight. "Methinks I have seen thy face before, young man."
"Yea, thou hast," said the youth, "for men call me David of Doncaster."

"Ha!" said Sir Richard; "I wonder that I knew thee not, David; but thy beard hath grown longer, and thou thyself art more set in manhood since this day twelvemonth. Come hither into the tent, David, and wash the blood from thy face. And thou, Ralph, bring him straightway a clean jerkin. Now I am sorry for thee, yet I am right glad that I have had a chance to pay a part of my debt of kindness to thy good master, Robin Hood, for it might have gone ill with thee had I not come, young man."
So saying, the Knight led David into the tent, and there the youth washed the blood from his face and put on the clean jerkin.

In the mean time a whisper had gone around from those that stood nearest that this was none other than the great David of Doncaster, the best wrestler in all the midcountry, who only last spring had cast stout Adam o' Lincoln in the ring at Selby, in Yorkshire, and now held the midcountry champion belt. Thus it happened that when young David came forth from the tent along with Sir Richard, the blood all washed from his face, and his soiled jerkin changed for a clean one, no sounds of anger were heard, but all pressed forward to see the young man, feeling proud that one of the great wrestlers of England should have entered the ring at Denby fair. For thus fickle is a mass of men.

Then Sir Richard called aloud, "Friends, this is David of Doncaster; so think it no shame that your Denby man was cast by such a wrestler. He beareth you no ill-will for what hath passed, but let it be a warning to you how ye treat strangers henceforth. Had ye slain him it would have been an ill day for you, for Robin Hood would have harried your town as the kestrel harries the dove-cote. I have bought the pipe of wine from him, and now I give it freely to you to drink as ye list. But never hereafterwards fall upon a man for being a stout yeoman."
At this all shouted amain; but in truth they thought more of the wine than of the Knight's words. Then Sir Richard, with David beside him and his men-at-arms around, turned about and left the fair.

But in after days, when the men that saw that wrestling bout were bent with age, they would shake their heads when they heard of any stalwart game, and say, "Ay, ay; but thou shouldst have seen the great David of Doncaster cast stout William with the Scar at Denby fair."

Robin Hood stood in the merry greenwood with Little John and most of his stout yeomen around him, awaiting Sir Richard's coming. At last a glint of steel was seen through the brown forest leaves, and forth from the covert into the open rode Sir Richard at the head of his men. He came straight forward to Robin Hood, and leaping from off his horse clasped the yeoman in his arms.
"Why, how now," said Robin, after a time, holding Sir Richard off and looking at him from top to toe; "methinks thou art a gayer bird than when I saw thee last."

"Yes, thanks to thee, Robin," said the Knight, laying his hand upon the yeoman's shoulder. "But for thee I would have been wandering in misery in a far country by this time. But I have kept my word, Robin, and have brought back the money that thou didst lend me, and which I have doubled four times over again, and so become rich once more. Along with this money I have brought a little gift to thee and thy brave men from my dear lady and myself." Then, turning to his men, he called aloud, "Bring forth the packhorses."

But Robin stopped them. "Nay, Sir Richard," said he, "think it not bold of me to cross thy bidding, but we of Sherwood do no business till after we have eaten and drank; whereupon, taking Sir Richard by the hand, he led him to the seat beneath the greenwood tree, whilst others of the chief men of the band came and seated themselves around. Then, quoth Robin, "How cometh it that I saw young David of Doncaster with thee and thy men, Sir Knight?"

Then straightway the Knight told all about his stay at Denby and of the happening at the fair, and how it was like to go hard with young David; so he told his tale, and quoth he, "It was this, good Robin, that kept me so late on the way, otherwise I would have been here an hour agone."

Then, when he had done speaking, Robin stretched out his hand and grasped the Knight's palm. Quoth he in a trembling voice, "I owe thee a debt I can never hope to repay, Sir Richard, for let me tell thee, I would rather lose my right hand than have such ill befall young David of Doncaster as seemed like to come upon him at Denby."

So they talked until after a while one came forward to say that the feast was spread; whereupon all arose and went thereto. When at last it was done, the Knight called upon his men to bring the packhorses forward, which they did according to his bidding. Then one of the men brought the Knight a strong box, which he opened and took from it a bag and counted out five hundred pounds, the sum of the money he had gotten from Robin.
"Sir Richard," quoth Robin, "thou wilt pleasure us all if thou wilt keep that money as a gift from us of Sherwood. Is it not so, my lads?"
Then all shouted "Ay" with a mighty voice.
"I thank you all deeply," said the Knight, earnestly, "but think it not ill of me if I cannot take it. Gladly have I borrowed it from you, but it may not be that I can take it as a gift."

Then Robin Hood said no more, but gave the money to Little John to put away in the treasury, for he had shrewdness enough to know that nought breeds ill-will and heart-bitterness like gifts forced upon one that cannot choose but take them.

days.title: Sir Richard: a carefully chosen thank-you (excerpt 5 of 5)
days.challenge: Infer the thought behind a gift from precise material details and connect a closing image with the chapter’s resolution.
days.focus: Gratitude is shown through attention to the receivers’ interests and needs.
days.context: Sir Richard has repaid his loan. He now presents gifts chosen for Robin and his companions, and the visit ends in a torchlit farewell. Read this brief closing scene twice, noticing both practical and decorative details.
days.contentNote: The gifts are bows and arrows, and the companions make a dramatic pledge of loyalty. Focus on gratitude and the difference between useful craftsmanship and boasting.

excerpt.locator: "How Sir Richard of the Lea paid his Debts to Emmet", 1883 Scribner edition; begins “Then Sir Richard had the packs laid upon the ground and opened, whereu”; ends “sfortunes, that else would have smothered the happiness from his life.”.

blocks.text: Then Sir Richard had the packs laid upon the ground and opened, whereupon a great shout went up that made the forest ring again, for lo, there were tenscore bows of finest Spanish yew, all burnished till they shone again, and each bow inlaid with fanciful figures in silver, yet not inlaid so as to mar their strength. Beside these were tenscore quivers of leather embroidered with golden thread, and in each quiver were a score of shafts with burnished heads that shone like silver; each shaft also was feathered with peacock's plumes and innocked with silver.
Sir Richard gave to each yeoman a bow and a quiver of arrows, but to Robin he gave a stout bow inlaid with the cunningest workmanship in gold, whilst each arrow in his quiver was innocked with gold.
Then all shouted again for joy of the fair gift, and all swore among themselves that they would die if need be for Sir Richard and his lady.

At last the time came when Sir Richard must go, whereupon Robin Hood called his band around him, and each man of the yeomen took a torch in his hand to light the way through the woodlands. So they came to the edge of Sherwood, and there the Knight kissed Robin upon the cheeks and left him and was gone.
Thus Robin Hood helped a noble knight out of his dire misfortunes, that else would have smothered the happiness from his life.
