questions.prompt: Which parts of the described pile have a practical protective function?
facilitatorNotes: Thorny branches and cactus around the small central nest can protect the entrance. The text distinguishes these from the shiny collected objects.
evidence: a narrow entrance well-guarded by an array of cactus spines

questions.prompt: Does an exchanged pine cone prove that a rat has a human sense of fairness?
facilitatorNotes: No. The writer reports replacement objects, then interprets them as conscience and trade. Ask what is observed and what the playful language adds.
evidence: As though it had a conscience

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: the beaver’s constructions (excerpt)
days.challenge: Connect each structure to its stated function while questioning an absolute claim.
days.focus: Human engineering terms organize an animal description.
days.context: Seton describes a beaver lodge, canal, and other structures after discussing the animal’s value to fur traders.
days.contentNote: Seton sometimes overstates: beavers eat several woody and aquatic plants, not only poplar. Modern comparison: the National Park Service Yellowstone beaver account (https://www.nps.gov/yell/learn/nature/beaver.htm). His “reinforced concrete” is an analogy for mixed building materials.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, The Industrious Beaver; begins “In some respects the Beaver is the most notable animal in the West. It was the search for Beaver ski”; ends “ food, is aspen, also called quaking asp or poplar; where there are no poplars there are no Beavers.”.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the two underwater lodge entrances in the account?
facilitatorNotes: One is winding for ordinary passage; one is straight for carrying wood. The specific functions help organize the description.
evidence: one straight for carrying in wood

questions.prompt: Why call the canal a “freight canal”?
facilitatorNotes: Its role is to move food logs from standing trees toward water and the lodge, much as a human canal carries goods.
evidence: for bringing in food-logs

questions.prompt: Which final claim is stronger than simply saying beavers like aspen?
facilitatorNotes: “Where there are no poplars there are no Beavers” is absolute. The preceding statement about a favorite food does not establish exclusive dependence.
evidence: where there are no poplars there are no Beavers.

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: abandoned dams (excerpt)
days.challenge: Use change over time to assess a proposed cause.
days.focus: A ruined structure can still be evidence of its builders.
days.context: Seton revisits places where he had seen active beaver ponds years earlier.
days.contentNote: This historical observation is not a claim that every abandoned dam has the same cause. The author’s measurements and dates describe his visits.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, The Dam; begins “Usually the Beavers start a dam on some stream, right opposite a good grove of poplars. When these a”; ends “It finishes the lodge outside with sticks, not mud.”.

questions.prompt: What changed between the visits to Yancey’s in 1897 and 1912?
facilitatorNotes: Earlier dams and ponds had become broken and dry, and former aspen groves were stumps. The paired dates establish the comparison.
evidence: the dams were broken, the ponds all dry.

questions.prompt: How does Seton connect the used-up trees with the broken dams?
facilitatorNotes: He argues the animals moved for food and stopped maintaining the old structures, so the dams failed. Distinguish the visible state from his causal explanation.
evidence: the Beavers used all the food and moved on.

questions.prompt: Why finish with a list of things beavers do not do?
facilitatorNotes: The list corrects dramatic human-style building myths and asks readers to replace attractive stories with closer observation.
evidence: It does not and cannot drive stakes.

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: an otter slide (excerpt)
days.challenge: Notice when vivid description becomes a confident claim about inner experience.
days.focus: Analogy invites sympathy while stretching beyond observation.
days.context: Seton compares otter play with children sliding down an icy hill.
days.contentNote: The writer generalizes about the temperaments of human fishing and hunting communities without supporting evidence. Treat that comparison and his claims about animal feelings critically.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, The Otter and His Slide; begins “Every one of us that ever was a small boy and rejoiced in belly-bumping down some icy hill, on a sle”; ends “y the sight of these merry creatures indulging in a game which closely parallels so many of our own.”.

questions.prompt: What physical features make the slide work?
facilitatorNotes: A steep bank leads into water and repeated use smooths it; snow or ice reduce friction further.
evidence: worn into a smooth shoot

questions.prompt: How does the account convey repeated, social play rather than a single trip into water?
facilitatorNotes: Otters follow each other, emerge, return, and chase, with older and younger animals together. Point to the recurring sequence.
evidence: plump into the water and out again

questions.prompt: What makes “unquestionably” worth questioning in this passage?
facilitatorNotes: Seton confidently assigns pure social joy as the motive. Observed play supports an interpretation, but cannot reveal every animal’s thoughts; his comparison with people is suggestive rather than proof.
evidence: unquestionably for the simple social joy

days.title: A Signal Through the Dark
days.challenge: Use changes in dialogue to follow fear, guilt, and a first practical plan.
days.focus: Problem solving under pressure
days.context: At sunset the children’s magical wings disappeared. They are trapped on a church tower with a locked door and the soda-water syphon they took from the clergyman’s house.
days.contentNote: The dialogue mentions imagined murder and prison. “Be a man” unfairly associates courage with gender; any child may be afraid or brave. A maid mistakenly believes she has seen a ghost.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 5; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 1–17; opens “Whether anyone cried or not, there was certainly an interval during which none of the part”; closes “ It was quite untrue, of course, but I suppose the girl's nerves were a little upset by the yelling.”.

questions.prompt: What has changed in Cyril’s judgment about taking the food and syphon?
facilitatorNotes: His new uncertainty follows the loss of an easy escape. Ask whether the action itself changed or his willingness to recognize its consequences changed.
evidence: I'm not sure now

questions.prompt: Why is Robert’s plan to throw away the syphon rejected?
facilitatorNotes: Cyril sees that hiding evidence could hurt someone below. Discuss why solving their immediate embarrassment is not the only concern a plan must address.
evidence: and hit some chap on the head

questions.prompt: How do they coordinate a signal, and why does its first effect differ from their hope?
facilitatorNotes: They assign noises and count together so they will be heard. The maid hears alarming sounds without seeing the situation, and interprets them as supernatural danger.
evidence: A four-fold yell rent the silent peace of the evening

days.title: Three Theories Below the Tower
days.challenge: Separate what each adult knows from what each adult assumes.
days.focus: Mistaken inference and suspense
days.context: The children’s coordinated cries have reached the clergyman’s house. The adults do not know that four stranded children are asking for help.
days.contentNote: Adults use stigmatizing historical language about mental illness and wrongly associate it with danger. A keeper carries a gun; no shot is fired. The story exposes their unsupported assumptions.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 5; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 18–44; opens “"One, two, three!" The Vicar was on his doorstep by this time, and there was no mistaking ”; closes “ne stair. And at the top of that there was a little door. And the door was bolted on the stair side.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the children shout again when the Vicar goes back inside? What does the reader know about his real reason?
facilitatorNotes: Cyril thinks he is dismissing the sound, but the Vicar is getting a hat and help. The misunderstanding creates louder cries and greater alarm.
evidence: He thinks he only fancied he heard something

questions.prompt: How do the Vicar, Andrew, and the keeper explain the same cries differently?
facilitatorNotes: The Vicar imagines a dangerous person, Andrew a trap, and the keeper expects less danger because noisy people seem less threatening to him. None has yet seen the children.
evidence: Great cry, little wool

questions.prompt: How does the narrator challenge Andrew’s later claim of bravery on the stairs?
facilitatorNotes: Andrew chooses the middle to avoid someone creeping up behind him. Compare the explanation he later gives with the motive the narrator reveals.
evidence: he did not like the idea of being behind the others

days.title: The Lantern Finds Children
days.challenge: Follow the moment when direct observation overturns a story people have invented.
days.focus: Revelation and concealed evidence
days.context: Three adults climb the tower expecting dangerous intruders. The children wait frightened on the other side of the bolted door.
days.contentNote: The armed keeper threatens to fire if attacked, before discovering the children. He does not fire and then helps them down. Cyril nearly loses his footing but does not fall.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 5; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 45–74; opens “The cook's cousin, who was a gamekeeper, kicked at the door, and said--”; closes “t they reached the bottom of the winding stair and stepped out on to the stones of the church-porch.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Cyril avoid answering with the simple fact that they flew up? What does he say instead?
facilitatorNotes: He expects the true magical explanation to be unbelievable, so supplies a partial account. Discuss what his answer includes and what it leaves unexplained.
evidence: We got up--and then we found the door was locked

questions.prompt: Which moment overturns the keeper’s picture of the people on the roof?
facilitatorNotes: The lantern reveals children; he lowers his gun and nearly drops the light. Reread the label “desperadoes” just before this change and explain its ironic effect.
evidence: if they ain't a pack of kiddies

questions.prompt: Why is going downstairs especially difficult for Cyril even after rescue?
facilitatorNotes: He conceals the syphon and cannot accept help freely. His attempt to hide the earlier act creates a new physical hazard when the bottle slips.
evidence: Cyril had to be independent because of the soda-water syphon

days.title: The Hidden Bottle Comes Out
days.challenge: Compare a partial account with a fuller admission.
days.focus: Dialogue, confession, and accountability
days.context: The adults have rescued the children from the tower and brought them into the Vicarage. Cyril is still trying to conceal the borrowed-without-permission syphon beneath his jacket.
days.contentNote: Adults physically hold the boys while leading them inside. Cyril fears prison. The discussion can evaluate his explanation without requiring children to disclose personal experiences.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 5; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 75–98; opens “Then suddenly the keeper caught Cyril and Robert each by an arm.”; closes “ing a disgrace. Well, don't you go and do it to us--that's all! We're as sorry as we can be. There!"”.

questions.prompt: Why is Robert’s reassurance that they have not hurt the Vicar funny from the reader’s point of view?
facilitatorNotes: The adults feared criminals while the children mainly feared being stranded. Robert responds literally to the wife’s worry, reversing who seems dangerous.
evidence: We haven't hurt them at all

questions.prompt: How does the keeper notice what the Vicar’s speech overlooks?
facilitatorNotes: The Vicar concentrates on a general lesson about good behavior; the keeper observes Cyril’s posture and hidden object. Specific observation brings the unresolved action into the discussion.
evidence: He knew all about poachers, of course, so he knew how people look when they're hiding something

questions.prompt: Which parts of Cyril’s admission accept responsibility, and which still try to excuse the act?
facilitatorNotes: He names the foods and says they took them and are sorry; he also stresses hunger, leaving money, and not taking sweets. Both acknowledgement and self-defense occur in the same speech.
evidence: Yes, we took this out of your larder

days.title: Forgiveness and a Ride Home
days.challenge: Recognize a resolution that depends on kindness even though some facts remain unknown.
days.focus: Partial truth and changing relationships
days.context: Cyril has admitted taking food and the syphon. The adults now hear an apology, but the children still will not tell them that magical wings brought them to the tower.
days.contentNote: The story uses historical dialect spellings. The children still receive a day indoors as a consequence; forgiveness does not mean that taking food was approved.

excerpt.locator: New York: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1905; Chapter 5; https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17314; consecutive transcript paragraphs 99–120; opens “"However did you get up to the larder window?" said Mrs. Vicar.”; closes “But that, too, is another story.”.

questions.prompt: What distinction does Jane make between something being true and being the whole truth?
facilitatorNotes: Their account contains no direct falsehood about climbing or sleeping, but excludes the magic. Ask what unanswered question remains for the adults.
evidence: it's all true, but it's not the whole truth

questions.prompt: Why do the adults become more sympathetic? Does their new explanation completely match the facts?
facilitatorNotes: They think the children are protecting a friend and admire their loyalty. Anthea thinks of the fairy, but the adults do not learn the actual mechanism; empathy grows despite a partly mistaken theory.
evidence: I expect it's a pal they're standing by

questions.prompt: How do the keeper’s actions show that the relationship has changed since the threatening rescue?
facilitatorNotes: He accompanies them, walks them to the door, and explains events to Martha. His care continues after the danger is over; contrast these actions with his earlier suspicion.
evidence: remained to explain to Martha and the cook and the housemaid exactly what had happened

days.title: Go Work in My Vineyard
days.challenge: Follow a dream that changes the meaning of a repeated work assignment.
days.focus: Care for overlooked people understood as valuable work.
days.context: The speaker first imagines harvesting crops, then dreams of a crowd ignoring people who fall. Read for the connection between bruised grain and those injured people.
days.contentNote: The poem expresses the historical speaker’s Christian beliefs. Discuss its imagery and reasoning without requiring agreement with those beliefs. The dream includes injured people and bleeding as non-graphic images of need.

excerpt.locator: Go Work in My Vineyard, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 31–33; complete poem; opens “Go work in my vineyard, said the Lord,”; closes “     There will be light at eventide.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker initially feel that the assigned task is discouraging?
facilitatorNotes: Other reapers seem to have taken the harvest, leaving bare stubble, while their joyful song contrasts with the speaker’s pain.
evidence: But the reapers had left the stubble bare,

questions.prompt: What does the busy crowd fail to do in the dream?
facilitatorNotes: It continues seeking pleasure and gain instead of stopping for injured people. This provides the turning point in understanding the task.
evidence: Too busy to pause or heed,

questions.prompt: Why can the speaker finally value the broken sheaves?
facilitatorNotes: They stand for helping vulnerable people; imperfect or overlooked lives are not worthless. The speaker’s own weakness does not prevent offering aid.
evidence: To feebler ones than mine,

days.title: Renewal of Strength
days.challenge: Recognize a body-house metaphor and compare changes in outward senses with inward confidence.
days.focus: A speaker’s account of aging without the loss of inner value.
days.context: The prison-house and pillars are figurative descriptions of the speaker’s aging body. Read each contrast slowly; no personal disclosure about illness is needed.
days.contentNote: A devotional reflection on aging and eventual death, expressed gently through a building metaphor.

excerpt.locator: Renewal of Strength, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 33–34; complete poem; opens “The prison-house in which I live”; closes “     Renews it day by day.”.

questions.prompt: What does the contrast between decay and renewed strength suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Physical weakness does not determine the speaker’s spiritual strength. The poem treats the body and inner life as connected but not identical.
evidence: But God renews my spirit's strength,

questions.prompt: How do sight and hearing each carry a contrast?
facilitatorNotes: Earthly light dims and earthly harmonies grow dull, while imagined heaven becomes clearer and its music nearer. The parallel structure reinforces the speaker’s outlook.
evidence: But heaven grows clearer to my view,

questions.prompt: Does the final stanza ask for the body to stop changing?
facilitatorNotes: No: it accepts the pillars’ fall while asserting daily renewal through love. Readers may describe this as courage, comfort or faith if they explain the ending.
evidence: Renews it day by day.

days.title: Truth
days.challenge: Follow an extended fable from a proud rock to a seed before interpreting its final statement.
days.focus: Quiet growth as an image for the power of truth against entrenched wrong.
days.context: Read the poem first as an imagined conflict in nature. On rereading, identify where it shifts explicitly from rock and seed to truth and wrong.

excerpt.locator: Truth, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 36–38; complete poem; opens “A rock, for ages, stern and high,”; closes “  The brightest blooms and fairest leaves.”.

questions.prompt: How does the beginning establish the rock’s confidence?
facilitatorNotes: It withstands storms and remains unmoved by both tender light and wrath. These details make the tiny seed seem unlikely to affect it.
evidence: And never bowed his haughty crest

questions.prompt: Why does the seed’s smallness matter to the later outcome?
facilitatorNotes: It is nearly invisible and begins in a low hiding-place, yet gradually spreads. The contrast makes slow, modest beginnings significant.
evidence: The keenest eye would hardly heed

questions.prompt: How does the ending change our understanding of the rock’s destruction?
facilitatorNotes: The rock becomes a figure for mighty wrong and the seed for truth. The new flowers suggest replacement and renewal, not destruction alone.
evidence: It saps its pillars proud and strong,

days.title: Thank God for Little Children
days.challenge: Compare several images for children and consider what each contributes to the adult’s perspective.
days.focus: Gratitude and responsibility joined in a short portrait of childhood.
days.context: Read aloud twice, listing the images of flowers, lifeboats, sunshine and jewels. The poem speaks from an adult caregiver’s viewpoint.
days.contentNote: The poem expresses the historical speaker’s Christian beliefs. Discuss its imagery and reasoning without requiring agreement with those beliefs.

excerpt.locator: Thank God for Little Children, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 47–48; complete poem; opens “Thank God for little children,”; closes “     To lay at Jesus' feet.”.

questions.prompt: How do flowers and lifeboats suggest different gifts children bring?
facilitatorNotes: Flowers suggest beauty and growth; lifeboats suggest comfort or support amid hardship. Ask readers to keep the differences instead of labelling all images simply positive.
evidence: The dancing, joyous lifeboats

questions.prompt: What changes when skies are cold and gray?
facilitatorNotes: Children’s presence is imagined as sunshine that relieves cares. The contrast is emotional as well as visual.
evidence: They come as sunshine to our hearts,

questions.prompt: Why does the last stanza move from thanks to a request that mothers guard the children?
facilitatorNotes: Affection brings responsibility for something precious. The jewel image helps connect delight with protection and care.
evidence: Dear mothers, guard these jewels,

days.title: Songs for the People
days.challenge: Explain a surprising battle-cry comparison that immediately rejects actual fighting.
days.focus: Music imagined as public care rather than entertainment alone.
days.context: Read the first two stanzas together before deciding what kind of force the speaker wants from songs. Then trace the different audiences the poem names.
days.contentNote: The poem mentions war and sorrow while arguing for peace, and uses a brief image of a heavenly resting place.

excerpt.locator: Songs for the People, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 69–70; complete poem; opens “Let me make the songs for the people,”; closes “     Girdle the world with peace.”.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to stop after the phrase “battle-cry”?
facilitatorNotes: The next stanza rejects clashing weapons and bloodshed. The speaker wants stirring energy directed toward fuller life rather than war.
evidence: Not for the clashing of sabres,

questions.prompt: How do the desired songs respond differently to weary people and children?
facilitatorNotes: They ease tension for the weary and offer guidance and love to children. The audiences have distinct needs rather than receiving one identical message.
evidence: Let me make the songs for the weary,

questions.prompt: What does the last image of hearts encircling the world suggest about a song’s possible reach?
facilitatorNotes: It imagines tenderness spreading beyond one listener toward peace across the world. Readers can discuss this as an aspiration without treating it as a guaranteed effect of music.
evidence: Girdle the world with peace.

days.title: What the Gardens Give
days.challenge: Compare results with the choices and care that produced them.
days.focus: Character revealed through work
days.context: Months have passed at Plumfield, and it is now harvest time. The children each have a garden plot, while Mrs. Jo helps them find ways to use and share what grows.
days.contentNote: Daisy repeats an old flower tale portraying a cruel stepmother; it is a folktale image, not a description of blended families. Preserve the quoted couplet as verse. The first edition prints “lowed” in the final sentence where the context calls for “loved”; the supplied text retains that printed form.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 18; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_18; consecutive transcript paragraphs 5–16; opens “THE gardens did well that summer, and in September the little crops were gathered in with ”; closes “Daisy made her own, and lowed the fanciful little friends who played their parts in her summer-life.”.

questions.prompt: How do the different uses of crops reveal different purposes for gardening?
facilitatorNotes: Compare potatoes sold to the household, corn given in gratitude, and vegetables chosen as gifts for grandparents. A harvest can have value beyond the money it earns.
evidence: We never can pay Uncle for all he has done for us

questions.prompt: Does Tommy’s decision to grow food for pets erase the reasons his earlier crops failed?
facilitatorNotes: His kindness is real, and so are his failures to water, weed and support plants. Hold both traits together rather than turning the ending into proof that he had planned everything well.
evidence: he let the poor things struggle with bugs and weeds

questions.prompt: How does Daisy use careful observation to turn flowers into an imaginary world?
facilitatorNotes: Find the detailed resemblances in flowers and the dolls and boats she makes. Her imagination builds from real forms and regular attention to her garden.
evidence: for finding that there were no elves, Daisy made her own

days.title: A Different Answer to a Mean Joke
days.challenge: Follow evidence of a prank and evaluate the response chosen for it.
days.focus: Conflict and alternatives to retaliation
days.context: Other harvest accounts occur between this scene and the previous garden excerpt. George, nicknamed Stuffy, has saved three watermelons to sell. Some disappointed boys damage their skins with an insulting word.
days.contentNote: The passage includes appetite-based name-calling and an insulting word carved into melons. The narrator’s body comments can be questioned. George talks of fighting but does not fight.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 18; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_18; consecutive transcript paragraphs 24–34; opens “Stuffy had various trials with his melons; for, being impatient to taste them, he had a so”; closes “ng, what all the rest agreed to, that Stuffy had taken a wise and merry way to return good for evil.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the carved word more than an ordinary joke?
facilitatorNotes: It insults George and damages something he has worked to grow and hopes to sell. Discuss the difference between laughing together and making one person bear the cost.
evidence: the word "Pig" cut in white letters on the green rind

questions.prompt: Which clues lead Mrs. Jo to suspect who did it? Are those clues equally strong?
facilitatorNotes: Separate observed whispers and nighttime movement from the cut finger and her interpretation. The later guilty response supports her suspicion; her initial conclusion begins as an inference.
evidence: a cut on Tommy's finger, all helped to confirm her suspicions

questions.prompt: How does George’s response change who controls the joke? What does his choice cost him?
facilitatorNotes: He adds a greeting, gives the melons to the pranksters and lets everyone share them. He gives up the sale, so readers can praise his generosity while considering whether further repair from the boys would be fair.
evidence: With the compliments of the pig

days.title: Dan’s Woodland Harvest
days.challenge: Reconsider what counts as a contribution when circumstances differ.
days.focus: Adaptation and descriptive detail
days.context: Dan has not had a garden because he was away or recovering from an injury much of the summer. He has helped with chores, but at harvest time wishes he had something visible to contribute.
days.contentNote: The passage mentions period plant remedies. “Lame” describes Dan’s temporary difficulty walking.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 18; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_18; consecutive transcript paragraphs 35–41; opens “Dan had no garden, for he was away or lame the greater part of the summer; so he had helpe”; closes “ beechnuts lay in separate compartments, getting brown, and dry, and sweet, ready for winter revels.”.

questions.prompt: What work has Dan already done before he feels he has little to show?
facilitatorNotes: List help for Silas, wood chopping, and lawn care. His disappointment concerns a visible harvest, not an absence of useful effort; make that distinction explicit.
evidence: helped Silas wherever he could, chopped wood for Asia, and taken care of the lawn

questions.prompt: How does he adapt the idea of a crop to his own knowledge and circumstances?
facilitatorNotes: He knows woodland places and seasonal materials, so gathers nuts, leaves and plants. Compare cultivated garden work with skilled observation and collecting.
evidence: a woodland harvest which no one would dispute with him

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Jo say Dan brings the woods to her? Which details make the expression feel concrete?
facilitatorNotes: Use colors, textures and shapes such as maple boughs, woodbine, ferns and cones. His gift lets someone at home experience qualities of a place she misses.
evidence: I need not sigh for the woods now, because Dan brings the woods to me

days.title: The Squirrels Keep Working
days.challenge: Track how time, weather, and work alter a competition.
days.focus: Consequences and perseverance
days.context: Rob and his little brother Teddy may keep the butternuts from one tree if they collect them themselves. At first the boys delay, while squirrels steadily carry the fallen nuts away.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 18; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_18; consecutive transcript paragraphs 42–60; opens “There was one butternut-tree on the place, and Rob and Teddy called it theirs. It bore wel”; closes “hieves with one grubby little hand, while he refreshed himself with the big apple held in the other.”.

questions.prompt: How does Rob’s first answer to Silas show the mistake in his planning?
facilitatorNotes: He relies on the large number of nuts and future effort while the squirrels work now. The falling supply and coming wind make delay costly.
evidence: we can beat them when we begin

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Bhaer refuse to let Rob skip lessons entirely? Is his compromise responsive to Rob’s problem?
facilitatorNotes: He connects the emergency with earlier neglected work, keeps the school obligation, and offers an hour. Readers can assess the balance of consequence and help using all three details.
evidence: You may go an hour earlier, but that is all

questions.prompt: What makes Teddy’s work important beyond the number of nuts he collects?
facilitatorNotes: He keeps helping while Rob is in class, despite fatigue. Mrs. Jo notices this generous persistence and helps carry, showing how another person responds to effort.
evidence: the kind little fellow who tried to help his brother

days.title: The Mystery of the Missing Nuts
days.challenge: Test a suspicion against observed movements, then interpret a closing metaphor.
days.focus: Evidence and the meaning of a harvest
days.context: Rob and Teddy have finally collected their butternuts and stored them in a locked corn-barn. A few days later many have vanished, and the boys try to discover how.
days.contentNote: Rob threatens to trap and kill a squirrel in anger, but follows Dan’s suggestion to watch instead. No animal is harmed in this excerpt.

excerpt.locator: Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1871; Chapter 18; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Little_Men/Chapter_18; consecutive transcript paragraphs 61–69; opens “Rob fell to work and the ground was cleared before two o'clock, the nuts safely in the cor”; closes “lt that their summer work had prospered well, and by and by had a harvest that made them very happy.”.

questions.prompt: Which possible explanations does Rob reject, and what observation starts a better investigation?
facilitatorNotes: The locked door seems to rule out boys; he dismisses birds and rats. Dick’s sighting of Frisky on the roof gives a lead that can be watched rather than guessed.
evidence: I saw Frisky on the roof of the corn-barn

questions.prompt: How does following the squirrels lead to a solution different from Rob’s first angry plan?
facilitatorNotes: Dan proposes watching; Rob finds the entry route and hiding place, retrieves the nuts, and changes storage. Observation allows prevention without carrying out the threatened killing.
evidence: if you watch, you can find out where he puts them

questions.prompt: What might the Bhaers’ “crop of a different sort” mean at the chapter’s end?
facilitatorNotes: Connect it to the children’s growing skill, generosity and judgment across the harvest scenes. Require an example from this scene or a recalled earlier selection, not just the abstract word goodness.
evidence: Father and Mother Bhaer's crop was of a different sort

days.title: The Insect Folk — Friend Cicada: A Cicada Is Not a Locust
days.challenge: Separate an association from a cause, and a familiar name from an identification.
days.focus: Careful looking that revises what people think they already know.
days.context: The loud insect is a cicada, often loosely called a locust in the conversation. The narrator uses bug in its narrower insect-group sense. Read the dialogue first for its corrections, then for the unanswered question about eyes.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — Friend Cicada: A Cicada Is Not a Locust; source transcription lines 4341–4430; opens “WHIR-R-R-R-RRRRR!!”; closes “They show very plainly with a magnifying glass.”.

questions.prompt: How do John and the narrator explain why the call makes May feel hotter?
facilitatorNotes: The weather is hot, and repeated experience has linked the call with hot summer days. An association in memory is different from the song physically warming the day.
evidence: we have learned to associate them with warm weather.

questions.prompt: Why are the names locust and harvest fly unreliable guides to this insect’s group?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator distinguishes it from grasshoppers and flies and points to mouth parts and closer examination. Familiar names alone are not the evidence used for identification.
evidence: its mouth parts are the mouth parts of the bug,

questions.prompt: What is useful about the teacher saying “I wish I knew, but I do not”?
facilitatorNotes: It separates an unknown count of eye facets from a different feature the teacher can describe: three small simple eyes. Admitting a limit does not prevent further observation.
evidence: I wish I knew, but I do not.

days.title: The Insect Folk — Friend Cicada: From Underground to Wings
days.challenge: Track changes of subject between sound-making, feeding and growth while preserving the life-cycle order.
days.focus: An adult and its discarded covering revealing different parts of a life.
days.context: The cicada is the loud insect sometimes called a locust in this book. “Dumb” here means silent. The underground duration given is the author’s example, not a duration shared by every cicada species; the young stage is now called a nymph.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific terminology and a species-dependent life-cycle estimate are retained as source text.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — Friend Cicada: From Underground to Wings; source transcription lines 4470–4540; opens “Our cicada has one organ that is very interesting; it is the little apparatus by which it sings.”; closes “It is a perfect cast of the cicada larva.”.

questions.prompt: How does the kettle-drum comparison explain the call?
facilitatorNotes: Membranes move rapidly with the action of muscles, making sound. The comparison directs attention to vibration rather than a human singing voice.
evidence: The membranes being set in rapid vibration

questions.prompt: What do the young and adult insects share about feeding despite their different surroundings?
facilitatorNotes: Both use piercing, sucking mouth parts for plant juices; the young feed on roots underground and adults on twigs or leaves in this account.
evidence: pierce holes in the roots of trees and suck out the juices.

questions.prompt: Why is John’s cast-off skin useful to the group?
facilitatorNotes: It preserves the young insect’s shape, including digging legs and small wing pads, so they can compare its earlier form with the winged adult.
evidence: It is a perfect cast of the cicada larva.

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Odd Spittle Insect: Who Made the Froth?
days.challenge: Follow a mistaken explanation through questioning, observation and a corrected account.
days.focus: An everyday name that survived from an earlier misunderstanding.
days.context: Nell has found foam on grass and knows the name frog spittle. The group investigates that explanation. Read the dialogue for the surprise, then reread for the evidence that actually changes their minds.
days.contentNote: Includes non-graphic insect predation. The historical author calls the young insect a larva; current terminology calls this stage a nymph.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Odd Spittle Insect: Who Made the Froth?; source transcription lines 4598–4652; opens “Why, little Nell! What is the matter?”; closes “The adult spittle insect is called a frog hopper, and it has the power of leaping very well.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the idea of frogs spitting on the grass doubtful even before the insect is found?
facilitatorNotes: The froth is high enough that the narrator jokes about unusually tall frogs. The question exposes a difficulty, though the insect supplies stronger evidence.
evidence: They must be tall frogs to reach up so high.

questions.prompt: What discovery replaces the original explanation?
facilitatorNotes: There is a young bug in the froth; the narrator connects the foam with its feeding on sap and its development.
evidence: there is something in the centre of it.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator mention wasps after describing the froth as protection?
facilitatorNotes: They provide an exception: some predators can get through. Protection can reduce danger without preventing every attack.
evidence: there are certain wasps that delight in invading the frothy masses

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Little Caddice Flies: A Moving House
days.challenge: Follow successive descriptions of the same object as observers discover what it is.
days.focus: A protective case understood through comparison with another animal’s shelter.
days.context: The children are looking into a clear brook. Caddice is the spelling used in this edition for caddis. Read once for Nell’s discovery, then reread the hermit-crab comparison to find both similarity and difference.
days.contentNote: Mentions potential insect predators. Read the historical observing scene as narrative; it does not require collecting or handling an insect.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Little Caddice Flies: A Moving House; source transcription lines 5697–5753; opens “Here we are in the woods again.”; closes “Its little black head is hard, but its body is soft, and that is why it does not like to expose itself to hungry larvae that might be living in the water.”.

questions.prompt: How does the explanation of the moving sand change as more is noticed?
facilitatorNotes: Nell sees bars of sand, Ned identifies tubes with a living thing inside, and the narrator explains the protective case and its occupant. The sequence moves from appearance toward explanation.
evidence: tubes of sand, containing a little live thing.

questions.prompt: In what important way is the case unlike the hermit crab’s shell?
facilitatorNotes: The crab uses an empty shell made by another animal; the caddis larva makes its own case. Both carry shelter and retreat into it.
evidence: it is a house of its own making.

questions.prompt: Why does the hard head matter to the explanation of remaining inside?
facilitatorNotes: The head is protected by its own hard covering but the body is soft and vulnerable to predators. The case shelters the part most in need of it.
evidence: Its little black head is hard, but its body is soft,

days.title: The Insect Folk — The Little Caddice Flies: Materials and Traces
days.challenge: Compare several constructions and work backward from tracks to possible makers.
days.focus: Evidence that becomes more informative when the observer follows it.
days.context: The group has already seen a caddis larva carrying a sand-grain case. This excerpt broadens the comparison to other materials and marks on the streambed. Reread to distinguish what the group sees from what the narrator infers.
days.contentNote: Includes insects eating other insects. Dietary statements are the historical author’s broad portrait; different caddis species have differing diets.

excerpt.locator: The Insect Folk — The Little Caddice Flies: Materials and Traces; source transcription lines 5815–5856; opens “Some caddice larvae build houses of wood instead of stone. They stick little twigs together, and some use little pieces of leaves.”; closes “They eat the larvae of the May flies when they can find them and no doubt they build these strong cases about themselves to prevent the May fly larvae from returning the compliment.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the cases a varied group rather than one identical kind of house?
facilitatorNotes: The account lists twigs, leaves, shells and sand and contrasts rough with neatly fitted cases. Several materials can serve the same general sheltering role.
evidence: Some caddice larvae build houses of wood instead of stone.

questions.prompt: Why is a line in the mud not enough by itself to identify a caddis larva?
facilitatorNotes: Snails can make similar tracks. Following a line may reveal its maker, adding evidence beyond a superficial resemblance.
evidence: Sometimes such lines are made by the little fresh-water snails;

questions.prompt: How does the phrase returning the compliment make the last claim playful rather than literally polite?
facilitatorNotes: It jokingly calls reciprocal predation a compliment. The narrator imagines prey becoming predators in return and proposes the case as protection; the wording is not an observed conversation between insects.
evidence: returning the compliment.

days.title: A New England Girlhood: the first verses (excerpt)
days.challenge: Read a child’s verse alongside the adult poet’s affectionate criticism.
days.focus: Practice can begin awkwardly and still become a lasting habit.
days.context: Larcom recalls discovering poetic meter in a dictionary and trying to write verses when she was about seven. An anticlimax is a drop from an exciting moment to something much less impressive.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, Glimpses of Poetry; begins “A tattered copy of Johnson's large Dictionary was a great delight to me, on account of the specimens”; ends “nt Hannah asked me to repeat my verses to her. I considered myself greatly honored by both requests.”.

questions.prompt: What unusual part of the dictionary interested Lucy most?
facilitatorNotes: Examples of poetic meter in the introduction, rather than simply definitions, gave her patterns to recite and imitate.
evidence: specimens of English versification

questions.prompt: Why does the adult writer call the second stanza an anticlimax?
facilitatorNotes: The first stanza builds a dramatic storm, while the second turns to the speaker merely feeling cooler. The scale drops from impressive weather to a small personal comfort.
evidence: I felt myself a little cooled

questions.prompt: What shows that embarrassment did not stop her writing?
facilitatorNotes: She kept making illustrated ballad books even while hiding them in floor cracks. Her wish to create continued alongside fear of being heard.
evidence: I went on writing little books of ballads

days.title: A New England Girlhood: taking a home to Lowell (excerpt)
days.challenge: Trace how concrete objects lead the writer to a larger claim about memory.
days.focus: A move changes surroundings while familiar possessions preserve connections.
days.context: After Lucy’s father died, her mother planned to run a boardinghouse for women working in Lowell’s mills. The family prepared to leave its coastal home.
days.contentNote: The family’s Christian books and practices are part of this personal account. One book’s disturbing historical illustrations are mentioned, without describing or reproducing them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, Beginning to Work; begins “After his death, my mother's thoughts naturally followed the direction his had taken; and seeing no ”; ends “r few Sabbath-day indulgences; and I cannot touch it now except with feelings of profound reverence.”.

questions.prompt: How do the sisters alter an unpleasant sewing task without abandoning it?
facilitatorNotes: They take the sheet into an apple tree and combine sewing with stories and riddles. They change the setting and companionship while still doing the work.
evidence: dragged a sheet up with us into an apple-tree

questions.prompt: Why is seeing old furniture in new rooms comforting?
facilitatorNotes: Recognizable objects carry family associations into the unfamiliar house. The secretary and books help make the rooms feel inhabited by their earlier life.
evidence: the novelty of seeing our old furniture settled in new rooms

questions.prompt: Why does Larcom distinguish family treasures from furniture that can be bought?
facilitatorNotes: Their special value comes from shared memories, which a buyer cannot purchase with the object. Her own examples develop that distinction.
evidence: Nobody can buy the old associations

days.title: A New England Girlhood: the mill and the school door (excerpt)
days.challenge: Hold an initially cheerful experience alongside the adult narrator’s later qualification.
days.focus: Economic necessity narrows a child’s educational choices.
days.context: Lucy’s family needed earnings, and she and a sister sought mill work. A bobbin holds thread; the mill-agent managed employment.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes nineteenth-century child labor and a family’s financial pressure. The adult narrator explicitly judges mill work unsuitable for a child.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, Beginning to Work; begins “There were many pros and cons between my mother and sisters before this was positively decided. The ”; ends “ow without enthusiasm. I had looked through an open door that I was not willing to see shut upon me.”.

questions.prompt: What condition does the mill-agent set before employing the two girls?
facilitatorNotes: They must attend school for the required number of months each year. The condition reveals that their schooling remained an issue even when work was allowed.
evidence: attend school the full number of months prescribed each year

questions.prompt: Why would it misrepresent this passage to quote only “nothing but fun”?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase describes Lucy’s first excitement. She later states factory life was not right for a child and describes losing a chance at high school. The whole passage complicates the first reaction.
evidence: could not be, the right sort of life for a child

questions.prompt: How does the open-door image explain her changed feelings when returning to work?
facilitatorNotes: Education has become a real possibility she wants; being forced back feels like losing access to it. She now works without the earlier enthusiasm.
evidence: an open door that I was not willing to see shut upon me

days.title: A New England Girlhood: the mill-girls’ magazines (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate causes of an organization’s beginning from judgments of its writing.
days.focus: Working women create outlets for thought and develop an audience.
days.context: As a young mill worker, Larcom participated in literary activities organized through her church. Two groups of workers published magazines that later joined.
days.contentNote: Church membership shaped these particular writing groups. The narrator’s account is one participant’s retrospective view, not a description of all mill workers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Mill-Girls’ Magazines; begins “Our minister joined us in our social gatherings, often inviting us to his own house, visiting us at ”; ends “hether spoken or written. This, no doubt, gave us a gravity of expression rather unnatural to youth.”.

questions.prompt: Why were two magazines started rather than one?
facilitatorNotes: Different church groups, locations, and social connections separated the contributors. Larcom suggests a combined effort could have worked better, but explains the practical division.
evidence: two magazines were started instead of one

questions.prompt: How did mechanical work help motivate Lucy to write?
facilitatorNotes: Her daily tasks left her thoughts unoccupied, and writing gave them an outlet. She describes it as a pastime before treating it as a literary career.
evidence: furnished no occupation for my thoughts

questions.prompt: What distinction does “plenty of pith, but it lacks point” make?
facilitatorNotes: The pieces contain serious substance, but may lack focused direction or a well-shaped purpose. The narrator connects this criticism to their sketchy, fragmentary character.
evidence: It has plenty of pith, but it lacks point.

days.title: A New England Girlhood: time for an education (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare two meanings assigned to the same practical resource.
days.focus: A worker weighs money, time, and intellectual freedom.
days.context: Larcom left one mill position for work with more pauses, though it paid less. Her family still needed earnings, and she wanted time to read and write.
days.contentNote: The thirteen-hour working day and very low wages belong to the historical setting. The narrator expresses her own religious and personal values about possessions.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, Reading and Studying; begins “Emilie found more profitable work elsewhere, and I found some that was less so, but far more satisfa”; ends “r way there during the frequent half-hours of waiting for the cloth to be brought in from the mills.”.

questions.prompt: How do the paymaster and Lucy give different meanings to her wish for time?
facilitatorNotes: He treats time as a way to earn money; she values it as a chance to learn. Their brief exchange exposes different priorities.
evidence: Time is education

questions.prompt: What limit does the narrator place on her own comments about being rich?
facilitatorNotes: She admits she has not experienced substantial wealth. That qualification helps distinguish her values from knowledge gained through experience.
evidence: I have never had the opportunity of knowing, by experience

questions.prompt: What details show that the new job fitted both her practical and imaginative aims?
facilitatorNotes: It involved counting and recording cloth, used pen and ink, and included waiting periods in which she could write verse. These features gave her useful work and mental space.
evidence: frequent half-hours of waiting for the cloth

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: storage and shelter (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare arrangements suited to different foods and habitats.
days.focus: Specific physical details explain a pattern of living.
days.context: Seton has described squirrels gathering mushrooms as an alternative to pine nuts. This excerpt begins with his account of how those foods are stored.
days.contentNote: This is historical animal observation, not a guide to identifying edible mushrooms. The family-history comparisons simplify evolution.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, The Cheeky Pine Squirrel; Chipmunks and Ground-squirrels; begins “Now if the provident Squirrel stored these up as he does the pinyons, in holes or underground, they ”; ends “irrels, that Mother Earth is a safer retreat in time of danger than the tallest tree that ever grew.”.

questions.prompt: Why store mushrooms in branches rather than in the same way as nuts?
facilitatorNotes: The writer says they would decay underground; branches allow drying. Placement also balances access by deer and exposure to wind.
evidence: where they dry out and remain good

questions.prompt: What makes the outside nest more organized than its first appearance suggests?
facilitatorNotes: Under the apparent rubbish are a warm chamber, a bark roof, and a concealed entrance. The description corrects a quick glance.
evidence: a convenient warm chamber

questions.prompt: How does the last paragraph position chipmunks between two other groups?
facilitatorNotes: They live near the boundary of woods and open land, can climb, but use underground refuge. This contrasts with tree-dwelling and ground-dwelling relatives.
evidence: the borderland between woods and prairie

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: the picket-pin (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate a nickname’s visual basis from the writer’s humorous judgment.
days.focus: A familiar object becomes a memorable animal name.
days.context: Seton recalls watching ground-squirrels near his Yellowstone cabin. A picket-pin is a stake used to tether an animal.
days.contentNote: The account’s judgments about an animal’s sleeping schedule are playful human judgments. Seasonal activity can vary; these are the author’s historical observations.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, The Ground-squirrel That Plays Picket-pin; begins “Conspicuous in its teeming numbers in the Yellowstone Park is the Picket-Pin Ground-squirrel. On eve”; ends “ in saying that there were ten families to the acre of land on all the level prairie in this valley.”.

questions.prompt: What posture makes the animal look like a stake?
facilitatorNotes: It stands very straight on its mound with paws pressed close to its ribs. The description explains the mistaken appearance.
evidence: pressing its paws tight to its ribs

questions.prompt: Why does the story about the newcomer and his horse explain the nickname especially well?
facilitatorNotes: The person mistakes the still animal for a useful stake until it chirrs and disappears. The sudden action reveals the illusion.
evidence: dives down out of sight

questions.prompt: How does Seton acknowledge a limit after criticizing the animal’s short active season?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines a defense and admits there are no facts to decide whether it has as many active hours as relatives. His disapproval is not a demonstrated biological defect.
evidence: we have no facts at present to determine.

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: what is still unknown about chipmunks? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Sort dated personal observations, predictions, and explicit gaps in knowledge.
days.focus: A nature account can invite investigation without claiming completeness.
days.context: Seton compares chipmunks he has watched in western mountain habitats with their eastern relatives.
days.contentNote: The account includes letting wild animals eat from plates. Species names and scientific knowledge have changed since this edition.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, A Four-legged Bird—The Northern Chipmunk; A Striped Pigmy—The Least Chipmunk; begins “The early naturalists who first made the acquaintance of the Eastern Ground-squirrel named it Tamias”; ends “hese things. Any exact observations you may make are sure to be acceptable contributions to science.”.

questions.prompt: What two roadside conditions does Seton offer to explain numerous chipmunks?
facilitatorNotes: Spilled oats supply food; discarded cut trees supply cover. Both relate to human alteration of the roadside.
evidence: the food, for oats are continually spilled

questions.prompt: What supports the claim that the chipmunks remain active in wintry weather?
facilitatorNotes: He gives specific dates and places where he saw them in snow. These examples are stronger evidence than simply calling them lively.
evidence: October 31st at Breckenridge, Col.

questions.prompt: Where does the author clearly separate a likely account from a proven one?
facilitatorNotes: For the least chipmunk he says its history is practically unknown and labels diet and brood size as probable, adding that none has been proved.
evidence: no one has proved any of these things.

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: the pika’s hay stores (excerpt)
days.challenge: Connect a long process description with evidence and tentative interpretation.
days.focus: An apparently barren place can be a well-suited home.
days.context: Seton describes a small relative of rabbits, also called a coney or calling hare, in rocky mountain habitat.
days.contentNote: The passage includes a reported claim that stored hay predicts winter severity. That report is not proof of prediction; distinguish it from the author’s examined hay stores.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, The Bump of Moss That Squeaks; begins “No matter how horrible a certain climate or surroundings may seem to us, they are sure to be the ide”; ends “fter year is shown by the abundance of pellets in several layers which were found in and about them.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the opening contrast a person’s view of bare rocks with the animal’s?
facilitatorNotes: A cold, bleak place that seems undesirable to a visitor is ideal habitat for this animal. The contrast challenges the reader’s first impression.
evidence: the paradise, the perfect place

questions.prompt: What steps turn growing plants into stored winter food in the account?
facilitatorNotes: The pika cuts and carries plants, spreads them in sun to dry, and stores the cured material in sheltered crevices. Follow the sequence without skipping drying.
evidence: When dry enough to be safe, he packs it away

questions.prompt: Which part of the “winter restaurant” idea is inferred rather than directly witnessed?
facilitatorNotes: Seton sees hollows within hay stores and suspects they are winter feeding places, rather than young-rearing nests. His repeated “I suspect” marks that limit.
evidence: a sort of winter restaurant

days.title: Wild Animals at Home: a night of unexpected work (excerpt)
days.challenge: Identify reported observations and imaginative reconstruction within the same paragraph.
days.focus: A surprising exception can revise an expectation.
days.context: After describing pikas drying and storing hay, Seton retells an observation attributed to naturalists C. Hart Merriam and Vernon Bailey.
days.contentNote: Seton did not witness this storm himself; he attributes the account to other naturalists and adds imaginative language about the animals’ experience.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, The Weatherwise Coney; begins “A very wise little people is this little people of the Rocks. Not only do they realize that in summe”; ends “rocks, and the wisdom of the Coney once more exemplified, with adequate energy to make it effective.”.

questions.prompt: Why is hearing pikas at night surprising in this account?
facilitatorNotes: Seton describes them as daytime animals and says he has not heard them after dark. The storm creates an exception to that expectation.
evidence: never heard a sound or seen a sign of their being about after dark

questions.prompt: What do the night sounds and changed hay piles together suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Activity during the storm and protected stores by morning support the inference that the animals moved their food. The observers need not have seen every trip.
evidence: every haycock had been removed to a safer place

questions.prompt: Which details turn the event into an imagined organized community?
facilitatorNotes: The call of older animals, warm beds, and “overtime” are human-style reconstruction. Distinguish those embellishments from the attributed night sounds and morning condition.
evidence: at the call of the older ones

days.title: Children
days.challenge: Follow a comparison between children and the parts of nature that bring warmth and light.
days.focus: The adult speaker’s renewal through play and companionship.
days.context: Read the poem as an adult’s address to children. During rereading, contrast the speaker’s autumn imagery with the children’s morning and springlike images.

excerpt.locator: Children; source transcription lines 19384–19431; opens “Come to me, O ye children!”; closes “  And all the rest are dead.”.

questions.prompt: What happens to the speaker’s puzzling questions when the children arrive?
facilitatorNotes: Their play and presence temporarily remove the speaker’s worries. The poem shows an emotional change rather than a literal answer to each question.
evidence: Have vanished quite away.

questions.prompt: Why compare children with leaves rather than with the tree’s trunk?
facilitatorNotes: Leaves receive light and air and bring fresh life to the tree; the comparison presents children as renewing the larger world.
evidence: What the leaves are to the forest,

questions.prompt: What does calling children “living poems” suggest about the speaker’s values?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker values direct companionship above books or art alone. Accept readings about creativity, joy or wonder that connect to the contrast with ballads.
evidence: For ye are living poems,

days.title: To the River Charles
days.challenge: Trace the different reasons the speaker gives for loving one place.
days.focus: A landscape made meaningful by changing feelings and remembered friends.
days.context: A river is addressed as though it could receive a gift. Reread to separate the river’s visible qualities from the memories the speaker brings to it.

excerpt.locator: To the River Charles; source transcription lines 2187–2240; opens “River! that in silence windest”; closes “  Take this idle song from me.”.

questions.prompt: What can the speaker give the river in return for its gifts?
facilitatorNotes: Only a song, which is the poem itself. This turns reading into an encounter with the speaker’s offering.
evidence: I can give thee but a song.

questions.prompt: How can the same river comfort sadness and accompany happiness?
facilitatorNotes: Its stillness calms the speaker in illness, while its gleaming movement matches brighter moods. The observed place supports more than one feeling.
evidence: I have felt my heart beat lighter,

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say the river’s colour is not the only reason for love?
facilitatorNotes: Friends who lived near it and friends recalled by its name make the place personally significant. Ask readers to use the shift from scenery to memory.
evidence: Friends I love have dwelt beside thee,

days.title: The Evening Star
days.challenge: Unpack a sonnet’s linked comparisons between a sunset window, a star and a beloved person.
days.focus: The way a repeated act of resting connects distant sky and familiar home.
days.context: An oriel is a projecting window, a casement is a window, and Hesperus names the evening star. Read the whole sonnet aloud, then reread its first and last windows.

excerpt.locator: The Evening Star; source transcription lines 7610–7627; opens “Lo! in the painted oriel of the West,”; closes “  And from thy darkened window fades the light.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the western sky resemble a coloured window?
facilitatorNotes: The setting sun reddens the sky’s panes, while the star appears like a person at a casement. The architectural words organize the scene.
evidence: in the painted oriel of the West,

questions.prompt: How is the star’s disappearance described as something a person might do?
facilitatorNotes: It seems to remove its radiant garments and recline behind the pines, turning a change in visibility into preparing for sleep.
evidence: Of all her radiant garments, and reclines

questions.prompt: How do the last lines bring the distant star close to home?
facilitatorNotes: The beloved retires and the light fades from her window, repeating the star’s retreat. Accept connections between affection, rest and the speaker’s attentive watching.
evidence: And from thy darkened window fades the light.

days.title: Autumn — the sonnet
days.challenge: Keep several royal-procession images connected within a compact fourteen-line poem.
days.focus: Autumn personified as a ruler who distributes gifts.
days.context: This is the complete sonnet beginning “Thou comest, Autumn,” not Longfellow’s earlier poem with the same title. A wain is a wagon; an almoner distributes gifts; Samarcand and Charlemagne appear as comparisons for splendour and kingship.
days.contentNote: The poem uses religious blessing and altar imagery within its portrait of the harvest.

excerpt.locator: Autumn — the sonnet; source transcription lines 7629–7646; opens “Thou comest, Autumn, heralded by the rain,”; closes “  Thine almoner, the wind, scatters the golden leaves!”.

questions.prompt: What things in the landscape become banners and a shield?
facilitatorNotes: Colourful leaves or autumn colours act as banners, and the red harvest moon becomes the shield. Ask readers to track how concrete details support the royal portrait.
evidence: Thy shield is the red harvest moon,

questions.prompt: How is this ruler connected with farmers rather than only with display?
facilitatorNotes: Oxen, harvest sheaves, blessings and farmers’ prayers link the procession to food and labour. The gifts have practical value as well as beauty.
evidence: Blessing the farms through all thy vast domain!

questions.prompt: Why is the wind an effective gift-distributor at the end?
facilitatorNotes: It scatters golden leaves, like a servant scattering gifts during a celebration. Different readings of the leaves’ value are welcome when tied to “golden” and the procession.
evidence: Thine almoner, the wind, scatters the golden leaves!

days.title: The Sparrow's Fall
days.challenge: Notice contrasts of size, colour and strength that build a devotional claim about attention.
days.focus: The importance of an ordinary, vulnerable creature.
days.context: The sparrow dies in this complete poem. Read gently, paying attention to why the speaker contrasts it with more spectacular animals.
days.contentNote: A bird’s death is described without graphic detail and followed by Christian reassurance. An adult may introduce the topic before reading.

excerpt.locator: The Sparrow's Fall, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 21–22; complete poem; opens “Too frail to soar--a feeble thing--”; closes “  Like children, on our Father's breast?”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker tell us that this is neither a colourful bird nor a strong eagle?
facilitatorNotes: The contrasts remove familiar reasons to admire the bird. Its worth does not depend on splendour or power in the speaker’s account.
evidence: Only a brown and weesome thing,

questions.prompt: How do the stars and lion enlarge the poem’s idea of care?
facilitatorNotes: The same divine attention is imagined as reaching stars, powerful animals and one tiny bird. Large and small are held together rather than ranked by importance.
evidence: Who hears the hungry lion's call,

questions.prompt: At what point does the speaker turn from the bird to a human listener, and why?
facilitatorNotes: The address to the restless heart turns the sparrow’s story into reassurance. The reader can explain that movement without needing to share its faith.
evidence: Oh, restless heart, learn thou to trust

days.title: The Skylark — Child’s Morning Hymn
days.challenge: Follow the bird’s physical ascent before interpreting the speaker’s spiritual comparison.
days.focus: An upward flight used to picture increasing joy.
days.context: This is a historical Christian hymn for children, supplied as literature. Read the first two stanzas for the bird’s action, then notice how the final stanza changes the subject.
days.contentNote: A Christian devotional poem; discuss the speaker’s belief as the poem’s viewpoint.

excerpt.locator: The Skylark — Child’s Morning Hymn; source transcription lines 59872–59893; opens “The skylark, when the dews of morn”; closes “    Most glad, when rising most to Thee!”.

questions.prompt: What is different about where the skylark sings compared with a bird on a branch?
facilitatorNotes: It sings while rising high above the morning cloud rather than resting on a leafy spray.
evidence: He rests not on the leafy spray

questions.prompt: How does height connect with the strength of the song?
facilitatorNotes: The bird’s sweetest notes come nearest the sky, linking ascent and intensified joy.
evidence: His notes of sweetest ecstasy.

questions.prompt: What does “Thus” ask readers to compare in the last stanza?
facilitatorNotes: It connects the bird’s upward flight with the speaker’s spirit rising toward the Creator. Readers need not share the belief to explain how the comparison works.
evidence: Thus, my Creator! thus the more

days.title: The Nightingale — Child’s Evening Hymn
days.challenge: Keep track of a delayed main action after three opening stanzas beginning with “When.”
days.focus: Night song as a model for peaceful reflection at day’s end.
days.context: Read the repeated “When” openings in one flowing sequence until the nightingale wakes. Then reread the movement from outdoor sounds to the speaker’s evening prayer.
days.contentNote: A Christian evening hymn; religious language belongs to the historical speaker’s perspective.

excerpt.locator: The Nightingale — Child’s Evening Hymn; source transcription lines 59898–59938; opens “When twilight’s gray and pensive hour”; closes “    Smile on Thy servant’s bed of rest.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the nightingale not appear immediately in the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The opening builds the twilight setting through flowers, mist, stars and glow-worms before the bird’s voice enters. This prepares the stillness its song will fill.
evidence: At that calm hour, so still, so pale,

questions.prompt: Which details show that evening is not a lifeless time?
facilitatorNotes: The primrose opens, glow-worms light the path, and the nightingale sings. The text presents different activity rather than simply an end to activity.
evidence: When evening’s primrose opes to shed

questions.prompt: How does the speaker connect the bird’s voice with a human evening practice?
facilitatorNotes: The bird’s twilight song becomes a pattern for songs of praise and prayer after daily cares. Ask readers to identify the transition to an addressed Father in heaven.
evidence: Thus may sweet songs of praise and prayer

days.title: The Rainbow
days.challenge: Separate sensory descriptions of a rainbow from the meaning assigned through a biblical allusion.
days.focus: A visible natural event interpreted as reassurance.
days.context: The source places a quotation from Genesis before the poem. Read it as the key to the speaker’s interpretation, then distinguish that belief from the observed colours and rain.
days.contentNote: The poem refers to the biblical flood and God’s covenant. Its religious interpretation is discussed as the speaker’s belief.

excerpt.locator: The Rainbow; source transcription lines 59499–59552; opens ““I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a”; closes “      The rainbow in the cloud!”.

questions.prompt: What does the rain do before the rainbow appears?
facilitatorNotes: It refreshes plants, brings buds into bloom and deepens colours. The shower is productive rather than only something to endure.
evidence: A thousand buds to day,

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker urge the child to hurry when the rainbow appears?
facilitatorNotes: The arch may vanish, so looking requires attention to a brief event. The urgency interrupts the calmer description of growth.
evidence: Haste, ere it vanish!--haste to view

questions.prompt: What extra meaning does the speaker read in the colours?
facilitatorNotes: The rainbow recalls a biblical promise of mercy and continuing seasons. Distinguish this stated religious reading from an explanation of how rainbows form.
evidence: And read God’s mercy there.

days.title: The Stars
days.challenge: Distinguish observation, imaginative speculation and reassurance within one address to a child.
days.focus: Vastness that first makes a person seem small and then offers care.
days.context: Read this nineteenth-century hymn as poetry, not an astronomy lesson. Its suggestion that every star has inhabited worlds is an imaginative claim, not an established fact. The opening Psalm quotation is retained.
days.contentNote: Christian devotional language and historical speculation about inhabited planets; distinguish poetic imagination from scientific evidence.

excerpt.locator: The Stars; source transcription lines 59638–59691; opens ““The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth his”; closes “    Is still in mercy turn’d on thee.”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker make the sky resemble both treasure and writing?
facilitatorNotes: Stars appear as gems, lamps and characters of flame. These comparisons make points of light seem precious and meaningful.
evidence: Inscribed in characters of flame?

questions.prompt: Which word signals that the description of beings on other worlds is a possibility rather than an observed report?
facilitatorNotes: Haply means perhaps. The speaker imagines their lives; the poem does not provide observations establishing them.
evidence: Haply, those glorious beings know

questions.prompt: Why compare a person with an insect or a drop before saying “Yet fear thou not”?
facilitatorNotes: The smallness images create a problem that the assurance of care answers. A reader can explain that turn without agreeing with its devotional conclusion.
evidence: Hath, e’en for thee, a Father’s care!

days.title: Mother's Treasures
days.challenge: Distinguish a parent’s questions about possible ambitions from the hopes finally endorsed.
days.focus: Character and service valued beyond status or ease.
days.context: A mother addresses her hopes for Edna and Will. The poem uses historical gender expectations in its questions; readers may compare them with its final wish for both children.
days.contentNote: Includes historical gender expectations and a final hope for reunion in heaven; discuss both as features of the speaker’s viewpoint.

excerpt.locator: Mother's Treasures, Atlanta Offering: Poems (Philadelphia, 1895), printed pages 56–58; complete poem; opens “Two little children sit by my side,”; closes “     "And the children Thou hast given."”.

questions.prompt: Why call the children Lily and Daffodil before giving their names?
facilitatorNotes: The flower names express affection and natural beauty, while Edna and Will make the children particular people.
evidence: One is Edna, the other is Will.

questions.prompt: Does the speaker ask for lives entirely free of pain?
facilitatorNotes: No: she explicitly declines that request and instead hopes the children remain faithful and true in difficulty.
evidence: I do not ask they shall never tread

questions.prompt: How does the final shared wish differ from the earlier separate questions about boy and girl?
facilitatorNotes: Earlier roles differ by gender, but the wish that both brighten and bless the world brings them together. Readers can reasonably question the old role division while noticing this shared aim.
evidence: This I ask for my boy and girl.
